descs.en: A trauma surgeon reborn as a governor’s daughter falls for the Emperor’s nephew from a balcony, and then does something very foolish to see him again. A warm historical romance told in stitches, letters and one river.

chapters.title: The Girl on the Balcony
chapters.desc: A general rides through Qingzhou in the rain, and an eighteen-year-old with a surgeon’s memory watches from her father’s balcony. He doesn’t look up.
chapters.epigraph: “He didn’t look at me. He looked at the roof.”
chapters.content:
The spring rains had stopped two days ago, and Qingzhou smelled of wet stone and fresh herbs. In eighteen years Yun Shiyu had decided it was the closest this world came to the clean, sharp smell of a hospital corridor, the one she still dreamed about some nights.

She was on the second-floor balcony of the governor’s residence with her elbows on the carved railing, pretending to study the herb garden. She was watching the street.

Little Lan came out with a cup of tea and the face of a maid who had been sent. “Miss. Madam says to come in.”

“I’m studying.”

“Madam said you’d say that.”

Shiyu took the tea. “Then Madam knows me. Stand here. You can tell the kitchen what he looks like before anyone else does.”

Little Lan put the tray down on the bench at once and came to the railing. “Cook says he finished the whole border war in one season.”

“Cook would know. She’s been to the border so often.”

“Her cousin’s son cooks for the army. He says the General never shouts. He says when the General is angry he goes quieter, and then everyone in the tent wishes he’d shout.”

“That’s useful.”

“Useful how?”

Shiyu leaned a little further over the railing. “Patients are like that too. The loud ones are usually fine. You worry about the ones who go still. What else did the cousin’s son say?”

Little Lan lowered her voice. “That he doesn’t drink. That he reads every report himself, all the way to the end, even the ones about broken carts. That he’s twenty-eight and nobody has ever seen him smile. And that he turned down the daughter of the Minister of Rites without even looking at her portrait.”

“How do they know he didn’t look at it?”

“It came back still tied.”

Shiyu laughed before she could stop herself, and from somewhere inside the house her mother’s voice rose.

“Shiyu! Come away from there. It’s unbecoming to stare at soldiers.”

“I’m looking at the herb garden, Mother.”

“The herb garden is on the south side of the house.”

“I’m looking at it from memory.”

There was a silence long enough for Little Lan to clap a hand over her mouth. Then Lady Ren’s footsteps went away towards the inner rooms, along with something about daughters who had inherited every one of their father’s habits.

“You’ll be in trouble, Miss.”

Shiyu set the tea down. “Later. Not now. Listen.”

Drums, at the far end of the street. Below them Qingzhou was already filling up: hawkers shifting their baskets, boys climbing the stone lions outside the tea house, an old man unrolling a mat on the cloth merchant’s step so he could watch sitting down.

The soldiers came first, two by two, in plain armour, with the faces of men who had been on the road a long time and wanted a bath more than a crowd. Then the banners. Then a gap, the way there’s always a gap before the thing everyone has come to see.

“That’s him. The black horse,” whispered Little Lan.

He didn’t look at the crowd. He rode like a man who’d been born in the saddle, his armour black with a thin silver edge and none of the gold the provincial officials liked, his helmet held against his hip. He said something to the officer beside him: a few words, no more. The officer nodded twice and dropped back.

“He’s so handsome,” said Little Lan, stricken.

“He’s exhausted. Look at his left hand. He keeps it off the reins. Something’s healing in that wrist and he doesn’t want anyone to know,” said Shiyu.

“Miss, how can you see his wrist from up here?”

“I can’t. I can see him not using it.”

Her father’s party came out through the front gate below, and the General turned his head to receive them. For the first time Shiyu saw his face clearly. She had expected handsome. Generals in stories were always handsome. She hadn’t expected sharp: a clean line of jaw, dark brows, dark eyes that went over her father and every official behind him in a single pass and took in everything. Exact, the way a good incision is exact.

He nodded once to her father. Then his gaze moved along the front of the house, the gate, the lanterns, the wall, and up. Shiyu forgot to breathe.

His eyes crossed the balcony and kept going. He hadn’t seen her. He was looking at the roofline, probably counting how many archers it would hold.

“Miss. Your face has gone red,” said Little Lan.

Shiyu pressed the back of her hand to her cheek. Warm. Pulse quick and a little uneven, which in a patient she’d have called interesting and in herself found extremely inconvenient. “It’s the sun.”

“There isn’t any sun. It’s rained all week.”

“Then it’s the tea.”

Little Lan looked at the cup on the bench. “You haven’t drunk any of the tea, Miss.”

“Then it’s the drums.”

Below them the procession moved on, down towards the river road and the north gate and whatever came after Qingzhou. The boys climbed down off the lions. The old man rolled up his mat. Within a quarter of an hour the city had gone back to selling fish.

Shiyu stayed at the railing, looking at the empty road where the black horse had been.

“Shall I tell the kitchen he looked at you?” said Little Lan hopefully.

“He didn’t look at me. He looked at the roof.”

“You’re nearly on the roof.”

Shiyu picked up the cold tea and drank it in one go. “Tell the kitchen he’s exhausted, he’s hurt his left wrist, and he doesn’t smile. And tell my mother I’ve finished studying the garden.”

“Are you coming in?”

“In a minute,” said Shiyu, and didn’t move.

chapters.title: The Return of Uncle Xiang
chapters.desc: Her uncle, the army’s chief physician, comes home for a few days, and she asks one question too many about the General.
chapters.epigraph: “I suppose someone in his position gets a great many marriage proposals.”
chapters.content:
Uncle Xiang arrived twelve days later, as he always did: with no warning, a great deal of energy, and the smell of medicinal smoke on his coat.

Yun Xiangyi was forty-eight, lean and quick, the chief physician of the Northern Army and her father’s younger brother. Visitors never believed they were related. Her father had grown gentle in Qingzhou, the way a good man with a peaceful life does. Her uncle had stayed sharp.

“You haven’t eaten,” said Lady Ren, before he was through the gate.

“I ate.”

“When?”

“Recently.”

“Yesterday is not recently, Xiangyi.”

He bowed to her, took the cup of tea she pushed into his hands, and turned to his brother, who had come out of the study with a book still open in one hand. “It was late yesterday. Chengde. You’ve got ink on your sleeve.”

“I always have ink on my sleeve.”

They held each other by the arms, the way they always did, and then her uncle saw Shiyu on the steps and his face changed completely. “I know. I’d worry if you didn’t. There’s my apprentice. Have you finished the Bencao yet?”

“Twice. Your notes in the margin are wrong about the willow bark,” said Shiyu.

“They are not.”

“Page forty. You say three qian. It should be two for a child.”

He stared at her, and then laughed and pulled a packet of dried northern herbs out of his coat for her, which was how she knew he’d been thinking about her on the road.

She waited all afternoon. She poured tea. She listened to the story of the cart that had lost a wheel at the river crossing and the story of the colonel who had tried to treat his own boil with a hot knife. She filled the cups when they were empty. She was the picture of a dutiful niece, and the whole time she was building a question, the way she’d once built a differential diagnosis.

Her chance came after dinner. Her mother went to speak to Cook about tomorrow, and her father got caught up in a polite disagreement with his brother about the proper drying time for angelica root. Shiyu put down her cup.

“Uncle. The General’s procession came through here twelve days ago.”

“Mm.” He didn’t look up from her father’s book.

“General Zhan Lingyun. You’ve served in his command for eight years, haven’t you?”

“About that.”

“He must be very demanding, to have a reputation like that at twenty-eight.”

Her uncle turned a page. “Precise. He holds everyone to the standard he holds himself to. His men follow him because they trust him, not because they’re frightened of him. That’s not a small difference.”

“His left wrist is hurt.”

That made him look up. “Who told you that?”

“Nobody. He rode through the whole city without putting that hand on the reins once.”

Her uncle looked at her for a long while. “Cracked bone, six weeks ago. He set it himself in the field because he didn’t want to wait for me. I reset it properly at the camp and he complained about that for three days. Don’t tell anyone.”

“Who would I tell?”

“Your maid. The kitchen. The whole of Qingzhou by the end of the week.” He went back to the book.

Shiyu folded her hands in her lap and arranged her face into something she hoped looked idle. “I suppose someone in his position gets a great many marriage proposals. From the families in the capital.”

The page didn’t turn. She kept her eyes on her hands. Across the table she could feel her uncle looking at her, and then she felt her father stop talking about angelica root.

“He’s declined every one. The Emperor doesn’t press him. Why do you ask?” said Uncle Xiang slowly.

“I was thinking about military logistics.”

“Were you.”

“Whether commanders without a family in the capital spend more time in the field. That has medical consequences. For the men.”

“Shiyu.”

His voice was gentle, completely and infuriatingly gentle. She looked up. He had his diagnostic face on, the one he wore when a patient’s story didn’t match their symptoms.

“It’s a reasonable question,” she said.

He turned the page at last. “It’s a very reasonable question. I’ll think about the logistics. Chengde, about this angelica.”

Out of the corner of her eye she saw her father and her uncle look at each other: one glance, the kind two brothers exchange after watching the same strange girl grow up for eighteen years. Her face went hot. She stared into her teacup and spent the rest of the evening behaving perfectly and trying not to think about dark eyes, or a cracked wrist set in a field by a man who couldn’t be bothered to wait.

She managed it some of the time. On her way to bed she stopped in the corridor outside her uncle’s room. The door was open a finger’s width, and the lamp was still lit.

“Uncle? When do you go back to the camp?”

There was a pause on the other side of the door. “Two weeks. Perhaps three.”

“And the camp is three days from here?”

“By supply cart. Why?”

“No reason. Good night, Uncle.”

“Shiyu.”

She stopped with one foot on the step.

“The answer to whatever you’re about to ask me tomorrow is no,” said her uncle through the door.

“I wasn’t going to ask you anything.”

“Good night, apprentice.”

She went to her room and lay on her back staring at the painted ceiling until the lamp in the corridor went out. Two weeks. Perhaps three.

In the morning, she promised herself, she was going to be entirely sensible about this.

chapters.title: The Decision
chapters.desc: There’s no sensible way to see him again, so she picks a foolish one, with Little Lan’s help.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m going to study military medicine.”
chapters.content:
She wasn’t, in the morning, entirely sensible. She tried the honest way first. After dinner, when her father was at his softest, she brought him a pot of the good tea and sat down across the low table from him in his study.

“Father. I’d like to go north with Uncle when he goes back.”

Yun Chengde put down his brush. “To the camp.”

“To the medical tent. He sees more wounds in a month than every physician in Qingzhou sees in a year. He’s worked out a way of cleaning and closing them that nobody down here has ever seen. I’ve read every book in this house twice. I can’t learn the rest from paper.”

He listened to all of it, which was one of the things she loved most about him. He never interrupted. When she’d finished he poured her a cup of the tea she’d brought him, and pushed it across.

“No,” he said.

“You haven’t said why.”

He looked at her over the cup. “You know why. You’re eighteen and unmarried, and a soldiers’ camp is no place for a governor’s daughter, however good her reasons are. And your reasons are good. That’s what worries me.”

“Why would good reasons worry you?”

“Because you only make this face when you have a second reason you aren’t telling me.”

She drank the tea and said nothing, which was its own answer, and her father sighed and went back to his brush.

She tried her uncle the next morning, in the herb shed, while he was sorting roots for the journey.

“No,” he said, before she’d finished her first sentence.

“I haven’t asked yet.”

“You were about to. The answer is the same as last night’s. I told you through the door.”

“I’d be useful. I can clean wounds. I can make up every poultice in your notes, including the ones you got wrong.”

He held up a root, frowned at it and put it in the reject pile. “I didn’t get any wrong. Shiyu, listen. A camp is no place for an unmarried girl from a family like ours, however good her hands are. Your mother would never forgive me. Your father would forgive me, which is worse.”

“And the General?”

He stopped sorting. “What about the General?”

“Would he mind?”

Her uncle picked up the next root, carefully. “The General has eleven thousand men to feed through a frontier spring. He’d mind a governor’s daughter in his medical tent the way he’d mind a goose in his war room. No.”

So she stopped asking. For four days she was the most cooperative daughter in Qingzhou. She did the household accounts with her mother without being asked twice. She copied out her father’s reports for the prefecture in her best hand. In the evenings she read medical texts with her uncle and argued only a little, and smiled at everyone, and showed no sign whatsoever of planning anything.

Little Lan saw through it on the second day.

“Miss, why is there a bundle under your bed?”

“There isn’t.”

“I dusted it. It has your blue jacket in it and the bone needles and two of your father’s books.”

Shiyu shut the door. “If I tell you, you can’t tell anyone.”

“I tell the kitchen everything.”

“Not this. Not even Cook.”

Little Lan looked at her, and then sat down on the end of the bed. “You’re going after him.”

“I’m going to study military medicine.”

“You’re going after him, Miss.”

“I’m going to study military medicine in the same camp as him which is a coincidence,” said Shiyu.

Little Lan put her face in her hands. When she took them away she looked like someone who had made a decision she would regret. “How?”

“The supply carts leave before dawn when Uncle goes. Three of them, medicines and dressings, for the General’s own tent. The last one has a storage box underneath, the size of a coffin. I measured it.”

“You measured a coffin.”

“I measured a box.”

“For three days?”

“They stop at relay stations every night. I’ll get out when they water the horses and back in before they load. I need water gourds that don’t slosh, dry food that doesn’t smell, and someone to put the letter on my mother’s dressing table after the carts have gone through the north gate.”

“What letter?”

“The one I haven’t written yet.”

It took her seven drafts. The first was so honest she burned it. The second was so calm it sounded like a lie, and she burned that too. The seventh said that she’d gone north with Uncle’s carts to study in the medical tent, that she was safe and would be under his care from the moment she arrived, that she was sorry for doing it this way, and that she loved them both. It didn’t say why. Her father would know why. He always did.

On the fourth night Little Lan brought three gourds wrapped in cloth, a parcel of dried dates and flatbread, and a small knitted blanket nobody had asked for.

“It’s cold in the north,” she said fiercely.

“It’s spring.”

“It’s still cold.”

Shiyu hugged her, which made Little Lan cry, which made Shiyu nearly cry, and then the watchman called the fourth hour and there wasn’t time for either.

The courtyard was dark and smelled of horses. The carts stood loaded by the side gate, and the drivers were in the kitchen getting their breakfast. She went under the last cart on her hands and knees, eased the box open and folded herself inside with the bundle against her chest, and Little Lan slid the lid shut over her face.

“Miss, if he sends you straight home, I’m telling Cook everything,” came the whisper through the wood.

“If he sends me straight home, you can tell her twice.”

Then the footsteps went away, and there was only the smell of dried medicine and the dark.

She had been a surgeon in her first life. She’d slept in call rooms, crouched under supply cabinets during a power cut, and once spent forty minutes holding an artery closed with two fingers in a lift that had stopped between floors. She wasn’t a woman who minded small dark spaces. She revised that opinion after about four hours.

The road out of Qingzhou was far less smooth than it looked from a carriage window. The smell of preserved medicine was so thick she could taste it. There were thin lines of grey light between the boards, enough to see her own hand, not enough to read by, which left her nothing to do but think. Once, at the north gate, she heard her uncle’s voice right outside, going through the inventory with the guard.

“Dressings, two crates. Wine for washing, four jars. Needles. The General’s own supply box.”

“You want it opened, Physician?”

Shiyu held her breath until her chest hurt.

“No. It was sealed in my brother’s courtyard. Let them through.”

The cart jolted forward. She let the breath go into her sleeve.

She thought about three things on that long first morning. That the plan had been foolish from the start. That she’d chosen it anyway, and would see it through. And that whatever happened when the lid came off, and she wasn’t naive about how it would happen, she had chosen that as well.

The rest, she supposed, would be up to him.

chapters.title: Discovered
chapters.desc: Three days hidden in a supply cart, and then the lid comes off at the camp checkpoint.
chapters.epigraph: “There’s a girl in the General’s supply box.”
chapters.content:
Three days, two relay stations and one cold night later, the lid came off.

She didn’t choose the moment. They had reached the camp’s outer checkpoint in the late afternoon, and a young soldier with a list was counting the General’s supplies box by box. Shiyu heard him coming down the line of carts, heard the clasp go, and then there was daylight on her face and a boy of about nineteen looking down at her with his mouth open.

She looked back up at him.

“There’s—” he said.

“I can explain,” said Shiyu, which wasn’t entirely true but was the only thing available.

He turned his head without taking his eyes off her. “There’s a girl in the General’s supply box.”

“There’s a what?” said someone further down the line.

“A girl. With a blanket.”

Her uncle arrived at something close to a run. He didn’t shout. His face had gone still, the face he wore over a patient whose wound had turned, and she had never wanted that face pointed at her.

“Shiyu.”

Just her name. In that voice. She climbed out as well as she could, which wasn’t well, because her legs had decided after three days that they’d rather not. There was a bruise coming on her elbow. She smelled of dried medicine so strongly that the soldier took a step back. She put her hands together, met her uncle’s eyes because looking away would be worse, and bowed.

“Uncle. I’m sorry about the way I arrived. I can explain my reasons—”

He didn’t answer. He turned to the soldiers who had started to gather and sent them back to their work with one look. He beckoned a runner. “Go to the command tent. Tell Chen Ye the Chief Physician is coming and why.”

“Why, sir?”

Her uncle looked at Shiyu. “He’ll see why.”

The runner ran.

“The General will want to see us. Both of us. Now,” said Uncle Xiang.

“I left a letter for Father and Mother.”

He started walking. “I know you did. Their rider passed us yesterday at the second station. Your father’s seal on the letter, your mother’s handwriting on the outside, and three lines from your father inside that I’m not going to repeat in front of soldiers. Come.”

She followed him through the camp. She had been in it for less time than it takes to drink a cup of tea, and already she could feel herself being looked at. Not the curious way Qingzhou looked at the governor’s odd daughter, but the trained way, the way a place full of soldiers looks at anything that wasn’t there yesterday. She was the thing that wasn’t there yesterday. She kept her chin up and her hands still.

“Uncle, how angry are you?” she said, low.

“I haven’t decided.”

“On a scale.”

He didn’t look at her. “Don’t give me a scale. I invented half the scales you know. Ask me again tonight, when I’ve worked out what to write to your father.”

The command tent was large and plain, lit by oil lamps even in daylight. Maps on the central table, weighted with stones. Nothing on the walls. A young officer at the entrance with a face that gave away nothing, who looked at her once and lifted the flap.

The General was seated at the far end of the table.

He was completely different from the man on the black horse, and exactly the same. From the balcony the distance had flattened him into a picture. In here there was no distance at all. He wore the black inner tunic of an officer off duty, silver at the collar and cuffs, and he sat the way he’d ridden, as if he didn’t need to show anyone who was in charge because it had never been in question. His left wrist was bound under the cuff. His dark eyes came up and settled on her, and the look in them was flat and attentive: the look of a man who had been handed something unexpected in the middle of a campaign and was deciding what to do with it.

Shiyu was glad of her habit of keeping her face calm. She was less glad that heat was climbing up her neck anyway, which was purely physiological and couldn’t be helped. She bowed, properly, as low as his rank and her situation called for, which was low.

“Chief Physician. Who is this?” said the General.

“My niece, General. Yun Shiyu. The Governor of Qingzhou’s daughter. She hid in the supply carts without my knowledge. The responsibility is mine.”

“In which cart?”

Her uncle’s pause was short and eloquent. “She concealed herself before we left Qingzhou, General.”

“In whose cart?”

“Yours.”

The young officer at the entrance made a noise that might have been a cough.

“Raise your head,” said the General.

She did.

He studied her for the space of a few breaths. “Your name.”

“Yun Shiyu.”

“Your age.”

“Eighteen, General.”

“Why?”

She’d had four days in Qingzhou and three in a box to prepare for that question. She gave him the answer she’d built: the army’s wounds, her uncle’s methods, everything a physician could learn here that she couldn’t learn at home. She said it well. She’d practised it on the inside of a lid.

“And you were refused so you had no other way,” said the General.

“Yes, General.”

“Your father refused.”

“Yes.”

“Your uncle refused.”

“Twice, General. Once through a door.”

His eyes went to her uncle, and something happened at the corner of his mouth that was gone before she could decide what it was. Then he stood and walked to the end of the tent, where an officer with a long scar down one cheek had been standing so still she hadn’t seen him. They spoke too low for her to hear.

Shiyu stood with her hands folded and tried to slow her breathing.

“Uncle, what’s he saying?” she whispered.

“Nothing you’ll like.”

“Will he send me home?”

Her uncle didn’t answer, and that was worse than any answer. Across the tent the scarred officer turned his head and looked at her, the way a man might look at a wall he’d been ordered to get through. Then the tent flap moved behind her, and the light changed, and she understood that more people had come in from both sides.

She was, she thought, in an enormous amount of trouble.

chapters.title: The Interrogation and the Truth
chapters.desc: Accused of spying, she has one defence left: the embarrassing truth, in front of six men.
chapters.epigraph: “The enemy’s people say they’re not spies. Do they also say they came to look at you?”
chapters.content:
There were five of them, and they had come in so silently that she hadn’t heard a single footstep.

The scarred officer stayed by the General. A slight man with ink on his fingers stood to her left. A broad, weathered older officer took the far wall. A restless one with a scout’s sunburn leaned on the tent pole like he’d been there all day. The young officer from the entrance stayed at the entrance. None of them were looking at her the way Qingzhou did. They were looking at her the way you look at a problem.

The scarred one spoke first. “A governor’s daughter in the General’s own supply box. Three days with the column. No pass, no escort, no letter. That isn’t curiosity. That’s an operation.”

“I’m not—” Shiyu began.

He had a voice like gravel being raked. “You hid on purpose. You stayed hidden until the camp. You knew exactly where you were going and made sure you weren’t found before you got there. A girl who runs away from home on a whim doesn’t do that. Someone who’s been sent does.”

“Wei Tiecheng. Vice-commander,” murmured her uncle.

“Thank you, Uncle. That helps.”

The ink-fingered man spoke without any heat at all. “For two years the border clans have been trying to put their own people into the army’s medical staff. You arrived in the medical supplies. You carry needles. You have training. The coincidence is notable.”

“Lin Wenyuan. Strategist,” said her uncle.

“I’d guessed.”

Nobody said the word spy. Nobody needed to. It hung in the tent like smoke. For the first time since the lid came off, Shiyu was frightened: not embarrassed, frightened. She could see exactly how it looked. If she’d been standing where they stood, it would have looked the same to her.

“I’m not a spy. I have no connection to anyone on the border.”

“The enemy’s people always say that. We wouldn’t be doing our work if we took your word,” said Wei Tiecheng, not unkindly.

The young officer at the entrance spoke for the first time. “Her uncle can vouch for who she is. The Governor of Qingzhou is trusted. But a trusted man can have someone in his house he doesn’t know about. And a clever operation would use the Chief Physician’s own niece. Think of the access.”

“I am not a spy,” said Shiyu, louder than she meant to.

Lin Wenyuan folded his ink-stained hands. “Then tell us what you are. A wish to study army medicine doesn’t explain the hiding, the timing, or the fact that you brought no letter, no request, nothing. A girl who wanted training would have asked her uncle in writing. You didn’t ask. You hid. So you knew the proper way wouldn’t give you what you wanted. What did you want?”

The silence after that was a particular kind of silence. All of them were looking at her. Her uncle had gone quiet beside her, and she understood that even he didn’t know what she was going to say.

She could still manage it. She had answers ready: she was desperate for real cases, she’d known her uncle would refuse, she was young and impatient and stupid. All of them were close to the truth without being the truth. All of them would probably get her sent home with a scolding instead of tied to a post. She looked up.

The General was watching her from his chair, and his watching wasn’t like theirs. They were waiting to judge her answer. He was waiting to see whether she’d lie.

She didn’t know how she knew that. She knew it. A good lie would work on the five of them. It wouldn’t work on him: not because he’d catch it, but because he’d know she had chosen it. All the careful answers came down at once.

“The enemy’s people say they’re not spies. Do they also say they came to look at you?” said Shiyu.

Nobody moved.

“I saw the General’s procession from my father’s balcony. Twelve days, fifteen now. I didn’t know you could see someone once and then not be able to stop thinking about them for fifteen days. I asked my uncle questions I shouldn’t have asked. He gave me his diagnostic face. My father looked at the ceiling. I knew what it was, and I didn’t know what to do with it, and it wouldn’t go away no matter how sensible I was. So I made a plan. It was a terrible plan. I can see now that it was a terrible plan. But I’m not a spy. I’m an eighteen-year-old woman who made the most impractical decision of her life because she couldn’t think of a better one.”

She stopped. She needed air.

The tent was completely silent. Wei Tiecheng’s mouth had come open; he shut it. Lin Wenyuan looked like a man whose careful model had just been handed something it had no column for. The weathered officer at the far wall stared at the tent roof with deep concentration. The scout made a small strangled sound and turned it, not very well, into a cough. The young officer at the entrance had gone so still that she’d later learn it was the sound of him not laughing. Beside her, her uncle let out one long breath through his nose.

And the General looked at her. For three heartbeats his face did something she hadn’t seen it do: it showed her surprise, real surprise, held in hard, as if he were stopping it from taking up any more room than he’d allowed it. It was the first unguarded thing she’d seen from him. Then it was gone, and he was flat and exact again, and he stood up.

“Chief Physician.”

“General.”

“Your niece will stay in the medical tent. The camp will understand that she arrived with the spring rotation of medical staff from the capital. Everyone in this tent will keep to that.”

The five of them said yes, General, nearly together. The scout’s voice cracked on it.

He came round the end of the table and stopped in front of her, close enough that she could see the bandage at his wrist and a small old scar through his left eyebrow she hadn’t been able to see from the balcony.

His voice was even and clear and had no warmth in it at all. “You’re here. Sending you straight back makes more trouble for your family than keeping you under supervision does. You’ll work for your uncle. You came for medicine. That’s what you’ll be here for. You won’t come to the command area unless you’re sent for. You won’t make difficulties for him. In six weeks you’ll go home with work worth having done. Do you understand?”

“Yes, General,” said Shiyu. It came out small.

“Good.”

He turned back to his maps. Her uncle’s hand settled on her shoulder and steered her out.

The afternoon outside was loud and cold and smelled of horses and woodsmoke, and the whole camp went about its business. Shiyu stopped walking in the middle of it.

“Uncle.”

“Mm.”

“Did I just say that out loud? In front of all of them?”

“You did.”

“All five?”

“And him. Don’t forget him,” said her uncle.

She covered her face with both hands.

“For what it’s worth, Wei Tiecheng has been vice-commander for nine years and I have never once seen his mouth fall open,” he said.

“That doesn’t help.”

“Zhou Hua will have told the whole scouting company by supper.”

“Uncle.”

He took her elbow, gently, the bruised one, and started her walking again. “He won’t tell them what you said. He’ll tell them you exist. Six weeks. Come on. I’ll show you where we keep the clean linen, and you can start by being better at this than anyone in the north.”

“I will be,” said Shiyu into her hands.

He sounded almost proud, which was the worst part. “I know. That isn’t what worries me.”

chapters.title: The Medical Tent
chapters.desc: Six weeks, a tent full of wounded men, and a chance to prove she belongs there.
chapters.epigraph: “Less swelling. Less heat. Less discharge.”
chapters.content:
The medical tent was large and divided into three: treatment at the front, stores and preparation in the middle, sleeping space at the back. Everything was labelled. Everything had its place. Shiyu recognised her uncle’s hand in all of it, the same order she’d watched him put into her father’s herb shed on every visit, scaled up for eleven thousand men.

She stood at the entrance with her bundle in her arms and tried to look like someone who hadn’t just told a general how she felt about him in front of his five most senior officers.

Her uncle came and stood beside her and said nothing. In eighteen years she’d learned that this was the worst of his displeasure. He never shouted. He let the silence do it.

“Uncle,” she said at last.

“Your bed is at the back, behind the screen. You’ll wear the assistant’s grey at all times while you’re working. It says medical staff and nothing else. Anyone who asks has been told you came from the capital with the spring rotation. Don’t add to it.”

“Yes, Uncle.”

He took a stack of papers off the nearest table and put them in her arms on top of the bundle. “We start at dawn. Every case is written up. The General requires it, reads it and uses it to run the health of the whole camp. It’s meticulous and it’s not optional. Last night’s watch. Read them. Then tell me what you’d do differently.”

“Tonight?”

“Now.”

She read them in the lamplight while he unpacked the carts. She hadn’t understood, until that first night, how much of an army physician’s day was writing things down. Every patient. Every complaint. Every herb weighed, every dressing changed, every follow-up. The format was strict and the language was exact and nothing was allowed to be left out.

The first report she handed him came back without a word, with his finger on a line where she’d summarised.

“I said the wound was improving.”

“Improving how?”

“Less swelling. Less heat. Less discharge.”

“Then write less swelling, less heat, less discharge, and how much less, and since when. Improving is what you thought. I want what you saw.”

She rewrote it. The second one came back two days later, a recovery note she’d been pleased with.

“You’ve written that he’s ready for light duty.”

“He is.”

“Says who?”

“Says me.”

Her uncle said it gently, which was how he said everything that mattered. “A conclusion without the observations under it is an opinion. And opinions aren’t evidence. Give me the grip strength, the range in the shoulder, whether he flinched when you pressed here.”

He pressed two fingers above her own collarbone, hard enough that she flinched.

“Like that. Write that.”

She rewrote that one too. By the end of the first week her reports came back with nothing on them but his initial. She took it as the highest praise the north had to offer.

The soldiers were easier than the paperwork. Most of them were boys from farms who had never been touched by a physician who was also a girl, and who blushed and stared at the tent roof while she cleaned their cuts, and lied about how much things hurt.

“It doesn’t hurt, Miss.”

“Then why are you holding your breath?”

“I’m not.”

“You’ve been holding it since I picked up the cloth. Breathe out. Now in. Now tell me where it hurts.”

“Everywhere a bit, Miss.”

“That’s more useful. Thank you.”

One of them, a corporal with a shoulder that wouldn’t lift, came back every second day for a week and brought his friends to watch.

“Can you lift it yet?”

“Higher than Tuesday, Miss.”

“Show me.”

He lifted it. His friends cheered. She wrote down the height against the tent pole in charcoal and the date beside it, and the next time he came the friends checked the mark before she did.

She didn’t see the General. That was exactly as it should be. He’d given her clear orders, and she was following them. There was no reason for her path to cross his, and she wasn’t inventing one.

She was also aware of him at roughly every other moment of every day. She heard him in the ordinary noise of the camp: soldiers talking while she dressed their wounds, a quartermaster complaining that the General had sent back the boot count because it didn’t add up, her uncle saying the General wants in the same tone he used for the weather.

On the fourth day, carrying an armful of clean linen down the western path to the drying racks, she saw him. He was walking with Wei Tiecheng towards the training ground, his hands behind his back, listening while the vice-commander talked. He didn’t look towards the path.

She didn’t slow down. She looked straight ahead at the drying racks and thought hard about the best temperature for drying wound dressings, and whether the wind was right for it. The part of her that hadn’t been told to think about temperatures did the same ridiculous thing it had done on the balcony. She hung the linen. She walked back.

“You’re red,” said her uncle, without looking up from his mortar.

“It’s windy.”

“It’s not windy.”

“It’s windy on the western path.”

He ground in silence for a while. “He went to the training ground to watch the archers. He does it every fourth day, after the morning council, if anyone ever needed to know.”

“Nobody needs to know.”

“Good. Then nobody will take the western path at the end of the morning council on the eighth day. Pass me the angelica,” said her uncle.

She passed him the angelica, and that evening she wrote an excellent report on the corporal’s shoulder, with three reasons for the improvement and every observation under each of them, and didn’t think about the western path at all. That was the first week.

chapters.title: He Reads the Reports
chapters.desc: Chen Ye lets slip what the General does with her reports in the evenings.
chapters.epigraph: “Chen Ye never makes conversation. Chen Ye delivers messages and pretends they’re conversation.”
chapters.content:
By the second week she knew the camp well enough to know which paths went near the command area. She told herself she wasn’t using that knowledge. Some mornings, she was.

There were two wells. The northern one was forty paces from the medical tent. The southern one was a hundred and sixty, and the path to it ran along the western edge of the command area. She used the northern well for anything urgent. For the water that could wait, she found herself, most mornings, taking the long way.

“The southern well again?” said her uncle on the sixth day, when she came back with the bucket.

“The water’s cleaner.”

“Is it?”

“The northern well’s closer to the stable drains. It’s a small difference. For wounds it matters.”

“That’s true,” said her uncle, and went back to his mortar, and she couldn’t tell whether he believed her, which meant he didn’t.

She never saw the General on those walks. The command tent was always busy, riders coming and going, voices inside, a map being carried in or out. Never him. She kept taking the long way anyway, and couldn’t have explained why even to herself.

On the ninth day Chen Ye came to the medical tent to collect the General’s personal supplies.

He was the young officer from the entrance, the one who’d gone so still while she was confessing. Up close he had a pleasant, forgettable face and observant eyes, and he leaned on the end of her table while she packed the box and watched her work as though he had nowhere in particular to be.

“You’ve settled in well, Miss Yun.”

“The work is good.”

“So I hear. The Chief Physician says your reports are unusually thorough.”

“He sends most of them back.”

Chen Ye picked up a roll of linen, looked at it, put it down again. “He used to. He’s stopped. Your trips to the southern well are very regular too, I’ve noticed. Every morning, just after the council breaks.”

Her hands didn’t stop. “The southern well gives cleaner water for medical preparation. The northern one’s too close to the stable drains.”

“Ah.”

“For wounds, it matters.”

“Of course it does. Thorough,” said Chen Ye, in the voice of a man finding an explanation completely reasonable and also completely transparent, and deciding not to say so.

She tied the box shut and pushed it across the table. “Two rolls of linen, the salve, the wine for washing, the fever powder in case. The wrist binding should be changed tonight. He won’t want to. Tell him my uncle said so.”

“Your uncle didn’t say so.”

“My uncle will say so, if anyone asks him.”

Chen Ye looked at her, and then he smiled, the first real smile she’d seen on anyone in the camp who wasn’t a patient, and tucked the box under his arm. “I’ll tell him exactly that.”

He went to the entrance. Then he stopped, with one hand on the flap, without turning round. She would learn that this was his habit: everything that mattered, Chen Ye said on his way out of a door.

He paused. “He reads them, you know. The medical reports. All of them, in the evenings, after the dispatches. The long ones most of all. The one where you followed eleven men through their recovery and wrote down what each of them had eaten. He writes in the margins.”

She looked up. The flap was already falling shut behind him.

She stood alone among the stores with a box of dried herbs in her hands and felt something turn over in her chest that she wasn’t going to put a name to. Then she put the herbs down and went back to work.

“Was that Chen Ye?” said her uncle from the front of the tent.

“He came for the supplies.”

“He stayed a while.”

“He was making conversation.”

Her uncle came round the screen with a bloody cloth in one hand and looked at her face. “Chen Ye never makes conversation. Chen Ye delivers messages and pretends they’re conversation. What did he tell you?”

“That the General reads the reports.”

“He does.”

“You knew?”

He threw the cloth in the basin. “I’ve known for eight years. I write half of them. He’s never written in the margins of mine.”

She didn’t know what to say to that, so she said nothing, and her uncle went back to his patient.

That evening she wrote her report by lamplight. It was more careful than any she’d written. Every observation had its number. Every conclusion stood on something she’d seen. She wasn’t trying to impress anyone. It was a matter of principle: if someone was going to read it with enough care to write in the margins, it deserved to be the best she could make it.

She didn’t think about dark eyes reading her handwriting by a lamp in the command tent. Not much.

The next morning she took the long way to the southern well, and on the way back, for the first time, the flap of the command tent was tied open, and there was a figure at the map table inside who looked up as she went past. She didn’t stop. She didn’t spill a drop.

“Cleaner water,” said her uncle, taking the bucket.

“Much,” said Shiyu.

chapters.title: The Battle, and What Came After
chapters.desc: The eastern flank breaks, the tent fills faster than she can count, and the General gives her leave with one condition.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll know if you don’t.”
chapters.content:
The rider came at midday, hard enough that she heard the hooves before she saw the dust.

She was grinding a compound at the back table. All over the camp men straightened at the sound before they knew why, and she put down the pestle. Her uncle was already at the entrance with his hand on the flap.

“Eastern flank. Clan cavalry came round the ridge at dawn. The General’s taken the main force out to meet them. There’ll be wounded by the afternoon,” said the rider, sliding off a horse white with sweat.

“How many?”

“Nobody knows yet, Physician.”

Her uncle turned round, and she saw his face change. The warmth went out of it. This was the Chief Physician of the Northern Army, not the man who brought her dried herbs in his coat.

“We prepare now. Everything. Every surface cleared, every pot of water on the fire, every roll of linen where you can reach it without looking. You know the system. Use it. If you’re unsure, make the safer choice and tell me after.”

“Yes.”

“Shiyu.”

She stopped with an armful of linen.

“You’ll see things today you haven’t seen in this life,” said her uncle.

“I’ve seen them in the other one.”

He looked at her a moment longer, and then nodded once, and they went to work.

They came in waves. First the walking wounded, holding their own arms, helping each other through the flap. She sorted them the way he’d taught her: the ones who could get worse first, the ones who’d keep sitting against the wall.

“You. What happened?”

“Lance, Miss. Glanced off.”

“Sit there. Press this on it. Harder. Don’t take it off to look, you’ll start it again.”

The next man was grey and holding his hand against his chest.

“You. Can you feel your fingers?”

“All but two.”

“Which two? Show me. Stay here, my uncle needs to see you.”

She cleaned wounds and closed them and washed them with the salt water and splinted a broken forearm while its owner swore at her in three dialects, and talked to him the whole time in the low, steady voice she’d built for this in a different life.

“You’re doing well.”

“I’m not, Miss, I’m screaming.”

“Screaming is doing well. It means your lungs work. One more. Ready?”

“No!”

“Good,” said Shiyu, and set it.

There wasn’t time to be frightened. She worked the way she’d worked in a trauma bay in a city that didn’t exist yet: one patient, then the next, then the next.

At the worst of it her uncle called her across.

“I need you on two at once. This one’s nicked an artery in the thigh, I’ve clamped it, someone has to keep it clamped while I close above. That one took a blade under the ribs and I can’t tell yet if it’s gone in. Can you?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t say yes because I’m asking.”

“I’m saying yes because I can.”

She held the clamp with one hand and pressed her ear to the other man’s chest, listening to the breath on both sides, counting, while her uncle worked beside her with his sleeves black to the elbow. The breath was even. The ribs had stopped the blade.

“He’s clear. It’s the muscle. It hasn’t gone into the cavity.”

“You’re sure?”

“I’d stake my licence on it.”

“Your what?”

“My reputation. Close the thigh, Uncle,” said Shiyu.

He closed the thigh. Only later, when the tent had gone quiet and her hands had finally stopped and her back hurt in a place she’d forgotten she owned, did she let herself think about whether she’d been able to do it. By then she already knew.

She was writing up the third-to-last case at the documentation table when her uncle came and stood beside her. He didn’t sit.

“The General’s been hit.”

Her brush stopped.

“Arrow. Upper left arm. Chen Ye says he’s walking and giving orders and refusing to sit down. I can’t leave. There are two out there I won’t trust to anyone else tonight.”

She was careful with her face. “I can go.”

“I know you can.”

“Arrow wound, upper arm. I’ve closed two of the same today. It’s straightforward. You’re needed here.”

Her uncle looked at her. She kept her face professional, which took more effort than anything else she’d done all day.

“You’ll treat the wound and only the wound,” said her uncle.

“Yes, Uncle.”

“You’ll go straight there and come straight back.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll conduct yourself with complete propriety.”

“Of course.”

“I’ll know if you don’t.”

“I know you will,” said Shiyu.

She packed the bag with hands that were steadier than she’d expected, and followed the runner out into the cold blue end of the afternoon, towards the command tent.

chapters.title: The Arrow and the Heartbeat
chapters.desc: She stitches the General’s arm, and her hands are steadier than her heart.
chapters.epigraph: “Is it just me, or did he not take his eyes off her the entire time?”
chapters.content:
He was standing.

She’d expected him to be sitting. Most men who’d lost blood and fought since dawn wanted to sit. He was at the map table with his left arm held carefully against his side, going over something with Lü Yue, the weathered officer from the far wall, who stood opposite him wearing the face of a man who had worked out exactly how likely his commander was to sit down if asked, and found it not worth the attempt.

She took in the wound from the doorway. A field binding on the upper arm, rough linen pulled tight, dried blood in a pattern that said the first bleed had been heavy and had slowed. He moved the arm when he pointed at the map, so the muscle worked and the bone was almost certainly whole. Good. That made everything simpler.

He looked up. His eyes went to her bag, then to her face, then back to the map, taking her in without stopping what he was doing.

“The Chief Physician is with two serious cases. He sent me. I’ve closed two arrow wounds of this kind today. I have everything I need. With your permission, General,” she said, before he could ask.

A pause. “Very well.”

Lü Yue gathered up his papers. On his way past her he said, low, “He’s been standing since the ridge. If you can make him sit, Miss Yun, the army will owe you a horse.”

“I’ll settle for a chair.”

“There’s one behind you.”

She set her things out on the corner of the map table: the salt water, clean cloths, the needles and thread, the salve, fresh linen. Then she looked at the binding. To get to the wound she’d need the sleeve off, which meant asking him to—

She picked up the shears. “I’ll cut the sleeve, General. It’s quicker, and I won’t disturb the binding until I’m ready.”

He looked at the shears. He looked at her. Then, without a word, he reached up with his right hand and began to undo his tunic.

She hadn’t prepared for that. She had prepared for a sleeve. A sleeve was sensible and clinical and kept everything simple. She hadn’t prepared for him to take off the whole thing, with the brisk, practical air of a man for whom his own body was just one more piece of equipment to be maintained.

The tunic came off. The undershirt followed, more slowly, because of the arm. He laid them on the map table and turned back to her and sat down in the chair, which Lü Yue would never know about.

Shiyu kept her eyes on the wound. She kept them there by an effort of will that she suspected showed on her face, and could do nothing about. The wound was in his upper left arm. The wound was what she’d come for. She was going to look at the wound, and the skin around the wound, and nothing else in the tent.

She was a physician. He was a patient. She could manage this.

She cut away the binding. The arrow had gone through the outer edge of the muscle and out the other side without catching anything that mattered. Whoever had bound it in the field knew what they were doing.

“Chen Ye?” she said.

“Zhou Hua. He’s quicker with linen than with a bow.”

She lifted the jar of salt water. “He’s good. Tell him I said so. This will sting.”

“I know.”

It stung. He drew one sharp breath through his nose and his jaw tightened, and then he made it stop, and didn’t move again while she washed the wound clean.

“This solution. The salt water. I’ve seen it in your reports,” he said, when she put the jar down.

“Salt makes it harder for rot to take hold in the wound. Wine first to clean it, salt water after.”

“By how much?”

“Of the wounds I’ve closed this way since I came, three in fifty festered. Of the ones closed with the old herbal compress before I came, it’s nearer one in five. I’ve been tracking it.”

“I know. I read it.”

She threaded the needle. Her hands were steady. Her heart wasn’t, but her hands were, and her hands were what mattered. He was still while she worked, the practised stillness of a man who’d been stitched enough times to know that moving only made it longer. She was on the seventh stitch when he spoke again, in exactly the same even voice.

“Your heartbeat.”

She placed the eighth stitch.

“I can feel it in your fingers when you work close to the skin. It’s been fast since you came into the tent.”

The observation landed exactly where he’d aimed it, which was the truth. Her face was hot. She didn’t need to touch it to know.

“It’s been a long day, General. The number of cases. The—”

“Your uncle says you were calm the whole afternoon in the medical tent. Calm and effective, he said. Those were his words.”

She tied off the eighth stitch.

“So it’s something particular to this tent,” said the General.

She began the ninth. She could feel him watching the side of her face. Not pressing; he hadn’t moved at all. Watching, the way he watched everything, with all of his attention and no hurry whatsoever.

“Yes. It’s something particular to this tent,” said Shiyu, when the pause had gone on longer than she meant it to.

It came out low and plain, without any of the careful framing she’d have liked to build round it. She’d used up every way of not saying it.

She placed the last stitch and tied it off, and sat back a little to look at the closure. Even tension. Clean edges. Her best work of the day; one of the cleanest closures she’d made in either life. Sitting back, she was aware of how close she’d been to him, the closeness the work had needed, and of the small distance between them now, across which she could see his face.

It was the same calm face he wore in front of his officers. But it was quieter, and there was something underneath it she couldn’t name and wasn’t going to try to.

“It’s closed. It’s clean. Don’t put any weight on the arm tonight. No fighting with it for five days at the very least. The stitches come out in ten,” she said.

“You’ll take them out.”

She looked up from the dressing.

“You put them in. Continuity of care. It makes sense,” said the General.

It did make sense. It was entirely reasonable. It was also the first thing he’d said to her that wasn’t an order or a clinical question, and she held it carefully with both hands.

“Ten days. I’ll come in the morning. Early.”

He looked at the dressing, and then at her. “The hour of the Rabbit. Before the morning drum. Come then.”

She wrapped the arm, packed her bag, bowed, and went out. Outside she stopped and pressed her palm flat against the cold canvas of the tent for three heartbeats, and breathed. Then she straightened her bag on her shoulder and started back towards the medical tent.

Behind her, round the side of the tent, she heard Lü Yue’s voice.

“Is it just me, or did he not take his eyes off her the entire time?”

“It’s not just you,” said Chen Ye.

“He sat down.”

“I saw.”

“I’ve been asking him to sit down since the ridge.”

“You didn’t have a needle,” said Chen Ye.

Shiyu walked faster.

chapters.title: The Hour of the Rabbit
chapters.desc: He tells her to come at dawn to take the stitches out. She’s early, and she was right about seven.
chapters.epigraph: “How do you know it was seven?”
chapters.content:
The camp at the hour of the Rabbit was a different place. The night watch was going off and the morning hadn’t properly started. Fires were being raked for breakfast, and the air had the dry, dusty smell of the frontier that she’d always connect, afterwards, with these weeks.

She’d come every morning since the arrow, to check the dressing. Every morning he was at the map table before her, with a cup of strong tea at his right hand and the night’s dispatches in a neat stack, and every morning he put down what he was reading when she came in and stood up.

“Sit, General.”

“I was going to.”

“You were going to stand until I asked. Sit.”

He sat. She’d learned that it mattered to say it. Not because he was difficult, but because the work needed him in one place, and it was cleaner to say so than to hope he’d choose it.

On the tenth morning she unwrapped the arm and looked at it for a while before she reached for the scissors. The wound had closed clean. The skin round the stitches was pink and cool, with no heat in it at all.

“Well?” said the General.

“Better than I’d hoped.”

“You don’t sound pleased.”

“I’m very pleased. I’m also annoyed, because you’ve been using it.”

“I haven’t.”

“There’s a mark on your sleeve from the bow string.”

He looked at his sleeve. She cut the first stitch and drew it out, turning it outwards so it wouldn’t drag.

“Your recovery notes. You added a proposal at the end. Changing the winter rations,” he said, while she worked.

“Yes.”

“More salt, more dried meat for the units on the hard rations. You think it’ll cut the cold-weather wound fevers.”

She drew out the fourth stitch. “The autumn and winter records say so. The units on short rations took longer to heal, every season, three seasons running. It isn’t a guess. It’s in your own tents.”

“Wei Tiecheng objects.”

“I know. On supply grounds. The contract’s fixed for the season and the quartermasters can’t change it halfway through without paying twice. He’s right. It should start with the next supply cycle, not now.”

He was quiet. “You’ve read the council’s notes on it,” he said.

She hesitated for one breath. “My uncle’s copy. He sees them because he runs the medical service. I read over his shoulder when they’re about my patients.”

That wasn’t the whole truth. She carried on to the sixth stitch without looking at his face.

“Lü Yue asked me how you decide which of your results can be trusted. I told him to ask you,” said the General.

Her hands stopped. She made them start again. “I’d be glad to answer him, if he ever asks.”

“He’ll ask. He reads your reports more carefully than anyone but me. He wants to know the method.”

She drew out the last one. Seven, not ten. She’d known by the fourth morning she wouldn’t need all ten, and hadn’t said so, because ten would have meant ten mornings and seven meant seven.

“It’s healed. You’ll have all the movement back in a week. Don’t pull a bow for another seven days. It’s knitted, but it isn’t strong yet,” she said.

“You said ten days for the stitches, at first.”

“I changed the estimate. It healed faster than I expected.”

“Is that why there were only seven?”

She looked up. He was watching her the way he’d watched her in the chair the night of the arrow: patient, with all of his attention.

“I said ten because ten is what a careful physician says. Seven was enough,” said Shiyu.

“And you came all ten mornings.”

“The dressing needed changing.”

“Every morning?”

“It’s best practice, General.”

The corner of his mouth moved. It was the closest she’d seen him come to smiling, and it was gone at once, and her heart behaved like it had been struck with a hammer.

She put on the last light wrap. Usually he stood the moment she said she’d finished, as if his body went straight back to readiness on its own. This time he didn’t move from the chair. He watched her pack the bag.

“Yun Shiyu.”

She looked up, because not looking up would have been a kind of hiding, and she’d promised herself she wouldn’t hide from him.

“Your uncle and I have talked about the camp’s records. Some of your work from these weeks is going into the formal system. Your way of tracking wound fever, especially. He thinks it should be standard in every tent.”

She waited.

“I’ve agreed. The method goes into the camp records under your name. Your uncle has orders to use it for every wound in the army.”

Her hands went still on the strap of her bag.

“Under my name. If the provincial office ever reads those records, General—” she said.

“Your name is already in them, as a physician’s assistant who served in the recovery after the eastern engagement. This adds to that. It doesn’t make anything new.”

He was giving her something that would outlast her: her name in the army’s own books, attached to work she’d done, there for as long as anyone kept records. She looked down at the strap and spent three breaths making sure her breathing was even.

“Thank you, General.”

He stood. She went to the flap, and then stopped, because something had to be said, and turned round. He was already back at the map table with a dispatch in his hand.

“I’m glad I came. I know the way I came was wrong. But the work was worth doing, and I’m glad I did it.”

He didn’t look up at once. When he did, his face was the quiet unreadable one, and it was real, and it wasn’t hers to claim.

“It was worth having done,” he said.

He hadn’t said what she’d said. She understood that he’d said it that way on purpose.

She walked back to the medical tent through the first noise of the morning. Her uncle was at the preparation table. He looked at her once, his diagnostic look, quick and complete, and went back to work without a word. She put her bag away and washed her hands and picked up the first case of the day.

She was smiling. She knew it, and didn’t try to stop, because her uncle had already seen and pretending would only insult him.

“Seven stitches?” he said, without looking round.

“How do you know it was seven?”

“Because you told me on the fourth day it would be seven and then went every morning for six more anyway,” said her uncle.

“Best practice.”

“Hm,” said her uncle, and it sounded like a man trying hard not to laugh.

chapters.title: The Last Week
chapters.desc: Her last days at the camp, the men who finally say what they think, and a kiss in the command tent the night before she goes.
chapters.epigraph: “Straight there and straight back?”
chapters.content:
The last weeks of her six went the way time goes when everyone can see the end of it and nobody mentions it. The wounded from the eastern flank healed or went home. The tent filled again with ordinary things: training sprains, coughs, a cook who’d taken the top off his thumb. Shiyu treated them all with the same care she’d given the arrow wounds. Somewhere along the way, without deciding to, she’d started thinking of them as her patients, not her uncle’s.

On the third day of the last week, Lü Yue came to the medical tent. Not for treatment. He came the way he did everything, like even a walk across the camp deserved to be done properly, and he sat down on the stool opposite her table and folded his weathered hands.

“The General tells me you have a method for deciding which of your results can be trusted.”

“I do.”

“I’d like to hear it.”

So she told him. How she counted every man, not just the ones who got better. How she wrote down what she expected before she knew the answer, so she couldn’t change her mind afterwards. How a result that happened once was a story and a result that happened eleven times in eleven men was something you could build on.

He listened to all of it without moving, with the attention of a man for whom understanding a thing properly mattered more than understanding it fast.

“And when it doesn’t happen eleven times?”

“Then I was wrong, and I write that down too.”

“You write down when you’re wrong?”

“Most of all then. That’s how you find out what you didn’t know.”

He asked two more questions. She answered both. Then he was silent for a while, looking at the stack of her records on the table.

“The logic is sound,” he said at last, and stood up, and bowed to her, a small exact bow, the kind a senior officer gives an equal.

From Lü Yue, she’d learn later, that was nearly a medal.

Wei Tiecheng came the next day. He stood in the entrance with his arms folded and the expression of a man about to say something he’d decided to say and didn’t enjoy saying.

“Miss Yun.”

“Vice-Commander.”

He looked at a point just past her left ear. “The salt water. You treated twelve of my men in the first days. None of them festered. Two had wounds I’ve seen kill men before, from the rot alone. You closed both clean.”

“The salt water made the difference in those two.”

He unfolded his arms, and then didn’t seem to know what to do with them, and folded them again. “Your hands made the difference. When you came, I said you were an operation.”

“I remember.”

“I was wrong.”

It was the longest personal speech she’d ever heard from him, and she could see what it had cost him to build.

“Thank you, Vice-Commander. That means a great deal.”

“Don’t tell Zhou Hua I said it,” said Wei Tiecheng, and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

On her last evening she wrote her final report. It was long: the whole recovery after the eastern engagement, every man, every wound, every number. At the end she added a section nobody had asked for, a plain account of the wound-cleaning method, written so that any physician who came after her could follow it without ever having met her. It didn’t matter that she’d worked it out. What mattered was that it worked.

She was tying the papers together when Chen Ye put his head round the flap.

“The General asks for the final report.”

“I’ll put it on the stack. It goes up in the morning with the others.”

“He asks for it tonight. Delivered in person,” said Chen Ye.

Her uncle, at the far table, didn’t look up from his mortar. “Go on.”

“Uncle—”

He ground something with more force than it needed. “It’s a report. You’re delivering it. Straight there and straight back. I’ll know.”

“I know you will.”

The command tent was lit low, one lamp on the map table and a brazier in the corner. He was alone. He stood when she came in, as he always did, and took the bundle of papers from her hands, and didn’t open it.

“Your uncle tells me you leave at first light.”

“Yes, General.”

“With the supply escort, by the south road.”

“Yes.”

“Sit down.”

She sat on the stool by the brazier. He didn’t sit. He stood by the map table with her report in his hands, and the lamp was behind him, so she couldn’t see his face properly.

“Your time here has been of value to the camp. I wanted you to know that I’ve noted it,” he said.

“Wei Tiecheng said nearly the same thing yesterday.”

Something moved at the corner of his mouth. “Wei Tiecheng said it first. He wanted that on the record.”

She laughed, and it came out shaky. She folded her hands in her lap to keep them still. “What will happen to the method? When I’ve gone?”

“It goes into every tent in the army. Under your name. Your uncle will write to you when it’s done.”

“And the winter rations?”

He put the report down on the table, carefully. “Next supply cycle. Wei Tiecheng’s already arguing with the quartermasters. What will you do, in Qingzhou?”

“Open a clinic.”

“Will your father let you?”

“Not at first. Then he will. He always does, if I’m patient enough and I’m right.”

“And your mother?”

“My mother will choose the sign.”

He was quiet. The brazier ticked. Somewhere outside a sentry called the hour.

“There will be proposals. Your uncle says so. Families who’ll hear about the governor’s daughter who studied with the army,” he said.

“My uncle says a great many things.”

“Is he wrong?”

She looked at the brazier, because she couldn’t look at him and say it. “No. There will be proposals. My mother will bring every one of them to me, and I’ll read every one of them, because she’ll ask me to. And then I’ll put them back in their envelopes.”

He didn’t say anything for so long that she thought she’d said too much, again, the way she had on the first day. Then he came round the end of the table, and crouched down in front of the stool so that his eyes were level with hers, and she saw that his face wasn’t calm at all.

His voice was even. “I’m going back to the border in a month. The clans haven’t finished. It could be a year. It could be three. I won’t ask you to wait for a man who can’t tell you when he’ll come back. I don’t have the right.”

“You’re not asking. I’m deciding,” said Shiyu.

He looked at her. She looked back. And she did the second most foolish thing she’d done that spring: she leaned forward and asked him, in a whisper, whether she could kiss him.

He didn’t answer. He put one hand against her cheek, warm and careful, the way she’d seen him handle a map that mattered, and kissed her first.

It was nothing like she’d imagined on the balcony. It was slower, and much less certain, and he tasted of strong tea, and his thumb moved once along her jaw as if he were learning it. When he drew back he stayed close, his forehead nearly touching hers.

“That’s an answer,” said Shiyu, a little breathless.

“It was a yes.”

“I’d gathered.”

He kissed her again, shorter, and stood up, and held out his hand to help her off the stool, and didn’t let go of it straight away.

“Straight back. Your uncle will know,” he said.

“He’ll know anyway.”

“Then go before he comes to get you.”

She went. At the flap she turned round. He was standing by the map table with his hand flat on her report, and he was looking at her, and he didn’t look away.

“General.”

“Lingyun. When there’s no one else in the tent,” he said.

She walked back to the medical tent through the cold with her face burning and her heart going like a war drum. Her uncle was exactly where she’d left him, grinding exactly the same root.

“Straight there and straight back?” he said, without looking round.

“Yes, Uncle.”

“You took a long time to put down some papers.”

“They were long papers.”

He ground the root for a while longer. Then he put down the pestle, came round the table, looked at her face, and sighed the sigh of a man who has seen it coming for six weeks and can’t, in all honesty, say he minds.

“Go to bed, apprentice. You’ve got a long road in the morning.”

chapters.title: The Road South
chapters.desc: She rides home without looking back. Almost. Her notebook gets one line about him, and then another.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll write every two weeks. With the northern dispatch. Read them all the way to the end.”
chapters.content:
The morning she left came up cold and clear, the sky a flat pale blue over the frontier. She’d said goodbye to her patients the evening before. Gao, the soldier whose forearm she’d closed in her first week, had taken her hand in both of his and held on, which wasn’t done, and she’d let him.

“Will you come back, Miss?”

“I don’t know, Gao.”

He’d held up the arm with its neat pink scar. “If I get another one of these, I want it done by you.”

“Then try not to get another one.”

“I’ll try, Miss. I’m not promising.”

Her uncle walked her to the southern gate. They didn’t say much. Somewhere in six weeks they’d got to a place that was more honest than anything either of them had said out loud. He’d watched her work, and been proud. He’d worried, too. Both were in his face.

At the gate he stopped. “Write to your mother. Every week, not every month. And when you get home, I mean this, Shiyu, don’t let what you’ve learned here go to waste in your father’s study. You have a physician’s mind and a physician’s hands. Use them.”

“I mean to.”

He looked down the road instead of at her. “I’ll write every two weeks. With the northern dispatch. Read them all the way to the end.”

“I always read your letters to the end.”

He cleared his throat. “These ones to the very end.”

She looked at him, and he looked at the road, and she understood that he was telling her something without telling her, the way he’d been telling her things her whole life.

“I will,” she said.

He put his hand on her shoulder, the way he had on the day she arrived, frightened and mortified and trying not to show either, and then he let her go.

“Travel safely, apprentice.”

“Are you still deciding whether to be angry with me?”

“I’ll let you know in a letter,” said her uncle.

She smiled. He gave her the small nod that was his version of a smile. She turned and walked to the escort and mounted, and didn’t look back at the medical tent.

She did look back once, when the escort cleared the last of the camp and the road bent east before it turned south. She looked at the whole camp, spread out over the brown hills, and searched it for the one figure she wanted to see.

He wasn’t at the gate. He wasn’t at the command tent, which she could pick out even from here. Of course he wasn’t. A general didn’t stand at the edge of his camp to watch a physician’s assistant ride away. He had a morning council. He’d said goodbye the night before, in the only way either of them could.

Then she saw the rider on the rise above the training ground. One man on a black horse, sitting perfectly still against the sky. He didn’t wave. He didn’t move at all. He stayed there until the road went down into the valley and the hill came up between them, and she watched him until she couldn’t.

“Miss? Something wrong?” said the escort sergeant.

“Nothing. The sun’s in my eyes,” said Shiyu.

The sergeant looked at the sky, where the sun was behind them, and wisely said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second evening, at the relay station, she wrote in her own notebook for the first time since Qingzhou. She wrote about the patients and the work. About Gao and the way he guarded his scar like a medal. About Lü Yue’s careful questions and Wei Tiecheng’s speech and what it had cost him. About Chen Ye, who said every true thing on his way out of a door. About her uncle’s face when she’d done something well.

About the General she wrote one line.

It was worth having done.

Then, under it, smaller:

He kissed me first.

She looked at that line, and closed the notebook, and slept with it under her pillow like a girl in a story, which she found humiliating and did anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

She reached Qingzhou on the third afternoon. Her mother met her at the gate, crying in the tidy, controlled way of a woman who has worried for six weeks and run out of the strength to hide it.

“I’m well, Mother,” said Shiyu into her shoulder.

“I know you’re well. I was still worried. Six weeks, Shiyu. Six weeks of your uncle’s letters saying you’d sewn up half the Northern Army.”

“Not half.”

“A third, then. Is that better?”

“About a quarter.”

Lady Ren held her at arm’s length and looked her over, every part, the way she’d once looked over a bolt of silk for flaws, and sniffed. “You’re thinner. Your hands are rough. You’ve been in the sun. And you smell of horses.”

“I’ve been on a horse for three days.”

“You look very well indeed. I’m still deciding whether to be angry with you. Come inside. Cook made the congee you like,” said her mother, and her voice wobbled and then steadied.

Her father came out into the courtyard with the face of a man feeling several things at once and dealing with it by being calm about all of them. He had ink on his sleeve. He looked at his daughter over his wife’s shoulder and gave her the small, fond, slightly bewildered nod he’d been giving her for eighteen years.

“You’re back.”

“I’m back.”

“Did you learn what you went to learn?”

“Yes, Father.”

He studied her face, and something in it made him look at the ceiling. “All of it?”

“More than I expected.”

“Hm,” said her father, and took her bundle from her, and carried it in himself.

Little Lan was waiting on the inner steps, hopping from one foot to the other. The moment Lady Ren had gone to see about the congee, she seized Shiyu’s sleeve.

“Miss. Miss. Did he send you home?”

“He didn’t send me home. I came home. At the end of six weeks. Like he said.”

“Did he say anything?”

Shiyu thought about the brazier and the stool and a hand against her cheek. “He said my work had been of value to the camp.”

Little Lan’s face fell. “That’s all?”

“That’s all he said,” said Shiyu, and went in to her congee before her face could give anything else away.

She slept for twelve hours that night. She hadn’t done that since she was five, and the soul she carried had first opened its eyes, bewildered, in this small body. When she woke she lay still for a while, looking at the ceiling she’d looked at her whole life in this world, and let the six weeks settle into the past where they belonged.

Then she got up. She had a clinic to build.

chapters.title: Three Years
chapters.desc: A clinic of her own at nineteen, a nickname she finds excessive, and letters that end with his paragraphs.
chapters.epigraph: “And proper lanterns. Two, not one. One looks like a noodle stall.”
chapters.content:
It took eight months to get from the day she first raised the clinic with her father to the day her first patient walked through its door.

“A clinic,” said Yun Chengde, the first time.

“In the eastern district. Near the river market, where the dockworkers live. They’ve got one physician for six streets, and he charges more than a week’s wages.”

“And who would work in it?”

“I would.”

He put down his brush. “As what?”

“As the physician.”

“Shiyu.”

“I’ve closed arrow wounds in a field tent, Father. Forty of them. I’ve got the records.”

He looked at her over the top of the lamp. “I know you have. Your uncle sent me copies. Let me think.”

She let him think. Then, over the next month, she brought him the numbers.

“Eleven thousand people in the eastern district, Father. Four hundred saw a physician last year. Ninety died of things that didn’t need to kill anyone.”

“Ninety.”

“Wound fever. Bad water. A cough left too long. Here’s the list of herbs I’d need, and where to get them cheapest. Here’s the building: the old dye-house by the second well. The roof’s sound.”

“And the money?”

“Here’s the money. A fee for those who can pay. Nothing for those who can’t. Uncle’s sent forty taels from his own salary as a loan, at no interest, which he says is the only foolish thing he’s ever done.”

“And when the respectable families of Qingzhou say a governor’s daughter has no business putting her hands on dockworkers?”

“Here’s what I’ll say to them,” said Shiyu, and put down a fourth sheet of paper.

Her father read it. He took his spectacles off. “You’ve answered that before I’d finished asking it.”

She was patient, the long way, the way she’d been patient with the General’s arm. “I’ve answered everything before you’ve finished asking it. I’ve had a month. Ask me the next one.”

In the seventh month her father said yes, the way he said yes to everything important she asked him: not with excitement, but slowly, like a man who has examined every argument against her and found none of them strong enough. Her mother was harder.

“A daughter of this house working with her own hands. In the eastern district. Where the boats come in,” said Lady Ren.

“Yes, Mother.”

“With men from the docks.”

“With anyone who’s sick.”

“What will people say?”

“They’ll say the governor’s daughter is odd. They already say that.”

Lady Ren looked at her across the embroidery frame. She’d spent eighteen years trying to make this daughter into something she could understand and had never once managed it. Shiyu watched her mother decide, slowly, to stop trying.

“Then it will need a proper sign. Something that looks established. Not one of those painted boards that peel in the first rain. We’ll ask Old Shen in the eastern district. He did the sign for the Grain Bureau,” said her mother at last.

“Mother.”

“And proper lanterns. Two, not one. One looks like a noodle stall.”

Shiyu went round the frame and put her arms round her mother, who said she was crushing the silk and didn’t let go.

Old Shen carved the name in camphor wood: Qingcloud Medical Hall. Her mother chose the blue. Shiyu was nineteen the day she stood under it for the first time, and something in her chest settled into place like a bone set right.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first year was hard in the way the first year of anything worth building is hard.

“I’ll wait for the physician,” said an old woman on the third day, sitting on the bench by the door with her swollen ankle propped on a basket.

“I am the physician.”

“You’re the governor’s girl.”

“I’m both. Let me see the ankle.”

“I’ll wait for the real one.”

Shiyu knelt down on the floor in front of the bench. “There isn’t another one. There’s me, and there’s the man on Willow Street who’ll charge you three strings of cash to tell you it’s swollen. I won’t charge you anything today. If I’m wrong, you can tell everyone in the market I’m a fraud.”

The old woman looked at her a long time, and then held out the ankle. It was badly sprained, not broken.
