Shiyu bound it and gave her a jar of the liniment she’d learned from her uncle and told her to come back in three days. She came back in two, with her daughter-in-law’s bad tooth and her neighbour’s cough.

The respectable families stayed away. They liked their physicians old and male and trained by famous masters. The dockworkers came, and the boatwomen, and the washerwomen from the river steps, and the children of all of them. She treated whoever walked in.

In the second year a river worker was carried in with his leg crushed between two hulls. Two physicians had already told his wife it would have to come off.

“Can you save it?” said the wife.

“I don’t know yet. I can try. It will take two months, and it will hurt, and he might still lose it.”

“And if he loses it?”

“Then he’ll lose it to me and not to them, and I’ll have tried everything first.”

Two months later he walked out through the clinic door on his own two feet, with a stick he didn’t really need, and his wife sent a basket of river fish every week for the next year.

That autumn half a street in the eastern district came down with a fever at once. Shiyu walked the street with a notebook, door to door, asking every family where they drew their water, and drew a map on the back of a prescription, and found that every fever came from the houses on one side of the old well by the dyer’s.

“Close it,” she told the district headman.

“On whose say?”

“On my father’s, if you need it. On mine, if you’ll take it.”

He took hers. The fever stopped at the well.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third year they were calling her the Fairy Physician.

“Miss, the fish man called you it again. And the boatman’s mother. And a man from the Grain Bureau,” said Little Lan, who’d come with her to the clinic and refused to go back to the house.

“It’s excessive.”

“It’s lovely.”

“I’m thorough. I’m honest about what I don’t know. I write everything down. None of that is magic.”

“It’s magic to them, Miss. You told the dyer’s well to stop and it stopped.”

“I told the headman to close it. It stopped because people stopped drinking from it.”

“That’s what fairies say,” said Little Lan, with great satisfaction, and went to answer the door.

She’d built a life. She’d built it on purpose, carefully, the way she did her medicine, and it was hers.

And every two weeks, with the northern dispatch, her uncle’s letter came.

She read them in the early mornings in the back room before the clinic opened, all the way through: the camp’s medical news, the spread of her method into every tent in the army, an argument with a quartermaster, a joke about Zhou Hua. At the end of each one there was a short paragraph, set apart from the rest, in her uncle’s handwriting, but not in her uncle’s voice.

The winter rations went to the outer units in the new cycle. Wei Tiecheng won his argument with the quartermasters. Fever cases down by a third. Someone asked me to tell you.

We moved the camp east in the thaw. The river here is wider than yours, and slower. The arm is fine. Someone asked me to tell you that, too.

I read your clinic’s first-year records. Your uncle sent a copy. You count the ones who die as carefully as the ones who live. Good.

She never answered them directly. She couldn’t. A governor’s unmarried daughter didn’t write to a man who wasn’t family, and every letter she sent north went through her uncle’s hands. But she began to add a paragraph to the end of her own letters to him, set a little apart.

Tell whoever asks that the dyer’s well is closed, and the fever stopped at it. Tell him I counted.

She kept every one of the letters in a camphor box under the window. She read the two-week ones at the window, too, because the light was better there. That was the reason. It was the only reason she had.

She wasn’t waiting. She was building, and the building was the point, and whatever she felt, which was still there, stubborn and unsettled the way some things are, lived beside the building instead of in place of it. She was twenty-one. She was the Fairy Physician of Qingzhou, and her clinic had the most careful civilian records in the province.

That was enough. She’d made it enough. She’d also, she could admit to herself, made it excellent, in case anyone was ever in a position to read it.

chapters.title: Mei Yun
chapters.desc: A fifteen-year-old talks her way into the clinic and notices far too much, starting with a cracked mortar.
chapters.epigraph: “Your mortar’s cracked on the inside. Near the lip. You’ll lose powder in it.”
chapters.content:
Mei Yun turned up at the clinic in the fourth month of the second year with a note from her mother and the face of a girl who had decided something and wasn’t going to be talked out of it.

“I want to learn medicine.”

“How old are you?”

She held out her hands, palms up, as evidence. “Fifteen. Nearly sixteen. I can clean, I can grind, I can carry, I can read. My mother sells tea eggs by the south bridge and she says I’m too clever to sell tea eggs. And I have good hands.”

Shiyu looked at them. They were small and steady, with short clean nails, and they didn’t shake under being looked at.

“Show me,” said Shiyu.

“Show you what?”

Shiyu put a lump of dried root and a pestle in front of her. “Grind it until it’s as fine as flour. Don’t spill any.”

Mei Yun ground it until it was finer than flour, and didn’t spill a grain, and then looked up and said, “Your mortar’s cracked on the inside. Near the lip. You’ll lose powder in it.”

Shiyu hired her on the spot. Not out of charity; the clinic needed a second pair of hands. She hired her because the girl reminded her of someone: a person who’d decided what mattered and went after it, without any of the polite fuss that usually came wrapped round a request like that.

She turned out to be observant to a degree that was occasionally inconvenient.

Her hands were as good as she’d claimed. She had a gift for the pressing and kneading that got stiff joints moving and poor circulation flowing, and within a few months half the old boatmen of the eastern district were asking for “the little one.” She had a good manner with frightened people, which can’t be taught, only grown in someone who already has it. She learned fast and asked real questions and made the right kind of mistakes, the kind you only make when you’re paying attention.

She also narrated the world to herself like it was a story she was reading, and sometimes did it out loud.

“The boatman’s son is in love with the dyer’s daughter,” she announced one morning, laying out the dressings.

“How do you know?”

“He’s had a sore shoulder four times this month, and he only comes on the days she brings her mother’s cough in.”

“Perhaps his shoulder is sore.”

“It’s never the same shoulder twice, Miss.”

Shiyu went to look at the record book, and it wasn’t.

About three months after she’d arrived, Mei Yun was grinding at the side table while Shiyu read the morning post, and said, without looking up, “You get a letter from your uncle every two weeks.”

“He writes regularly.”

“And one a month from your father’s brother in the capital, and one a season from your mother’s cousin in Hangzhou.”

“My family writes letters.”

Mei Yun tapped the pestle on the rim. “The two-week ones are different. You read the monthly ones at the record table. You read the two-week ones at the window.”

Shiyu put down the letter she’d been holding. “Mei Yun.”

“I’m only observing.”

“Observe the angelica. It’s burning.”

It wasn’t burning. Mei Yun looked at it anyway, serenely, and went back to grinding, and Shiyu picked up the letter again and found she’d lost her place in it.

She hadn’t lost her place in the paragraph at the end. She never did.

The east camp has a well on a slope, and the latrines are above it, and nobody but me thinks this is a problem. I quoted the dyer’s well to the quartermaster. He asked who the physician was. I told him. He moved the latrines.

She read it twice. Then she folded it and put it in the camphor box with the others.

“Is that the one from your uncle?” said Mei Yun.

“Yes.”

“He writes very nicely at the end.”

“Mei Yun.”

Mei Yun ground. “I said nothing. I’m grinding. Is your uncle tall?”

“Why would that matter?”

“No reason, Miss. I was just wondering what the person who writes the end of your uncle’s letters looks like.”

Shiyu put the box away under the window, and shut the lid, and turned round, and found Mei Yun looking at her with an expression of perfect innocence and enormous delight.

“He has dark eyes. And a scar through his eyebrow. And he’s very bad at sitting down when he’s told to,” said Shiyu, before she could stop herself.

Mei Yun put the pestle down. “Miss.”

“Grind.”

“Miss, is he a soldier?”

“He’s a patient. Was. Three years ago. Grind the angelica.”

“Is he coming back?”

The light from the window fell across the box under it. In the street outside a boat bell rang, and somebody was shouting about the price of eels.

“I don’t know. He’s at the border. He’s been at the border for two years. The border doesn’t care whether anyone in Qingzhou is waiting,” said Shiyu, which was the truest thing she’d said all week.

“Are you waiting?”

“I’m running a clinic.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Shiyu looked at her for a long while: fifteen, sharp as a needle, and kind under all of it.

“I’m running a clinic. And I read the end of the letters at the window. Because the light is better there,” she said again, more gently.

Mei Yun picked up the pestle. “The light is much better there,” she agreed, and didn’t say another word about it all morning.

She said one more thing at the end of the day, though, while they were locking up and Shiyu was reaching for the second lantern.

“Miss? When he comes back, I’d like to be there.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to see whether he reads the end of your letters at the window too.”

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.desc: The Northern Army comes through Qingzhou with a wounded officer, and the General is at the window.
chapters.epigraph: “My hands are always steady.”
chapters.content:
Her father came to the clinic door on an ordinary afternoon early in the autumn of the third year, and one look at his face told her the day was about to stop being ordinary.

“Father? Is Mother well?”

He came in, ducking under the drying herbs, and stood by the record table in a way that meant he was carrying news he wasn’t sure how to put down. “Your mother is perfectly well. She’s choosing new lanterns for the clinic. Again. There’s a procession coming through the city. The Northern Army, on its way to the capital. The campaign’s over.”

Shiyu’s hands stopped on the bandage she was rolling.

“The General is with them. One of his officers took an arrow in the leg four days ago, and it’s gone bad on the road. The garrison captain came to the residence an hour ago. He asked for the Fairy Physician. By name,” said her father carefully.

Behind her, Mei Yun dropped a jar. It didn’t break. Mei Yun picked it up and set it down again with exaggerated care and didn’t say anything at all, which for Mei Yun was a kind of shouting.

Shiyu thought, with the clear head of someone who’d spent three years becoming a physician people trusted: there’s a man with a wound that needs treating. She thought, with the honesty she kept for herself alone: he’s in my city. And she thought, with the good sense of someone who had built something real and wasn’t going to wreck it by panicking: I’m the physician they asked for, and I’m going to go and treat the wound.

She took off her apron and folded it.

“Where?”

“The Jade Phoenix. The eastern suite.”

“Mei Yun, bring the big case. And the oils for the circulation work.”

“Yes, Miss.” Mei Yun was already moving, and her eyes were enormous.

Her father stood aside to let her past, and then caught her sleeve, lightly, at the door.

“Shiyu.”

“Father?”

He looked at her, and then at the ceiling, and then at her again. “Your mother chose the blue for the sign. I’d like you to know I chose the camphor wood. It lasts.”

She didn’t know what to say to that, so she squeezed his ink-stained hand and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Jade Phoenix had the best address on the central avenue: dark timber, pale plaster, three storeys, the kind of quiet quality that said expensive without saying it out loud. The innkeeper had the hunted look of a man whose house had been full of a general’s people for four hours and who was coping with it well at some cost to himself.

“The physician? Thank the gods. Up the stairs, end of the corridor. They’ve moved the furniture. I didn’t ask why.”

“Treatment,” said Shiyu.

“I didn’t ask,” said the innkeeper again, and fled.

At the top of the stairs she stopped and adjusted the strap of her bag. She let out one breath through her nose.

“Miss. Your hands are steady,” whispered Mei Yun.

“My hands are always steady.”

“Your face isn’t.”

“Thank you, Mei Yun.”

“You’re welcome, Miss.”

She went in. The room had been set up properly. She saw that before anything else: the bed moved out from the wall so a physician could get to both sides, the table by the window cleared and covered with a clean cloth, extra lamps brought in even though it was still daylight. Someone had thought about this. Someone in his household always thought about this.

Zhou Hua lay on the bed with his right leg propped on folded blankets and the face of a man in a good deal of pain pretending to be in none. He’d been twenty-nine in the camp. At thirty-two he was leaner, more sun-dark than ever, and a shade too pale under it. The field dressing on his thigh was stiff with old blood.

Four of the Five stood round him. Wei Tiecheng by the window with his arms folded, as broad as ever, the scar on his cheek the same colour it had always been. Lin Wenyuan in the only chair, holding a document at an angle that meant he hadn’t read a word of it in some time. Lü Yue at the bedside, standing guard the way he did everything, gravely. Chen Ye against the far wall.

Chen Ye’s face changed first. She saw it: the smallest flicker of surprise, folded at once into something more polite.

And at the window in the far corner, with his back to the room—

She didn’t look. Not yet. She went straight to the bed.

“Commander Zhou. I’m the physician from the Qingcloud Medical Hall. I need to look at the wound. Can you tell me how it happened?”

Zhou Hua squinted up at her with the look of a man whose memory was working towards something it hadn’t quite reached.

“She’s the Fairy Physician,” said Mei Yun helpfully, from just behind Shiyu’s left shoulder, in the voice of someone presenting a qualification.

Wei Tiecheng’s head turned from the window. Lin Wenyuan put down his document. Lü Yue looked at her the way a man looks at a sum he’s just checked and found correct.

Chen Ye pushed himself off the wall, and let the pieces fall into place one by one. “The Qingcloud Medical Hall. Eastern district. Opened about two and a half years ago. Yun Shiyu.”

Her name, in that room. She didn’t turn towards the window. She looked at Zhou Hua and kept her hands busy opening the case.

“The arrow. When it hit you, which way were you facing?”

Zhou Hua blinked. Then, with the quickness of a man who’d spent his life following sudden changes of plan, he started to tell her: the ambush in the gorge, the clan archer on the ridge, the way he’d turned his horse.

“Turned left or right?”

“Left.”

She pressed two fingers above the dressing. “So it came in from the outside. Good. That’s further from the big vessels. Does this hurt?”

“No.”

“Does this?”

“Yes. Gods. Yes.”

“Thank you. That’s very helpful.”

“It didn’t feel helpful,” said Zhou Hua weakly.

Behind her, from the window corner, she heard nothing. Not a word, not a step. Only the presence of him, which she’d learned three years ago to feel the way you feel weather: not always visible, always there.

She began the examination. Her hands were steady. She was a physician and this was her work, and she didn’t look towards the window for the first quarter of an hour.

Then she reached across for a clean instrument, and turned a little to do it, and found that he wasn’t at the window any more.

He’d moved. He stood at the edge of the room now, nearer the bed. Not close enough to be in her way. Close enough to see. He wasn’t looking at her face.

He was watching her hands, the way he’d watched them in the command tent three years ago, the night of the arrow, with all of his attention.

She turned back to the case and took out the wine and the salt water and the needles, and she did her work.

chapters.title: The Five Days
chapters.desc: She treats Zhou Hua’s leg and doesn’t look at the window. Four voices agree to pretend.
chapters.epigraph: “So. Are we all going to pretend we didn’t see that?”
chapters.content:
The wound was serious but manageable. The arrow had gone into the outer thigh at an angle and through the muscle without touching the bone. The field dressing had done its work: the bleeding had stopped, and the rot hadn’t properly started yet, though it was thinking about it.

She turned to Zhou Hua. “I’m going to wash it first. With wine, and then salt water. It’ll sting.”

“How much?”

“More than you’d like. Less than the arrow.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

“It’s accurate. Then I’ll close it in two layers. Deep first, then the skin. I’ll tell you before each one.”

She washed it as thoroughly as it needed, which was thoroughly, and Zhou Hua swore at the ceiling in a steady, educated stream. She talked him through the deep layer, a stitch at a time, warning him before each pull, keeping her voice at the level that said everything was under control and he needn’t worry. It was the voice she used for patients who were more frightened than they’d admit.

“You’re good at that. The talking. Telling me what’s coming before it comes,” said Zhou Hua, between stitches.

“If you know what’s next, your body doesn’t brace for the version you’ve invented. The invented version is always worse.”

He squinted at the ceiling. “Hm. You remind me of someone. A physician’s assistant we had, three years ago. After the eastern engagement. Except she was younger. I think.”

Behind her, a document rustled. Lin Wenyuan had been reading the same page for a quarter of an hour. “The salt water. That’s the same preparation.”

She placed the next stitch.

“It’s her. I told you when she walked in,” said Chen Ye from the wall.

“You said ‘it’s the physician,’” said Zhou Hua.

“I said it in a particular tone.”

“You say everything in a particular tone.”

“Hold still, Commander,” said Shiyu.

From the edge of the room, the General said nothing at all.

She closed the outer layer with the patience of someone who wasn’t going to let the quality of the work suffer for anything that was happening in the room. Even tension. Clean edges. She laid on the salve and began the dressing.

“Mei Yun. Start on the circulation in the foot and calf.”

Mei Yun was already warming the oil between her palms. She took Zhou Hua’s foot in both hands and pressed her thumbs into the arch, and he jerked upright on his elbows.

“That’s—that’s very strong.”

“Your circulation’s been squeezed by where the wound is. The work keeps the leg from stiffening and lowers the risk of a clot. It’ll be uncomfortable at first,” said Shiyu.

“Uncomfortable? Is that the word you’re looking for?”

“It’s the accurate one.”

From the window came a sound, almost nothing. A breath let out through the nose by someone stopping himself from reacting. If she was reading it right, and she thought she was, it was close to amusement.

She didn’t look up from her notes. But she felt, the way she felt where he was in a room without looking, that the sound had been warm. Knowing she’d caused it, without trying to, settled in her chest like something small and warm that she wasn’t going to examine just now. Later. Later she’d examine it.

She turned to the room. “The Commander needs complete rest for at least a week. No weight on the leg. The dressing has to be changed morning and evening, and I’ll come and do it. Watch for fever, and any change in the feeling below the knee. He should eat properly. Meat, eggs, broth, plenty to drink. Not rations out of a cart. Real food, cooked properly.”

She looked at Wei Tiecheng as she said the last part, because he was the man in the room most likely to think rations would do, and most likely to fix it if told directly.

He looked back at her with the face of a man receiving tactical orders. “Real food.”

“From the inn kitchen. Twice a day.”

“Twice a day,” said Wei Tiecheng, and she could see him filing it.

“No travel for a week. If it heals well I’ll look again at five days. That isn’t up for discussion.”

“His Majesty expects us in the capital within ten days,” said Lü Yue, as information, not objection.

“Then you have five days here and five days on the road, if it heals the way I expect. That’s possible, if he rests now.”

“I can rest. I’m very good at resting. Ask anyone,” said Zhou Hua.

“He’s terrible at resting,” said Wei Tiecheng.

“Then someone will sit on him,” said Shiyu, and began to pack her case.

The room went quiet in a way that meant several people were thinking about something nobody was going to mention in front of a patient who needed sleep. She snapped the case shut and turned to go.

“Physician.”

The word came from the window. His voice. She hadn’t heard it since she’d left the camp three years ago, and it went into her exactly the way it always had: even, a voice that carried without trying, and one she’d never once managed to hear calmly.

She turned round, and looked at him properly for the first time since she’d come into the room nearly an hour ago.

Three years had taken something that was already a great deal and added three more years of whatever made it what it was. He was thirty-one. He’d taken off his armour for the evening and wore the black inner tunic with the silver at the collar. Not in a command tent with his maps; in an inn room in her city. He’d been watching her work for most of an hour, and his face was the calm, careful face she knew, which she’d learned wasn’t the absence of something but the holding of it.

His eyes were exactly the same. She let none of it reach her face. She was a physician, and she’d just done her work well, and she was going to carry herself the way that work deserved.

“Yes, General.”

“Your fee. The innkeeper will settle it. Tell him the amount.”

“Mei Yun knows the amounts. She keeps the clinic accounts.”

“Good.”

He held her eyes a moment longer. One breath. Then he looked away, towards the window, and it was over.

She walked out. In the corridor she pressed her free hand flat to the wall for three heartbeats and felt the cool of the plaster under her palm. Then she straightened, settled the strap of her bag, and went to find the innkeeper.

Behind her, from the suite, came Zhou Hua’s voice, entirely recovered.

“So. Are we all going to pretend we didn’t see that?”

“Yes,” said four voices at once.

She didn’t slow down to hear the rest.

chapters.title: Morning Rounds and a Moved Chair
chapters.desc: Someone has moved a chair to where she sits. She knows who. Page nine.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s in the summary. Page nine.”
chapters.content:
She went back the next morning before the inn was properly awake. The sky was the flat silver of an autumn dawn, the kind of light that makes everything look as if it’s been pressed overnight between clean sheets.

“Did you sleep, Miss?” said Mei Yun, carrying the dressing basket.

“Adequately.”

“That means no.”

“It means adequately. Three years ago I’d have lain awake counting. I’m older now. I manage.”

“Manage what?”

“The distance between what I feel and what I’m allowed to do about it.”

Mei Yun walked in silence for half a street, which was a record. “That sounds very tiring, Miss.”

“It is. Carry the basket,” said Shiyu.

The dressing change was simple. The wound was clean and pink at the edges, with no heat and no smell, and the flesh was knitting exactly as she’d hoped. She changed the salve, laid on fresh linen, and wrote her notes. Zhou Hua complained about the inn food, which he said was too much like real food, and Wei Tiecheng, from the corner, said he’d eat it or Wei Tiecheng would feed it to him personally.

The second morning was the same. On the third morning something changed, though she couldn’t have said exactly when it started. It started with the chair.

Someone had moved it from the window to the table where she wrote her notes, so that when she sat down after the dressing, it was there beside the table instead of across the room. It was a small thing. A practical thing. A physician needs somewhere to sit when she writes, and the light at the table was better. She sat in it and wrote.

The General was in the room that morning. He’d asked two questions about the wound while she worked, and the questions were so specific that she knew he’d been reading medical books in the evenings. Now he took the other chair from the wall, set it at the end of the table at an angle you’d choose for talking, and sat down.

He didn’t say anything at first. Neither did she. She wrote. His silence, after three mornings, felt less like a commander managing a situation and more like someone comfortable with the quiet of a person doing close work.

After a while he spoke. “In your methods summary you wrote that the civilian diet makes it harder to control for nourishment than in a camp.”

“Yes. In the camp the ration lists give you a baseline. I don’t have one. I have to guess at what my patients eat from other things: what they tell me, how they look when they come in, what season it is. It’s less exact.”

“But your results look the same as the camp’s.”

“Which means the link is probably real. If two different ways of measuring show you the same pattern, the pattern’s more likely to be true.”

He was quiet a moment. “That’s the argument I made eight years ago, when I asked the Emperor to let me track the health of the whole camp. Several kinds of records pointing to the same pattern,” he said.

She looked up. He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at the table, with the face of a man who’d noticed something and was deciding what he thought of it.

“I know. My uncle told me about the proposal. I recognised the logic when I read the camp records. It was good reasoning,” said Shiyu.

That made him look at her: the flat, measuring look. Then something in it shifted, by a degree, the way light changes a surface without changing the surface.

“You read the camp records.”

She looked back at her notes. “My uncle sends me copies of the medical reports. I’ve followed the system for three years. It’s the best way of tracking the health of a large number of people I know of. I’ve taken things from it for the clinic. I added a column of my own. For rain.”

“Rain?”

“Fevers go up in the eastern district two weeks after the river floods. Every year. I’ve got three years of it now.”

“Two weeks.”

“Twelve to sixteen days. The wells take that long to foul.”

He sat back in the chair. She could feel him looking at her, and she kept writing, and her brush only shook once.

“You should send that to the camp,” he said.

“It’s in the summary. Page nine.”

“I haven’t reached page nine.”

“You’ve had it for three days.”

“I’ve read the first eight pages four times,” said the General.

Her brush stopped altogether. She looked up. He was looking straight at her, and his face was quite calm, and there was colour at the top of his ears that hadn’t been there a moment before.

Across the room, Zhou Hua began loudly to describe the inn’s soup to Mei Yun.

Shiyu put down her brush. She read her notes over once, out of habit, not need, and put them in the case.

“The Commander’s healing well. At this rate the five-day review will go in his favour. My uncle would have been glad to see his own method work so cleanly.” She stood up.

“He taught you well,” said the General, and it was her he was looking at when he said it.

She didn’t answer, because answering would have needed a steadiness she wasn’t sure she had just then. She picked up the case and went to the door, and at the door she turned, the way she always seemed to turn at the doors of that inn.

“Page nine. The rain,” she said.

“Tonight,” he said.

All the way back to the clinic, through morning air that smelled of the season turning cold, Mei Yun said nothing whatsoever, in a way that was louder than speech.

“Say it,” said Shiyu, at the corner by the herb market.

“I wasn’t going to say anything, Miss.”

“Say it before you burst.”

Mei Yun took a deep breath. “He moved the chair.”

“Someone moved the chair.”

Mei Yun counted them off on her fingers. “Miss, the Vice-Commander doesn’t move chairs. The Commander can’t walk. The quiet one with the papers was sitting in the other one. The one who leans on walls was leaning on a wall. That leaves one person.”

“The innkeeper.”

“The innkeeper hasn’t been upstairs since we got there. He’s frightened of them.”

Shiyu walked faster. Mei Yun trotted to keep up, and then, being Mei Yun, delivered the rest of it on the doorstep of the clinic, with her hand on the latch.

“And he went red, Miss. At the ears. I saw it.”

“You were looking at Commander Zhou’s soup.”

“I can look at two things,” said Mei Yun, and went in.

chapters.title: Chen Ye’s One True Thing
chapters.desc: On his way out of the inn, Chen Ye says one true thing, and someone finally asks whether he’s kissed her.
chapters.epigraph: “Miss. Has he kissed you?”
chapters.content:
On the fourth evening Chen Ye fell into step beside her as she was leaving the inn.

She hadn’t expected it. He’d been there for the afternoon dressing and said almost nothing, leaning in his usual corner, but there’d been something deliberate in the way he’d watched her pack her case. She let him walk with her. Three years ago she’d learned that Chen Ye said one true thing on his way out of a room, and that it was usually worth hearing.

They went down through the main hall without speaking. Outside, the evening had turned cold, the first real cold of the autumn. She pulled her wrap closer.

“He hasn’t slept properly since we got to Qingzhou. I keep his days in order. Including the parts he thinks are private. He’s been up late. Later than usual, and he doesn’t sleep much to begin with,” said Chen Ye.

She kept her pace even. “Is he unwell?”

“No.”

“Then why are you telling his physician?”

He looked at the lanterns in the courtyard. “I’m not. I’m telling you. He’s been reading the camp records from the eastern recovery. Three years ago. The ones with your name on them. And page nine of your summary, last night, until the lamp ran out.”

Her carriage was waiting by the gate. She stopped short of it.

“Chen Ye. What do you want me to understand?”

He turned, and he wasn’t smiling. He was the young officer from the supply tent, sharper about people than anyone gave him credit for, choosing when to use it.

“Three years ago he let you stay in that camp and called it a practical decision about staffing. I was standing at the entrance. I could see what it was: a man who’d never been confused by anything in his life, doing the only thing he knew how to do with confusion, which was to make it useful. Then he put your method in the records under your name. Nobody asked him to. It took longer than it should have, because he wrote the citation himself instead of giving it to a clerk.”

“I didn’t know that.”

He paused. “You weren’t meant to. And on your last night in camp, he sent me for your report and told me to stand guard outside the tent and let nobody in. I’ve stood guard outside that tent for nine years. He’s never once asked me to keep people out.”

The cold went right through her wrap. She didn’t notice it.

“He’s spent three years putting what he feels about you in its proper box. He labelled it. He managed it. He worked very well round it. Then he walked into that room upstairs and watched you work for an hour, and from what I can see the box has stopped closing. I’m not telling you this so you’ll do anything. I’m telling you so you know what’s happening. Accurately. Instead of guessing at him through whatever you think is possible,” said Chen Ye.

“And what is possible?”

Chen Ye looked back at the inn door. “I don’t know. He’s never been here before. Neither have you. There are real things in the way. His rank. The Emperor. His sense of duty, which isn’t a performance. It’s who he is. But I’ve served him for nine years, and I had never seen him move a chair.”

She looked at him. He looked back, with the face of a man who’d said his one true thing and was finished.

He was formal again, at once, a man ending a professional conversation. “Good evening, Physician. I understand the Commander continues to improve.”

“He does. Good evening, Captain.”

Her voice shook at the edges. She hoped the dark hid it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat in the carriage with the lanterns of Qingzhou going past the little window, and breathed slowly, and let herself think, for the first time since her father had come to the clinic door, about what she was doing.

Not the medicine. The medicine was real and important and exactly what she said it was. The other thing. The thing she’d been carrying beside the medicine all week like a second lamp she was trying not to look at.

She’d built something in three years. She was a physician people knew by name. She wasn’t the girl who’d hidden in a supply box because a man on a horse had done something to her chest. She was the woman who’d turned that into a clinic, and records, and a dyer’s well closed in time.

She was also, under all of it, someone who hadn’t once in three years felt anything for anyone else. She’d tried, honestly. Her mother had brought her four proposals, and she’d read every one of them, and put each one back in its envelope. She’d been open, she thought, to the idea that someone in Qingzhou might matter to her. Nobody had.

Little Lan was waiting up at the residence, with tea and an expression.

“Well, Miss?”

“Well what?”

“Did he say anything today?”

“He asked about the dressing. And the rain.”

“The rain?”

“Fevers. After floods. It’s on page nine.”

Little Lan sat down on the end of the bed. “Miss. Has he kissed you?”

Shiyu put the tea down carefully. “Why would you ask that?”

“Because you came home from the north three years ago and slept with a notebook under your pillow, and I’m the one who changes the pillows.”

There was a long silence.

“Once. Three years ago. The night before I left,” said Shiyu.

Little Lan’s hands flew to her mouth. “Miss!”

“Don’t tell the kitchen.”

“I’d never—”

“Don’t tell Mei Yun.”

Little Lan leaned forward. “Mei Yun already knows, Miss, she’s been looking at you like a cat at a fish since the first day at the inn. And now?”

Shiyu lay back on the bed and looked at the painted ceiling. “And now he’s in my city, and he’s moved a chair, and he reads my summary until the lamp runs out, and he hasn’t said one word about that night. Neither have I. Tomorrow is the fifth day. If the leg is ready, I’ll clear Commander Zhou to travel. And then they’ll all go to the capital, and Qingzhou will go back to selling fish.”

“Will you say something?”

“I don’t know.”

“Miss you hid in a box for three days. You can say something,” said Little Lan, very seriously.

She lay awake an hour after she should have been asleep. In the dark she found that what kept her awake wasn’t worry or sadness, but something she didn’t have a clean word for: the feeling of standing at the edge of something whose shape she could sense but not yet see, the way important things sometimes make themselves known before they arrive.

She slept in the end. She woke early. She dressed with care, and Little Lan, without a word, put her grandmother’s jade comb into her hair, and she let her.

Then she went to the inn for the fifth day.

chapters.title: The Fifth Day
chapters.desc: The officer is fit to travel, the General asks for all of her records, and the plum tree sees a second kiss.
chapters.epigraph: “Because none of them read my reports all the way to the end.”
chapters.content:
She was slow and thorough that morning. She took the wound through every step, checked it against her notes from the first day, measured the healing against what she’d expected, and looked for the signs that said the flesh was strong enough for a careful journey.

It was ready. She’d known from the evening before that it would be, but knowing and confirming weren’t the same thing.

She stood back. All five of them were in the room that morning, which hadn’t happened once before. She noticed it and said nothing. The General was by the window in the morning light.

“Well? Am I going to the capital or am I staying here to be fed soup by the Vice-Commander for the rest of my life?” said Zhou Hua.

“You’re going to the capital.”

Zhou Hua lay back and addressed the ceiling with feeling. “Thank every god in the sky.”

She looked round the room. “By carriage. Stop every two hours. No weight on the leg, none, not even to get down for the latrine. Someone carries you. I’ll write out the instructions for the road, and a letter for my uncle with the wound’s state, so he knows what he’s getting.”

“He’ll have it,” said Lü Yue, in the voice of a man who never said anything he couldn’t stand behind.

“And the methods summary. The final version. You said you’d have it ready,” said Lin Wenyuan.

“Tonight. It needs one more pass. It’ll be here before you leave. My uncle will have opinions about it, and I’d rather he had them about the finished version.”

Lin Wenyuan almost smiled. It was the first time she’d seen him do even that much.

She turned to go, and then turned back. It was becoming a habit, at the doors of that inn, and she couldn’t seem to stop it.

“General. I wanted to say thank you. For the attribution in the camp records, three years ago. My uncle told me it was formally entered, with my name. I don’t think I thanked you properly at the time. I had a great many other things to manage that morning.”

“You thanked me.”

“I thanked you correctly. I’m not sure I thanked you really.”

“It was deserved,” said the General.

It neither accepted the thanks nor brushed it away: the plain fact, the thing he’d always say, on its merits.

“I know. It still mattered to me,” said Shiyu.

She had her hand on the door when he spoke again.

“Your clinic records. The three years. Would you send copies to the camp? Not only the summary. All of them.”

“All of them,” she repeated.

“If you can spare a clerk.”

“I’ll copy them myself,” said Shiyu, and wished she’d said it a little less quickly.

Behind her, Zhou Hua made a noise like a kettle. Wei Tiecheng hit him with a pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was halfway across the inn’s back courtyard, under the bare plum tree by the well, when she heard footsteps behind her that she’d have known anywhere. She stopped. She didn’t turn round.

“You forgot this,” said the General.

He was holding out her brush case. She hadn’t forgotten it. She’d left it on the table by the moved chair, on purpose or not on purpose, she honestly didn’t know.

She took it. Their fingers didn’t touch, and somehow it was worse than if they had.

“Thank you.”

He didn’t go. He stood under the plum tree with his hands behind his back, looking at her the way he’d looked at her across the brazier three years ago, and the courtyard was empty except for a cat on the well cover and the smell of someone’s breakfast.

“You haven’t mentioned it,” he said.

“Mentioned what?”

“The night before you left the camp.”

Her heart did what it always did. “Neither have you.”

His voice was even, which she’d learned meant it wasn’t even at all. “I didn’t know whether you’d want me to. Three years is a long time. You were eighteen. You’d done one foolish brave thing and then you’d gone home and done a great many sensible ones. I thought you might have decided the foolish one was a mistake.”

“I put four proposals back in their envelopes.”

He went still.

“My mother brought me four. In three years. A magistrate’s son. A salt merchant’s nephew. A scholar who sent me a poem about my eyebrows. And a widower with two children who needed a mother more than a wife. I read every one of them, because she asked me to. And then I put them back in their envelopes, every time,” said Shiyu.

“Why?”

She looked up at him. She’d told him the truth on the first day, in front of everyone. She could tell him the truth now, under a plum tree, with only a cat for a witness.

“Because none of them read my reports all the way to the end.”

For three heartbeats his face did the thing it had done in the command tent: it showed her everything, and he didn’t stop it. Then he stepped forward and put one hand against her cheek, the same careful hand, and kissed her.

The first time had been a question. This was an answer three years coming, slower and surer, and she held on to the front of his tunic with the hand that wasn’t holding the brush case and kissed him back until the cat got bored and left. When he drew back he didn’t go far.

“I can’t write to you. Not yet. Not without a reason anyone could read. You’re the governor’s daughter. I’m a man your father has met once,” he said, against her hair.

“I know.”

“I’ll write to your uncle.”

“Then I’ll read to the end,” said Shiyu.

He laughed. It was low and short and completely unexpected, and she’d never heard it before, and she thought she’d probably be willing to hide in a great many boxes to hear it again.

“Go and see your patients. Before Chen Ye comes looking for me and finds out he was right,” he said.

“He already knows he was right.”

“I know he does. I’d rather he didn’t see it.”

She went. She walked back through the morning streets of Qingzhou, which smelled the way they always did of river water and osmanthus and a city that had been growing medicine for a hundred years, and she breathed all of it in.

He wanted her records. All of them. He hadn’t asked through Lin Wenyuan or through her uncle. He’d asked himself. And then he’d followed her into a courtyard with a brush case she hadn’t forgotten.

She saw her afternoon patients. At dinner her father asked how the Commander was doing, and she answered calmly and ate Cook’s congee, and her mother looked at her face and then at her father, and her father looked at the ceiling.

Afterwards she lit the lamp in her room and took out the methods summary for its last pass. She worked until midnight. She made it excellent.

At dawn she sent Mei Yun to the inn with it, and the first bundle of copied records, tied with cord. Mei Yun came back an hour later with a small, flat parcel wrapped in plain cloth.

“From the General, Miss. He said it’s for the clinic, and you’re not to read anything into it.”

It was a new mortar, white stone, heavy, with no crack anywhere inside it.

chapters.title: What Arrives Three Days Later
chapters.desc: The General hears about a cracked mortar, and her uncle’s letter ends with a commission.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t know he’d tell anyone! I thought he was being polite!”
chapters.content:
On the morning of the sixth day the procession gathered in the inn courtyard to leave. She wasn’t there to see it. Her morning patients came first, the way they always did. The clinic door opened at the usual hour, and Old Master Feng was waiting on the bench with his bad knee and a cloth bundle of persimmons.

“You’re late,” he said.

“I’m exactly on time.”

He looked at her over the persimmons. “You’re usually early. You’ve been early every day for two years. The army’s leaving this morning. Half the street’s gone to the avenue to watch.”

“Then it’s a good morning to have your knee seen without a queue. Sit down.”

She treated his knee as carefully as it deserved and accepted the persimmons as graciously as they deserved, and she didn’t cross the city to the Jade Phoenix to watch a procession ride away.

Mei Yun said nothing about it. She had the tact to know that some silences were worth more than anything she could observe. She lasted until the middle of the afternoon.

“Miss. Can I tell you something?”

“Is it about the persimmons?”

“It’s about the mortar.”

Shiyu put down the record book. Mei Yun was standing in the doorway of the back room, twisting a bandage round her fingers.

“On the second day at the inn the one who leans on walls asked me what the clinic needed. I thought he meant for the accounts. I told him a new mortar, because ours is cracked inside, near the lip,” said Mei Yun.

“You told Chen Ye about the mortar.”

“I didn’t know he’d tell anyone! I thought he was being polite!”

“Chen Ye is never only being polite.”

Mei Yun looked stricken and delighted at the same time, which was a thing only Mei Yun’s face could do. “I know that now, Miss. Are you angry?”

Shiyu looked at the new mortar on the shelf, white and heavy, with its perfect unbroken inside. “No. I’m not angry.”

In the quiet after the last patient that evening she stood in the preparation room and let herself feel it. Mei Yun was wiping down the bench, and didn’t pretend not to be watching.

“You’ve been standing there since the bell, Miss.”

“I’m thinking.”

“About the officer’s leg?”

“About the officer’s leg. Which healed. And the records, which I sent. And the courtyard,” said Shiyu.

Mei Yun wrung out her cloth. “And the plum tree. The cat saw everything. I saw the cat.”

“He’s riding north with eleven thousand men and an Emperor waiting, Mei Yun. I don’t know when I’ll see him again. I don’t know how. I don’t know whether anything a governor’s daughter and the Emperor’s nephew want could ever be something a court would allow.”

“Then don’t know it tonight. Know it in the morning. You’re always cleverer in the morning,” said Mei Yun.

Shiyu turned to Mei Yun, who was rolling bandages. “If nothing comes of it, I’ll still have known something real. What it’s like to care about someone that much, and to be cared about back. That isn’t nothing, even if it doesn’t go anywhere.”

She said it in the steady voice she kept for exactly this, and she meant it.

Mei Yun didn’t look up. “Of course, Miss.”

“You don’t believe me.”

“I believe you mean it, Miss.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No, Miss,” said Mei Yun, and kept rolling.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days after the procession left, a letter came by the military post. It came in through the garrison at the east gate with the camp’s seal on it, addressed to the Qingcloud Medical Hall in the stiff phrases of an official dispatch.

She opened it at the writing table, alone, early, before the clinic opened. It was from her uncle. Three pages, full of exactly what she’d expected: detailed opinions on the methods summary, questions about how she’d counted, two suggestions for extra controls, and a note of real appreciation for the three-year view, which he said filled a gap in the camp’s records he’d been trying to fill for years. It was the kind of letter her uncle wrote when a problem had got its teeth into him.

On the last page, after the method was done with, there was a small space, and then a paragraph.

The General went through your summary himself before he passed it to me. He made three notes in the margin, which I’ve marked for you. He asked me to tell you that your figures are going into the camp’s formal records as a comparative study, credited in full to the Qingcloud Medical Hall and to you by name.
He also asked, and I note that he asked me to put it in a letter rather than in any official record, which is a choice worth noticing, whether you were well. Whether the clinic was well. Whether Qingzhou suited you.
I told him you were more than well. I told him the clinic was excellent. I told him Qingzhou suits you the way a place always suits a person who has built something in it.
He didn’t answer that. But the next morning, in the daily medical council, he asked me whether the civilian medical commission I’ve been proposing for two years had any suitable candidates from outside the capital.
I haven’t answered him yet. I thought you should know he’d asked.

She read it twice. Then she put it down on the table, carefully, and looked at the wall.

A civilian medical commission. Suitable candidates from outside the capital.

He couldn’t write to her. He’d said so, under the plum tree. Not without a reason anyone could read. So he’d gone and found one. Not a reason to court her. A reason to work with her, in the open, with letters that any clerk in the army could read and find nothing in but records and method.

“Mei Yun!”

Mei Yun appeared in the doorway so fast she must have been standing just outside it. “Miss?”

“What would you say to the clinic having a second physician? If I had to be away sometimes. For work.”

Mei Yun’s eyes went wide. “Away where, Miss?”

“North. Perhaps. Sometimes. For a commission.”

“A commission with the army,” said Mei Yun slowly.

“With the army’s civilian medical office. Which doesn’t exist yet.”

“Which the General’s thinking about.”

“Which my uncle has been proposing for two years.”

“Which the General asked your uncle about three days after he left,” said Mei Yun.

Shiyu didn’t answer. Mei Yun put both hands over her mouth, and then took them away.

“I’d say yes, Miss. I’d say I could run the massage days on my own already, and the boatwomen like me, and Little Lan can do the accounts if I teach her the abacus properly. I’d say go.”

Shiyu picked up her brush. She opened a fresh sheet. She thought for a while about the right thing to say in a letter to her uncle about method, if you also wanted to answer a question that had been asked in a different letter, through a different person, so that nobody could ever point at it.

At the end of her long reply about controls and counting, she left a small space, and wrote:

Please tell the General that I’m very well. The clinic is excellent. And that if the commission he mentioned needs a physician who has been building a careful way of tracking a city’s health, I’d like to talk about what that might involve.

She sealed it. She took it to the garrison herself instead of sending Mei Yun, and handed it over the counter to the clerk, and watched him put it in the northern bag.

She walked back through the morning with her hands at her sides and the cold air on her face and something rising in her chest that wasn’t certainty and wasn’t the end of anything. It was, if she was honest, the first beginning of a beginning, the kind that could still come to nothing. It would need patience, and work, and being willing to stay inside not knowing for as long as it took.

She’d had practice. Three years of it, and eleven before that, and a whole other life before that, which had taught her, among a great many other things, that the work worth doing was almost never quick.

She turned the corner into the clinic’s street. Old Shen’s sign caught the morning light over the door: Qingcloud Medical Hall, in clear even strokes, in the blue her mother had chosen.

She stopped and looked at it. Then she went in, and opened the clinic for the day.

chapters.title: The Letter He Writes Himself
chapters.desc: For the first time, the handwriting on the letter is his.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s very long for entirely about the commission. You’ve been reading it for a quarter of an hour.”
chapters.content:
The appointment came first, in the deep of the winter: a heavy document with the army’s seal on it and her name in it, Yun Shiyu, Chief Civilian Physician to the Civilian Medical Commission of the Northern Army.

She read it twice standing up in her outdoor coat, still damp from a house call in the river district. Then she took off the coat, made tea, and sat down with it.

“Is it real?” said Little Lan, hovering.

“It’s real.”

“Does it say Fairy Physician?”

“It says Chief Civilian Physician.”

“That’s longer. Longer is better,” said Little Lan, pleased.

Her father came down from the residence at midday with ink on both sleeves, having heard, because the garrison clerk’s wife bought her vegetables from Cook’s cousin and nothing in Qingzhou stayed secret past lunch.

“Show me.”

She gave it to him. He read it standing in the doorway with his spectacles pushed up on his forehead, which meant he wasn’t reading the words so much as looking at the seal.

“Chief Civilian Physician,” he said.

“Yes, Father.”

“To the Northern Army.”

“To its civilian commission. It’s new. I’d still be here most of the year. I’d go north for the seasonal reviews.”

“And who suggested this commission should look outside the capital for its physicians?”

“Uncle has been proposing it for two years.”

Her father handed the document back. “Your uncle has been proposing a great many things for two years. Nobody listened to any of them until this autumn. You’ll need a proper case for your papers. Something that doesn’t let in the rain.”

“Father.”

He looked at her over the top of his spectacles, and his face did the thing it had done her whole life, fond and bewildered and very proud. “Your mother will want to choose it. Let her. Three years ago you hid in a box.”

“I remember.”

“I’m glad the box was the right size,” said Yun Chengde, and went back up the hill to tell his wife.

Three years of work, and someone who mattered had seen all of it, for the right reasons. She was still sitting with that when the second letter came.

It wasn’t from her uncle. She knew the handwriting on the outside before Mei Yun had even put it down. She’d seen it in the margins of her own summary, three notes, small and precise. She’d looked at those three notes for longer than she would ever admit to anyone.

Mei Yun set the letter on the cleared end of the preparation table with enormous care, as though it might go off.

“I’ll finish the compound, Miss,” she said, and took the pestle out of Shiyu’s hands before she was asked.

Shiyu carried the letter to the writing table. She opened it steadily; her hands had never been the problem. One page. His own hand, not a secretary’s. She knew the difference: the characters pressed a little closer when he wrote fast, and spread when he was being careful. He’d been careful.

To Chief Civilian Physician Yun, at the Qingcloud Medical Hall.
Your appointment is confirmed by the Emperor’s seal and takes effect at the new year. You will report to the Chief Physician of the Northern Army on matters of method, and to the commission on matters of structure. The camp’s records officer is Lin Wenyuan. You have met him.
Direct letters on this channel are appropriate where they concern the commission’s method or structure. The Chief Physician has been told.
Zhan Lingyun

She read the last part three times.

He’d made a channel between them. Not through her uncle: between them. And he’d told her uncle, which meant it wasn’t hidden. He’d decided, the careful way he decided everything, that this was something he was willing to have known. Nobody had made him. He had clerks and secretaries and every sort of official distance at his disposal, and he’d set them all aside and written to her in his own hand, and then made it a matter of record so that no one could ever say it was improper.

“Well?” said Mei Yun, from the doorway, holding the pestle.

“It’s about the commission.”

“Of course it is, Miss.”

“It’s entirely about the commission.”

“It’s very long for entirely about the commission. You’ve been reading it for a quarter of an hour.”

“It’s one page.”

“Yes, Miss,” said Mei Yun, and went back to grinding before Shiyu could throw something.

She was twenty-one, not eighteen, and not on a balcony any more. And she was still exactly as undone by him as she’d ever been.

She wrote back that same afternoon. Two real questions about how he wanted the records laid out. A note about the clinic’s baseline figures that the commission would need. And at the end, in exactly the same voice as everything above it:

The clinic’s records begin in the month it opened, two years and four months ago. They include season-by-season figures the commission’s current baseline doesn’t capture. If the structure can take an expanded baseline, the first seasonal report will be more useful. Please advise.
Yun Shiyu

She read it over. It was correct and useful and entirely about method. She looked at it a while longer and then, under her name, in smaller characters, added one more line.

The mortar is excellent. It has no cracks at all.

She sealed it before she could change her mind. She carried it to the garrison herself, because using the channel wasn’t too soon and she’d decided that two readings ago, and walked back through the winter streets. The osmanthus trees were bare. The river district smelled of cold stone and water slowing towards ice. She passed Old Shen’s workshop, the herb market, the corner where Old Master Feng sat with his persimmons when the weather was better.

He’d written it himself. He’d made a channel and told her uncle and called it administrative. She knew exactly what that was.

At dinner her mother asked careful questions about the appointment, and Shiyu answered them honestly, and watched her mother’s eyes, and didn’t comment on what she saw in them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four days later, before dawn, in the camp office, he read her letter.

He read it once. He put it down. He read it again.

The questions about the records were exact. She’d found the same two gaps in the commission’s rules that Lin Wenyuan had flagged a month ago and he hadn’t yet fixed. She’d found them in four days from a single reading. He drafted the corrections before breakfast. Then he read the last line again.

Chen Ye came in with the morning tea and found him sitting at the table with the letter in one hand, not reading it, looking at the wall.

“Bad news from Qingzhou, General?”

“No.”

“The commission?”

“The mortar has no cracks at all,” said the General.

Chen Ye set down the tea carefully. He said nothing. He’d made a career of knowing when to say nothing.

The General wrote back that afternoon, which wasn’t his usual hour for letters. He answered her questions and confirmed the expanded baseline. At the end he wrote a line, and crossed it out, and wrote it again, and sent it.

The records format is at your discretion. You know them better than the commission’s rules do.

He sealed it and gave it to the dispatch rider himself. Chen Ye, who happened to be in the corridor at exactly that moment, watched the rider go and went back to his own desk, where he allowed himself the small private expression of a man who was entirely pleased with how a particular story was going.

“Something amusing, Captain?” said Lin Wenyuan, passing.

“The weather,” said Chen Ye.

Lin Wenyuan looked out of the window at the sleet, and then at Chen Ye, and then, being Lin Wenyuan, wrote something down.

chapters.title: Two Weeks
chapters.desc: The letters come every two weeks, she locks a drawer, and her mother airs the green coat.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve got a drawer that you lock now.”
chapters.content:
The letters came every two weeks. The northern dispatch ran weekly. He wrote every second one. Four weeks would have been plenty for the commission’s business. She didn’t let herself ask why he’d chosen two, and put the answer in the box of things she understood without needing to explain. She wrote back on the same rhythm. She stopped pretending she didn’t watch for the garrison runner.

Every letter was about the commission, and every word of the commission part was real. And every letter, at the end, had one line that wasn’t only about the commission.

The Vice-Commander has asked me to tell you he is eating real food. I have not seen him do it.

Lü Yue read your rain column twice and then went to look at the camp’s own well. He says nothing about it. He has moved the latrines again.

It snowed here last night. The river froze at the edges. I thought of yours.

She kept them in the drawer of her writing table, in order. Not with the rest of the commission papers.

“You’ve got a drawer,” said Mei Yun, in the second month.

“I’ve always had a drawer.”

“You’ve got a drawer that you lock now.”

“Papers can be confidential.”

“Commission papers go in the commission box on the shelf, Miss. I file them. That drawer has eleven letters in it and you take them out at night.”

“How do you know there are eleven?”

“Because there have been eleven and you haven’t put one of them in the box,” said Mei Yun.

✦ ✦ ✦

One evening in the second month, her mother came and stood in the doorway of the back room while Shiyu was going over the season’s figures by lamplight.

“You’ve been at that for three hours.”

“The seasonal report is due next week.”

“You finished the seasonal report two days ago. I watched you seal it.”

Shiyu put down her brush. Her mother came in and sat on Mei Yun’s stool, the one by the grinding table, and folded her hands in her lap and looked at her daughter with twenty-one years of plain, loving attention.

“I’m not going to ask you anything. I’m going to say one thing, and then I’m going to bed,” said Lady Ren.

“Mother—”

“I’ve watched you for twenty-one years. I watched you the day you came home from that camp at eighteen and wrote in your little notebook for an hour and said nothing to anyone. I watched you put four perfectly good proposals back in their envelopes and thank me for every one of them. I’ve watched you build something extraordinary for three years and tell everyone, yourself included, that the building was enough.”

“It is enough.”

Her mother stood up and smoothed her skirt. “It is. You’re right. A life like yours would be enough for almost anyone. But for two months I’ve also watched you write letters at the window in the morning light. I know you, Shiyu. You don’t write anything at that window unless it matters to you.”

Shiyu opened her mouth, and found she had nothing to put in it.

Her mother went to the door. Then she stopped, with the timing Shiyu had inherited from her and never once used as well, and turned round.

“When you go to the capital, wear the green coat. And your grandmother’s jade hairpin. And for once in your life let someone see you wanting something,” said Lady Ren.

“Who says I’m going to the capital?”

Her mother’s face did something complicated. “Your uncle. In a letter to your father. There’s to be a presentation at court when the commission’s first year is finished. Your father’s been unbearable about it for a week. He thinks they might let him into the Imperial Library. And the General’s household has written to the garrison to arrange our passage. All of us. So that we don’t have to arrange our own.”

“The General’s household?”

Her mother looked at her. “Captain Chen. Very polite. He spelled your father’s name correctly, which nobody from the capital has managed in twenty years. Good night, Shiyu.”

“Good night, Mother.”

She sat alone in the lamplight afterwards with the quiet all round her: the clinic smell, the sound of Qingzhou settling into the night, a boatman calling something to another boatman down on the river. She let herself think about what she’d been carefully not thinking about for two months.

She was moving towards him. She’d been moving towards him since she wrote the first letter on the channel he’d made and walked it to the garrison herself. She wasn’t waiting any more. She was going.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took out her brush. It was a commission week, and the letter she wrote was about commission business, every line of it, except the last.

My mother says I’m to wear the green coat in the capital. I’m telling you so that you’ll know it was her idea, and not mine.

The answer came back two weeks later, at the end of a long and dry page about the funding schedule.

Your mother is correct. I have no objection to the coat. I have no objection to any of it.

She read it at the window, because the light was better there.

Then she went and found her mother, who was supervising the lanterns in the front courtyard, and stood beside her for a while in silence, watching the lamplighter on his ladder.

“Mother.”

“Mm.”

“Where’s the green coat?”

Lady Ren didn’t look round. But Shiyu saw the corner of her mouth move, in exactly the way that someone else’s did, and she thought: so that’s where I learned to see it.

“In the cedar chest. I had it aired last week. Just in case,” said her mother.

chapters.title: What the Emperor Hears
chapters.desc: The Emperor asks one question about the physician, and his nephew remembers a page from an eleven-year-old report.
chapters.epigraph: “Tell me about the consulting physician.”
chapters.content:
The private audience lasted longer than approving the commission needed.

That was the part that mattered. Approving it took less time than a cup of tea takes to cool. It was a well-built proposal with good evidence behind it and no politics in it. Emperor Zhan Hong read it, signed it, put it to one side, and then said, in the tone that was never quite as idle as it sounded, “Tell me about the consulting physician.”

Zhan Lingyun answered.

“She opened her clinic at nineteen. Her own records are its founding documents. Her method of cleaning wounds cut deaths after the eastern engagement by a third while she was in the camp, three years ago. Her three years of records are the most careful civilian health records in the province. The circulation treatment her assistant uses is in the northern field manual now, and we’ve used it on forty-one men this season. She tracks fever against the river floods. Twelve to sixteen days. Nobody else in the empire has thought to count it.”

He kept going. He didn’t notice, until several sentences later, that he hadn’t stopped.

The Emperor listened, and let him keep going. He’d been managing men for thirty years and understood that what a man doesn’t know he’s telling you is the most accurate thing he’ll ever tell you.

Because his nephew never ran on. In sixteen years, since the boy had come to live in the palace at fifteen with his father two months dead and his face like a closed door, the Emperor had never once heard him say more words than a situation required. His reports were models of compression. He answered the question and stopped. He wasn’t stopping.

“She thinks in a way I’ve never seen. As if she’d already read a book none of us has. I don’t know where she learned it. I’ve stopped expecting to find out,” said Zhan Lingyun.

The Emperor turned a page he wasn’t reading. “You find that troubling?”

“I find it interesting.”

“Interesting.”

“Yes, Majesty.”

The Emperor put the page down. In sixteen years of watching his nephew make his way through a palace full of people who wanted things from him, he’d learned to hear the reckoning underneath everything Lingyun said about anyone: the constant low weighing of threat and motive. There was no cruelty in it, only the scaffolding a boy builds when he’s been orphaned into a house of wolves.

There was none of it here. There was only forty-one men and a field manual and a column for rain, and something Chen Ye had mentioned to him months ago in a corridor, sideways and deniably and entirely accurately, about three heartbeats in a command tent.

“The commission’s first year should be presented at court when it ends. In person. A written report won’t carry the weight. The officials who hold the purse for the expansion need to hear it from her own mouth,” said the Emperor.

There was a pause. A short one: the pause of a man taking in information.

“I’ll tell the commission staff, Majesty.”

The Emperor picked up the next document. “Good. And include the Yun household in the invitation. The physician’s family. It’s the proper courtesy for a commission of this size. Qingzhou is a fine city. I’ve always thought it was undervisited.”

“Yes, Majesty.”

“Lingyun.”

His nephew stopped at the door.

“Your wrist. The one you set yourself in the field and let a physician reset afterwards. Does it trouble you?” said the Emperor, without looking up.

“No, Majesty.”

“Who reset it?”

“The Chief Physician.”

“And who has been checking it since?” said the Emperor, still reading.

There was a silence by the door that lasted exactly one breath too long.

“Go. Before I think of another question,” said the Emperor.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the corridor outside, Chen Ye fell in at his shoulder. “The audience ran long.”

“His Majesty had questions about the commission.”

“Of course he did. He ordered an in-person presentation, I hear.”

“It’s standard for a commission of this size.”

Chen Ye looked into the middle distance with the face of a man composing a sentence in his head and finding it extremely satisfying. “Entirely standard. And the household?”

“He wants the Yun family invited. All of them.”

“Shall I arrange it?”

“Through the Qingzhou garrison. Make sure they don’t have to arrange their own passage. The road north of the river is bad in spring. Find out which of the relay stations still have decent rooms.”

“Yes, General.”

“And the Governor has been trying to get into the Imperial Medical Library for eleven years.”

Chen Ye didn’t break stride. “Has he?”

“The Tang classifications. The originals. He wrote to the library twice and they lost both letters.”

“How do you know that, General?”

“It’s in the Governor’s annual report. Eleven years ago. Page forty.”

Chen Ye walked on in silence for some time. “Shall I arrange that as well?”

“I’ll do it myself,” said Zhan Lingyun.

Chen Ye said nothing for the rest of the corridor, which was long. In the privacy of his own head he was so pleased he could barely walk straight.

They reached the stairs. Lin Wenyuan was coming up them with a stack of dispatches, and stopped, and looked at Chen Ye’s face, and then at the General’s back going on ahead, and then at Chen Ye again.

“What happened?”

“He talked,” said Chen Ye.

“For how long?”

“Long enough that His Majesty asked about his wrist.”

Lin Wenyuan considered this. Then he took a brush from behind his ear, and opened the top dispatch, and in the margin, in his beautiful calligraphy, wrote a date.

chapters.title: Three Months
chapters.desc: Six drafts, a library pass for her father, and a question he’d like a day to think about.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody reads the annual report. I’m not sure the prefecture reads the annual report.”
chapters.content:
The presentation was set for the third month of the new year. Three months away. Shiyu wrote the date in her planning book in exactly the same hand she used for seasonal reports and the spring rush of coughs, and gave it exactly the same weight. She knew that wasn’t entirely honest.

The letters kept coming every two weeks. The commission questions were real, and she worked at them properly. But in the last lines, the ones that weren’t only about the commission, something had changed. Not in what he said: in the weight of it, like the shift in the air before the weather turns.

In the sixth week she sent him the first draft of her court presentation, because the commission said he had to review it. She sent five more after that, because every one came back with notes down the margins in his hand, and the notes were always better than the draft deserved.

“Sixth draft,” said Mei Yun, sealing it.

“The commission requires review.”

“Of every draft?”

“Of the final draft.”

“This isn’t the final draft, Miss. You said that about the fourth one.”

“Seal it, please.”

In the eighth week, at the end:

The cold-weather notes from your camp records went to every medical tent this winter. They held. Fevers down again.

In the tenth week:

The river worker from your third case. His outcome is in the commission’s baseline now. You were right to include him. Nobody will ever be able to say a leg like that should come off without reading about his.

In the twelfth week there was nothing at the end at all: only the commission business, clean and professional. She read the place where the last line should have been three times, and told herself it meant nothing, and didn’t believe herself.

“Is something wrong, Miss?” said Little Lan.

“No.”

“You’ve been looking at the bottom of that page since breakfast.”

“There’s nothing at the bottom of it.”

“That’s what I mean,” said Little Lan.

Two days later another letter came. Not on the commission channel: by the ordinary military post, addressed to the Qingcloud Medical Hall, formal and correct, with the commission’s seal. But the hand on the outside was his.

She opened it at the window, because her mother was apparently right about the window.

The presentation will be on the ninth day of the third month. The garrison will bring your household north. Rooms have been taken for you in the eastern quarter. You will not be asked to arrange anything.
The Governor has been granted access to the Imperial Medical Library for the length of his stay. The Tang classifications are held in the inner room. The librarian has been told to expect him, and to bring him tea, and to not, under any circumstances, lose his letter.
Zhan Lingyun

She read it twice. He hadn’t needed to think about her father at all. Inviting the household was already more than the bare minimum. And then, separately, he’d found out what her father had been trying to reach for eleven years and made it happen. And he’d told the librarian not to lose the letter.

She thought about a moved chair in an inn. A method entered in the records under her name before anyone asked. A white mortar with no crack in it.

He’d been doing this the whole time, through the proper channels, with the proper reasons, every one of which also happened to be exactly what she needed.

“Mei Yun. Where’s my father?”

“At the residence, Miss. Copying something. He’s been copying it since dawn.”

“Close the clinic for an hour.”

“We’ve got the boatman’s mother at—”

“Close it for an hour.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yun Chengde was in his study with ink to the elbows and the same herb text he’d been fighting with for eleven years open in front of him. He looked up when she came in, and took his spectacles off.

“Is someone hurt?”

“No. Father, read this.”

She gave him the letter. He read it once, quickly, the way he read anything that looked official. Then he read the second paragraph again, slowly. Then he put the letter down on top of the herb text and took off his spectacles again, though they were already off, and looked at them in his hand.

“The inner room,” he said.

“Yes.”

“The originals.”

“Yes, Father.”

“I wrote to them. Twice. They lost both letters.”

“I know. So does he.”

Her father looked at the letter. “How does he know that?”

“It was in your annual report. Eleven years ago.”

“Nobody reads the annual report. I’m not sure the prefecture reads the annual report.”

“He read it,” said Shiyu.

Her father didn’t say anything. He put the letter down gently, and smoothed it flat with his ink-stained fingers, and then he stood up and went to the window and stood with his back to her for a while. When he turned round his eyes were wet.

“He told the librarian to bring me tea,” said Yun Chengde.

“I saw.”

He wiped his eyes with the back of his sleeve, and left a streak of ink across his cheek, and didn’t notice. “Nobody’s ever told anyone to bring me tea. Shiyu. This young man.”

“Yes, Father?”

“Is he going to ask me something? In the capital?”

The question went through her like cold water. “I don’t know.”

“Hm. If he does, I’d like a day to think about it,” said her father, and looked at the ceiling, and then at her, and then sat down again.

“A day?”

“Your mother will want three. I’ll want one. And then I expect we’ll say what we always say to you, which is yes, eventually, because you’re always right in the end. Go back to your clinic. I have eleven years of questions to write down before the ninth day of the third month,” said her father, picking up his brush.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wrote back on the commission channel. She answered every commission question first, properly. And at the end:

My father has been trying to read those books for eleven years. He cried. He got ink on his face. I wanted you to know it reached the right person.

She sealed it and took it to the garrison herself, and walked home through the winter morning. Her mother was at the gate with a basket of winter greens.

“You’ve been to the garrison.”

“I’ve written to the General. About the presentation.”

“About the presentation,” said Lady Ren, in a voice with no opinion in it at all.

Shiyu took the basket from her. “And about Father’s library pass. And about the green coat. Mother. I’m not only going to the capital to present.”

“I know.”

“I’m going to him. And I’m going as myself. Not the girl on the balcony. Not the girl in the box.”

Her mother looked at her, and then reached up and tucked a strand of hair behind her daughter’s ear, the way she had when Shiyu was small.

“Good. The girl in the box would have worn the wrong coat,” said Lady Ren.

Three months. She was good at patience. She’d also, at last, stopped pretending it was only patience.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read her letter in the morning quiet and sat with the last paragraph for longer than he usually sat with anything. He wrote back that evening. Commission business first. Then:

I read your father’s survey of the regional herbs, in the Governor’s report, eleven years ago. It was careful work. He should have had the sources then.

He read it over once. He’d read a provincial governor’s annual report, years before he’d ever seen Qingzhou, and remembered it, and he was telling her so: no commission reason, no official cover. Only the plain fact of a man who’d read something and kept it.

He didn’t change a word. He sent it as it was.

chapters.title: The Capital
chapters.desc: A green coat, a jade hairpin, and the Emperor’s questions at dinner. He’s coming to Qingzhou first.
chapters.epigraph: “I know. I’ve read every page of it. Your father’s found his scholar.”
chapters.content:
The capital announced itself before anyone could see it. Shiyu had read about it all her life and built it in her head from pieces. What no book had given her was the size of it: the smell reaching the carriage first, cooking smoke and stone and something medicinal blowing from the Imperial Herb Market, and then the sound, the fullness of a city that never entirely went quiet.

Her mother sat beside her, managing her wonder with the composed dignity of a woman who had decided before leaving Qingzhou that she wouldn’t look overwhelmed. It was working about half the time.

“Close your mouth, Mother.”

“My mouth is closed.”

“It’s open. Very slightly. At the wall.”

“It’s a large wall,” said Lady Ren with dignity, and closed her mouth.

Her father hadn’t looked up from his notes since the north gate of Qingzhou four days ago. He had eleven years of questions written out in a fresh book and was adding to them at every relay station.

“Father, look. The Drum Tower.”

“In a moment.”

“You’ve been saying that since the river.”

“There’s a reference to fritillary bulb in the Tang texts that I’ve been wrong about since before you were born. In a moment,” said her father.

Mei Yun sat by the window and watched everything with her bright, storing attention, and occasionally said “Oh” under her breath.

The house was in the eastern quarter: white plaster, dark tiles, lanterns already lit at the gate in the grey afternoon. Her parents’ rooms looked south onto the garden, which she’d asked for through the garrison and which had been confirmed in two days by a desk she didn’t need to name. Her own room had the best light in the house: an eastern window, a south wall. Someone had chosen it with care.
