She unpacked. She put on the green coat and stood in front of the polished bronze mirror. Her mother came to the door and looked at her and said nothing at all, and then came in and pressed her grandmother’s jade hairpin into her hand.

“It suits you.”

“It’s the presentation coat. I’ll wear it tomorrow.”

“You’ll wear it tonight. There’s a dinner.”

“What dinner?”

Her mother turned her round by the shoulders and pinned the hair herself. “His Majesty’s dinner, for the commission and their families. In the smaller hall. The invitation came while you were unpacking. It was in Captain Chen’s handwriting. He’s the only man in the capital who can spell your father’s name.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went down. He was already there. She’d known he would be. She’d prepared for it for three months, the way she prepared for a difficult operation: know what you’re there to do, trust your training, trust yourself.

She came into the room and found him at once, not because she was looking but because she always knew where he was in a room, the way you know where the door is in a house you’ve lived in. He was across the hall, speaking to Lü Yue. He hadn’t seen her yet.

She went to her uncle first. He was near the Emperor’s end of the room, and he turned and took in the whole of her, his niece at twenty-one in the capital in the green coat and the jade, and for once his diagnostic face had nothing to diagnose.

“You look like someone who’s built something,” he said.

“I have.”

He put a hand on her arm. “I know. I’ve read every page of it. Your father’s found his scholar.”

From somewhere behind them came Yun Chengde’s voice, rising with joy, explaining to a startled court historian exactly why everyone had been wrong about fritillary for two hundred years.

“He’ll still be talking when the household goes to bed,” said Shiyu.

“He’ll still be talking when the household gets up,” said her uncle.

At the first course she found herself where the seating put her, and across the table and three places to the left was his profile. She was aware of him the way she’d been aware of him in rooms, and in letters, for three years.

Then the Emperor said, in the light voice of a man arranging something, “The wound-cleaning method in the field manual. Physician Yun. The mechanism interests me.”

The whole table turned to her. She answered. The Emperor asked good questions, better than most of the officials she’d face in the morning, and she answered them properly, because they deserved it.

“Why salt?”

“Because the things that make a wound rot don’t like it, Majesty. They don’t grow as well. Wine first to clean, salt water after to keep it clean.”

“And you knew this how?”

“I counted, Majesty.”

“Counted what?”

“Every wound I closed. Which ones went bad and which ones didn’t. Three in fifty with salt. One in five without.”

The Emperor put his cup down. “You counted every wound.”

“Every one I could. A physician who only counts the ones that get better is telling herself a story.”

The Emperor looked at her for a long while, and then turned his head a fraction and looked three places to the left. “Hm,” he said, to nobody, and went back to his soup.

At the edge of her eye, across the table, the profile had turned. Not towards her. In her direction.

She thought: the shrewdest man in this room isn’t the General.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, in the inner courtyard where the guests staying in the palace drifted out into the cool spring night, she was talking to one of the camp physicians when she felt someone at her left shoulder. Close enough to be deliberate. She finished her sentence, and turned.

He was standing at the angle she knew: near enough to be meaning it, at the distance of a man who had decided to speak to her and no one else.

“His Majesty was interested in the mechanism,” he said.

“He asked good questions.”

He paused. Somewhere inside, her father’s voice was explaining something, enthusiastically. “He always reads everything first. Then he asks. Your father found his conversation.”

“In about a breath. He’ll be talking till dawn.”

Something moved at the corner of his mouth. Not quite a smile. The nearest thing to one, and in person, in lantern light, on a spring night, it was a great deal more than she’d prepared for.

“The seasonal reviews. For the commission’s first year. In person. Records are easier to argue about across a table,” he said.

“I agree.”

“Alternating. Qingzhou and the capital.”

Alternating. He’d come to Qingzhou. Not only ask her to come to him; come to her city, the way he’d come to the Jade Phoenix, into the world she’d built.

“Qingzhou first,” she said.

He looked at her. Not his council face, not his careful professional face: the look of a man who has made a decision and is looking straight at the reason for it.

“Qingzhou first,” he agreed.

Across the courtyard Lin Wenyuan called his name with a question about the morning. He turned his head towards it. Then back to her, for one breath.

“Tomorrow,” he said.

She nodded. He went. Mei Yun materialised at her elbow as if she’d been folded into the shadows.

She let a pause go by. “I was on the other side of the courtyard, Miss. I couldn’t hear a word. I didn’t need to. He looked back. After the quiet one called him. Before he’d got halfway across. He looked back at you.”

Shiyu said nothing.

“Like you’re the one fixed point and everything else is just the map,” said Mei Yun.

She went inside. Shiyu stood in the courtyard a little longer and let herself feel exactly what she felt, without making it smaller. The capital was real. The presentation was tomorrow. The green coat was right. Her father was talking to a historian about bulbs, her mother had put a jade pin in her hair, and across the courtyard a man who’d read a provincial annual report eleven years ago and remembered it had just told her he was coming to Qingzhou.

Not for the commission. Or not only. She went in. She went through the case studies one last time, until the lamp burned low and she was satisfied. Then she slept.

chapters.title: The Presentation
chapters.desc: She stands before the court with three years of work and an appendix. Page seven.
chapters.epigraph: “Because the army’s medical service has measurably better outcomes since it took up the clinic’s methods.”
chapters.content:
She wore the green coat. The presentation hall was built to make people feel the weight of what was decided in it: high ceilings, stone floors, the proportions of a room that had held five hundred years of important outcomes. She noticed it, adjusted for it, and kept walking.

The Emperor was at the head of the long table. She’d known he might be. She hadn’t let herself picture it until she was standing in the room and the man her uncle called shrewd but not cruel was looking at her with the expression of someone who’d been told things about this physician and was now checking them.

She held herself properly. She met his eyes with the steadiness the room required. She didn’t look at the side of the hall.

“Nervous?” murmured her uncle, beside her.

“No.”

“Liar.”

“A little.”

“Good. The ones who aren’t nervous at court are the ones who’ve stopped paying attention.” He stood up to give the overview, and spoke for a quarter of an hour about the commission’s structure, and then turned and called her work something the army’s medical service had never seen before, and sat down.

She stood.

She’d known this material for three years. She’d built it from the inside. Every number she gave them had a patient behind it she could have named. Every conclusion was honest about what it showed and what it couldn’t show yet. She took the officials through the figures with nothing hidden, put the limits next to the strengths, and brought the case studies to life: not sentimentally, but with the plain weight of real people who had walked into her clinic one way and out of it another.

She felt proud. Not performing it: the clean, steady pride of someone showing work that’s exactly as good as she’s saying it is.

The cost section drew the most fire. A thin official near the end of the table, with a scholar’s stoop and a long grey beard, leaned forward.

“Physician Yun. Forgive me. Why should a provincial clinic physician be taken as a serious authority on the medical service of an imperial army?”

“Because the army’s medical service has measurably better outcomes since it took up the clinic’s methods. Page seven of the appendix. If you find it unpersuasive, I’d welcome a critique of the method.”

There was a short silence in the hall.

“Page seven,” said the Emperor, from the head of the table, mildly.

The official turned to page seven. He read it. He asked no more questions on that point. A younger man beside him asked about the cost of salt in a bad year, and she had the figures for that too, three bad years running, and the cost of the fevers it would have prevented set against it.

“You’ve costed the fevers?” said the young man.

“Every one I could count. A fever costs a man’s wages for the days he can’t work and his family’s food for the days he doesn’t earn. Salt costs less.”

“That’s—” the young man began, and stopped, and wrote something down.

The Emperor approved the commission. Full implementation; expanded funding. The hall began to move: robes, papers, officials turning to other business. Her uncle pressed her arm once, the same hand that had been steadying her since she was seven, and went out without a word, because he didn’t need one.

She let herself look at the side of the hall.

He was talking to Lin Wenyuan about something in the papers. He wasn’t looking at her.

And then, as if he’d felt where her attention had gone, or had known all along and was only now letting himself admit it, he looked up.

The hall was full of people going somewhere else. He looked at her across all of it and held it. None of the brief professional nod, none of the one-beat glance before looking away. He held her eyes like a man who’d decided this was a moment he wasn’t going to turn from, and his face, which she read carefully, because he didn’t give things easily and when he did they were real, wasn’t calm at all.

Something had come up to the surface of it, short of a smile, something she didn’t have a word for: the face of a man who’d just watched her be everything he’d told the Emperor she was. It said, in the only language he was fully fluent in: yes. This. Exactly this.

She held it. For the first time since the inn in Qingzhou, she didn’t look away first.

He did. He turned back to Lin Wenyuan and the papers. She turned back to her own composure, which she had, but only just. Mei Yun was at her elbow.

“The Emperor approved it.”

“He did.”

“Page seven. I saw the old one’s face. Like someone had sat on his hat,” said Mei Yun, with enormous satisfaction.

“Mei Yun.”

“And Miss, you looked very well in the green coat.”

“Mei Yun.”

“I’m only observing that the coat was exactly right for the room,” said Mei Yun serenely.

✦ ✦ ✦

The thin official with the grey beard caught her in the colonnade on the way out. He was older than she’d thought, and he bowed to her lower than the occasion called for, and straightened slowly.

He stopped, and his face worked. “Physician. Page seven. I read the whole appendix while the others were talking. My wife’s brother lost a leg to wound fever at the northern passes. Twenty years ago. If your method had been in the field manual then—”

He couldn’t finish. He bowed again, and went. She stood in the colonnade with her papers against her chest. After a moment a shadow fell beside hers on the stones.

“He’ll speak for the funding next year,” said the General.

“He didn’t finish what he was saying.”

He stood beside her, looking at the courtyard, not at her. “He won’t. But he’ll speak for the funding. Page seven.”

“You’d read it.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “I’d read it six times. I wanted to see whether anyone else in that hall had. One man. He’s the one who’ll matter.”

She walked back to the house through the capital streets in the thin, clear early spring light, with the city moving round her in all its layers, and she was, without any qualification, without managing it into something smaller, completely and specifically happy.

chapters.title: The Dinner and What Follows
chapters.desc: A list from an old official, and in a lantern-lit courtyard, a kiss under the plum tree. And for other reasons.
chapters.epigraph: “I know your language. I’ve been learning it for a long time.”
chapters.content:
The celebration that evening was smaller than the night before: the commission staff, their families, and a handful of officials who’d asked good questions. Her uncle sat near the Emperor. Her father was reunited with his historian and lost to the world within a breath. Her mother wore the face of a woman storing everything away to think about later.

The seating had been arranged, the way these things are arranged, with care. Shiyu found herself where it put her, and across the table and three places to the left was his profile.

She ate her soup. She talked to the physician on her right, a woman from the capital’s charity hospital who wanted to know everything about the rain column.

“Twelve to sixteen days?”

“Every year. Three years running.”

“We have the same river. It floods the southern wards in the fifth month. We’ve never counted,” said the woman slowly.

“Count this year. Write down every fever, and where they drew their water. Send it to me. I’ll send you the form,” said Shiyu.

“The commission has a form?”

“It does now,” said Shiyu, and three places to the left the profile turned, a degree, in her direction.

Halfway through the meal the thin official from the morning came round the table again. He didn’t say anything this time. He only stopped by her chair, and put a small folded paper beside her bowl, and bowed, and went back to his seat. She opened it under the edge of the table. It was a list, in a shaky, careful hand: the names of six men who sat on the Revenue Board, and beside each one, a note of what they cared about. Salt prices. His son is a soldier. Deaf in the left ear, sit on his right.

She folded it again and put it in her sleeve, and when she looked up the General was looking at her sleeve.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, in the inner courtyard, she found him beside her without having seen him cross the room. The lanterns were lit, the spring night was cool, and from inside came her father’s voice, enthusiastic and unstoppable, a man who’d been given exactly the conversation he’d come for.

“He gave you something,” said the General.

She took it out and showed him. “A list. Who sits on the Revenue Board, and what they care about. And which ear to sit by.”

He read it. “That’s worth more than the presentation.”

“I know.”

“He’s never given anyone anything in twenty years at court.”

“His wife’s brother lost a leg.”

He gave the list back. “Then keep it somewhere safe.”

The corner of his mouth again: the thing that wasn’t quite a smile. She’d been looking at him for months in letters and for three years before that in memory, and she was looking at him now in a courtyard in the capital, and the not-quite-smile was undoing her so thoroughly that she was only managing because she’d had practice.

“The presentation,” he said, and stopped.

The pause was longer than his pauses ever were: the pause of a man who’d prepared what he meant to say and found, at the moment of saying it, that the prepared version wasn’t good enough.

She waited. She knew how to wait for him.

He tried again. “The presentation was—”

Shiyu spoke before he could try a third time. “I know. I know what the six drafts were telling me. I know what the field manual was. I know what the library was, and the librarian with the tea. I know your language. I’ve been learning it for a long time.”

The silence after that was different from all the silences before it: two people who’d both, in the same moment, admitted what they knew.

“You’re going back to Qingzhou,” he said at last.

“The day after tomorrow. The expanded commission starts next month.”

“Qingzhou first. For the seasonal review. I said I’d come.”

“You did.”

He looked at her with a directness that had been building through the whole visit: not a man presiding over a meeting, but the full particular attention of someone who has decided whom he’s going to look at.

“I’ll come for the review,” he said.

A breath.

“And for other reasons.”

She breathed. It was the plainest thing he’d ever said to her about anything that wasn’t work, in all the years she’d known him, without any of the official language he used to cover things. And for other reasons. She valued honesty above nearly everything. She’d proved it once, in a tent, in front of six men, when a lie would have been easier. She’d honour it now.

“Good. I’ll be there,” she said.

The courtyard was empty except for the two of them and a stone lion with moss on its paws. He looked at the door to the hall, where the light and the voices were. Then he looked at her. Then he stepped round the lion, into the shadow of the plum tree beside it, and held out his hand, and she took it and let him draw her in under the branches.

“Someone will come out,” she whispered.

“Then be quick,” said the General, and kissed her.

It was quick, and it wasn’t. It was his hand at the back of her neck, under the jade pin, and the smell of the plum blossom and the cold, and her own hand flat against his chest where she could feel his heart going exactly as fast as hers, which she’d never once suspected, and which delighted her so much she laughed into his mouth.

He drew back. “What?”

“Your heartbeat. It’s fast,” said Shiyu.

He looked at her in the half-dark. “It’s been fast since you came into the hall.”

“So it’s something particular to this courtyard?”

“It’s something particular to you. It has been since a supply box,” said the General.

Footsteps at the hall door. A palace attendant, peering out into the lantern light.

“General? His Majesty asks for you.”

He let her go. He stepped back out round the lion into the light, perfectly composed, and only someone standing close would have seen that his collar was crooked. He glanced back at her once, for the length of something being kept, and crossed the courtyard and went in.

Shiyu stood in the shadow of the plum tree and pressed both hands to her face.

Mei Yun appeared at her side so fast she must have been behind a pillar.

“And for other reasons,” said Mei Yun, in a voice that made it clear she had excellent hearing and no remorse whatsoever.

“Mei Yun.”

“I’m only—”

“I know exactly what you’re doing.”

“I’m going in. I only want you to know that I’ve been right about this since the Jade Phoenix, and I expect to go on being right. And the jade pin was perfect. And his collar’s crooked. Someone should tell him before His Majesty does,” said Mei Yun.

She went. Shiyu stood alone in the cool capital night and let herself feel it, all of it, without qualification: the enormous feeling of something that had been building for three years finally moving.

She was going home the day after tomorrow. He was coming to Qingzhou. And for other reasons.

chapters.title: The Morning of Departure
chapters.desc: He checked the road before dawn. She asks what the other reasons are, and he answers in one word.
chapters.epigraph: “You said, and for other reasons. What are the other reasons?”
chapters.content:
She was packed before the household woke. She’d never left packing until the last moment; who she was didn’t allow it. The case was in order, the presentation papers filed, the herb samples from the capital market wrapped and stowed, and her father’s library parcel, three days of notes from the Tang texts he’d waited eleven years for, sat on top where he’d find it first.

Her father had already gone to the Medical Library for a final hour before the carriage. Her mother was at the breakfast table with tea and the clear head she always had in the mornings.

“The capital suits you.”

“It’s a remarkable city.”

Lady Ren poured for her. “I didn’t mean the city. You were different last night. Not less yourself. More. The way people are when they’re in a room with someone who sees them properly.”

Shiyu drank her tea.

“Mother.”

Her mother refilled her own cup. “I’m not asking anything. I told you what I needed to tell you two months ago. I’m only noting that you listened. And that the jade pin was the right choice.”

“It was. Thank you.”

“And that someone’s collar was crooked when he went back in to His Majesty. Mei Yun mentioned it. She mentions everything.”

“Mother!”

“I said nothing at the time,” said Lady Ren, and smiled into her cup with the warmth of a woman who’d wanted things for her daughter and trusted her daughter to find them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The commission’s closing session was short and administrative. Her uncle ran it briskly: papers confirmed, schedules aligned, the eastern physicians given their roles. She signed what needed signing. The General was there, as he’d said he would be, and said little. He answered one question from the court’s administrative officer so precisely that the matter closed for good.

When the room cleared she was gathering her papers and heard someone stop beside her. Not behind. Beside. She finished gathering, and looked up.

The room was empty. Her uncle had shepherded everyone out with the efficiency of a man who’d been managing situations for years, and had shut the door.

“The carriage leaves at midday,” said the General.

“Yes.”

“The road from the south gate’s clear. The weather will hold for three days.”

“I know. My uncle told me last night.”

“Your uncle didn’t check the gate this morning.”

She looked at him. He’d gone to the south gate before the session, in the dark before the city woke, to look at the road her carriage would take.

“You didn’t have to do that.”

“No,” he said.

Not: it was nothing. Not: it was practical. Just no. He took the document case out of her hands and set it on the table behind her, the way a man moves something she doesn’t need to be holding right now. Her hands were empty, and he was close.

“I read your first draft. Two months before the revisions, when the second section was still rough and half the case studies weren’t finished. It was already the most rigorous piece of civilian health work I’d ever seen,” he said.

“It was nowhere near finished.”

He held her gaze. “You gave it three more revisions. Not because it needed them. Because you were making it as good as it could be, not as good as it had to be. That’s why.”

“Why what?”

He paused. “Why the gate. Why the six drafts. Why your name went on the title page where they’d see it first. Why I moved a chair in an inn.”

She understood it then the way the significant things always landed, not loudly but with weight. She’d been doing this since she was eighteen on a road outside a camp, telling the truth when a lie would have been safer. He’d seen it on the first day.

“I need to ask you something. Not for the commission,” she said.

He waited.

“Last night. Qingzhou, the seasonal review. You said, and for other reasons. What are the other reasons?”

The room was quiet. He looked at her, and then, on purpose, he set the control aside. Not all of it. He was still himself. But enough.

“You,” he said.

One word. Plain and complete, and from this man, in this room, the most significant thing she’d ever heard him say.

Her voice was even. She was managing, only just, and had stopped caring about only just. “All right. Then I’ll be there. And not only for the commission.”

“I know you will,” said the General, and put both hands round her face and kissed her.

This one wasn’t quick. There was no palace attendant at the door, and her uncle had shut it on purpose, and the morning light came in long across the empty table. She held on to the front of his coat and kissed him back, and when they stopped she didn’t step away. She stayed where she was, her forehead against his collar, which was straight today.

“Three months. That’s a long time to wait for a review,” she said into it.

His thumb moved once along her jaw. “I’ve waited longer. I’ll write.”

“About the commission?”

His mouth moved. “About anything. Every week. Not the commission’s letters with a paragraph at the end. Mine. I’ve already told Lin Wenyuan he’ll have to stop reading them before they go.”

She laughed, and he let her go, and she picked up her document case and went to the door.

“Shiyu.”

She stopped and turned. He hadn’t moved. He was standing where she’d left him, looking at her with the whole of his attention and, under it, something with no performance in it at all: just him, looking at her, and letting her see him do it.

“Midday. I’ll be at the gate,” he said.

“To check the road again?”

“To check that you’re on it,” he said.

She went into the corridor at her ordinary pace. She breathed the capital air, lacquer and old stone, and thought about one word said flat and certain in a quiet room. She wasn’t managing any more. She let herself feel the full weight of it, and it was enormous, and she carried it easily, because it was exactly the right size for who she’d become.

chapters.title: The Road Home
chapters.desc: Mei Yun confirms it the whole way home, and her father turns out to have known since the inn.
chapters.epigraph: “I know you were there. I want to hear you say it.”
chapters.content:
The carriage moved. The capital drew back behind its walls: the great gate, then the approach road, then the city’s layered smell giving way to open air. He’d been at the gate, as he’d said. He hadn’t come to the carriage window. He’d only stood beside the guard post with his hands behind his back, and when the carriage passed he’d inclined his head to her father, and to her mother, and then to her, a fraction longer.

Her father hummed. He’d found the herb he was looking for at a roadside stop on the way in, it had settled a classification argument he’d been having for most of his adult life, and he was profoundly, thoroughly happy.

Mei Yun sat across from her, looking out of the window. She lasted until the first milestone.

“You.”

“I know,” said Shiyu.

“He said you.”

“I know.”

“In a room by yourselves, to a direct question, he said—”

“Mei Yun.”

“I’m only confirming.”

“You don’t need to confirm. I was there.”

“I know you were there. I want to hear you say it.”

Shiyu looked out at the road south, the new grass on the plains, the sky the flat pale blue she’d always connected with the northern frontier, and had come to understand was his sky.

“He said you,” she said.

“Yes. And then?” said Mei Yun, with great satisfaction.

“And then nothing.”

“Miss. Your uncle shut the door. I watched him do it. He stood outside it with his arms folded like a temple guardian and told the court’s administrative officer that the room was being aired.”

“Was it?”

Mei Yun turned back to the window. “The officer didn’t think so either. Your hairpin was crooked when you came out. I fixed it on the stairs. You didn’t notice.”

Her mother, beside her, had been studying the road with the composure of a woman who’d heard every word and was making no comment, which was itself a comment.

“The congee at the first overnight stop was good last time. Plain rice, ginger, a little salted egg. We should stop there again,” said Lady Ren.

“Yes, Mother.”

“And Mei Yun, you’ll sit facing forward tomorrow. You’ll make yourself sick facing backwards and talking.”

“I’m never sick, Lady Ren.”

“You’ve never talked this much,” said Lady Ren.

Two li further on her father rapped on the frame and asked the driver to stop.

“Father. We’ll be late to the overnight stop.”

He was already out and crouching in the roadside grass. “A moment. The classification of that specimen’s ambiguous in every standard text, and I’ve been looking for a living example for years. This settles the secondary identification entirely. Where’s my notebook?”

“On the seat, Master Yun,” said Mei Yun, handing it down.

Her mother sighed the sigh of a woman who’d married this man knowing exactly who he was. Shiyu leaned against the carriage frame and watched her father sketch a weed with the focused joy of a man who’d waited eleven years to do exactly this.

“Shiyu. Your General,” he said, without looking up.

She went still. “Father?”

He shaded a leaf. “He came to the Medical Library yesterday afternoon. While you were at the closing session. He sat down at my table and asked what I was reading. I told him. He listened to all of it. Nobody listens to all of it.”

“What did he say?”

Her father blew on the page. “Very little. He asked one question at the end. He asked whether I’d mind if he wrote to you. Not about the commission. About anything.”

Her mother turned her head slowly.

“What did you tell him?” said Shiyu.

He closed the notebook. “I said you were twenty-one and a physician with her own clinic and a commission, and you could decide for yourself who wrote to you, and that I’d be very glad if it were him. Then I told him about fritillary for another half an hour. He stayed for all of it. I thought that was a good sign.”

He climbed back in, beaming, and the carriage moved on. Her mother looked at her father.

“Yun Chengde. You’ve known about this since yesterday afternoon?” she said.

“I’ve known about it since the inn. I’m not blind, Ren. I’m only reading,” said her father mildly.

Mei Yun put her face in her sleeve and shook silently all the way to the overnight stop.

Shiyu sat back in the warmth of it: her father’s happiness, her mother’s composure undone for once, Mei Yun’s terrible delight, and under all of it, running through everything, one word in a quiet room. She was going home to her clinic, her city, her work. She’d treat Old Master Feng’s knee and accept whatever fruit he decided she needed, and in a week a letter would come in the handwriting she knew. Not about the commission. About anything.

And in three months the door of her clinic would open.

She’d waited three years. This wasn’t the same kind of waiting at all.

chapters.title: Three Months Later
chapters.desc: The clinic door opens on the first morning of the sixth month, and the General is standing in her front room.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to find the words for it. I know.”
chapters.content:
The clinic door opened on the first morning of the sixth month. She heard it from the preparation room, where she was compounding the week’s first batch with the white mortar.

“I’ll let the physician know you’re here,” said Mei Yun, at the front.

“There’s no hurry. She can finish what she’s doing,” said a voice she’d have known through a wall of stone.

Shiyu set down the pestle. She untied her apron, straightened her inner coat, and pressed both hands flat on the table for a breath, feeling three years of her own work worn into the wood. Then she went through.

He was standing in her front room, in the clinic she’d opened at nineteen with her own records and her own reasoning and the best carpenter in Qingzhou. He wore the plain travelling coat from the inn, not the uniform. He hadn’t brought the Five or his staff: one horse in the little courtyard, one guard at the gate, and him, reading the labels on her herb jars with the attention he gave to things he wanted to understand.

He looked up. She’d been preparing for this for three months, and found, now it had come, that she wasn’t nervous at all.

“General.”

“Physician.”

“The seasonal review.”

“Yes.”

“And the other reasons.”

“Yes,” he said, and crossed the room, and in front of Mei Yun and the herb jars and the open door to the street, kissed her.

Mei Yun turned round and became extremely interested in the supply shelf.

“There’s a patient at eight,” said Shiyu, when she could.

“How long have we got?”

“An hour.”

“An hour’s enough.”

“For the review.”

“Among other things,” he said, and didn’t let go of her hand.

She took him to the consultation table, the one with the lamp placed exactly right for reading records, and pulled out a chair. He sat. She sat across from him, and they looked at each other over the table in the morning light, and she thought of every distance there had been between them, a balcony and a road and a tent and three years and five hundred li of letters, and how it had all come down at last to a table and two chairs and an hour before the first patient, in a room that was entirely hers.

“Your letters came every week,” she said.

“I said they would.”

“You wrote about the weather in the third one. Two pages about the weather.”

“It was remarkable weather.”

“It was rain.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “It was rain at the camp, and I was thinking about your fever column, and I wanted to tell you what the river looked like. Lin Wenyuan would’ve cut it.”

“I’m glad he didn’t see it.”

“So am I,” said the General, and opened the season’s file.

The work was good. It had always been good. It was theirs now: built between two people who’d been building towards each other in the only language they both spoke fluently, the work and the precision of the work.

An hour went by. Mei Yun knocked and put her head round the door.

“First patient, Miss.”

“Thank you.”

The door shut. He didn’t stand. He was looking at the season’s records between them.

“The summer projections are conservative,” he said.

“They are. I’d rather underestimate and exceed than overestimate and disappoint.”

He looked up. “I know. I’ve known about you since the supply cart.”

“I know you have.”

He turned a page without looking at it. “Before that. Your uncle showed me your first report, the night you arrived. He was proud of it, which was enough to make me read it. I’ve read everything since. The camp records. The clinic records he forwarded. The seasonal reports. All of it.”

She held his eyes. “Chen Ye told me. At the inn. He said you annotated them in the evenings. I’ve been writing to you since the first report. Before I even knew you were reading.”

He was quiet for a breath.

“When the procession left Qingzhou three years ago, I told myself there was no purpose in coming here. You were eighteen. The constraints were real. The distance was real. I was right about all of it.”

“You were.”

“The constraints are still real.”

“I know.”

“The distance is still real.”

“I know.”

“And I’m here anyway. That’s the part I got wrong.”

“Yes. You are,” said Shiyu.

In the waiting room the old chair creaked under Old Master Feng’s considerable weight.

“The patient’s waiting,” she said.

“Go.”

She stood and took Feng’s file from the shelf, and paused at the door.

“Tonight. My parents are expecting you for dinner.”

“Your parents know I’m here?”

“My father knew before you did. My mother’s known for months. She’s had the cook practising since the fourth month.”

The corner of his mouth: the thing that wasn’t quite a smile, and which she’d decided was one of the most significant expressions she’d ever seen on a human face.

“Tonight,” he said.

She went through.

“Master Feng. The knee?”

Old Master Feng held up a basket of loquats. “Better every week, Physician. And these are for you, and for whoever’s in the consultation room, because I heard two voices in there and neither of them was Mei Yun.”

“Thank you, Master Feng. Let’s look at that knee.”

“It’s the General, isn’t it? From the capital? My grandson saw a horse with an army saddle.”

“Your knee, Master Feng.”

“I’m only asking because I’d like to shake his hand. He sent you back to us. Plenty of men would’ve kept you up there,” said Old Master Feng, with dignity.

In the corner Mei Yun was arranging the morning’s supply trays with the concentration of a woman defusing something.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midday Shiyu came through to the preparation room and found him there, not in the consultation room, having been shown the herb cabinet by Mei Yun, who’d evidently decided that the General’s visit called for a full tour. He was reading the label on a jar of dried mugwort.

“Mei Yun gave you a tour.”

“She was thorough.”

“She’s always thorough.”

He set the jar down. “She showed me the white mortar. She told me who’d brought it and how long it took to find. She told me you use it every day.”

“I do.”

He looked at her across the room, with the cabinet behind him and three years of her work on the shelves, and his face had no guard on it at all. “The work is—”

“Don’t. You don’t have to find the words for it. I know.”

He was quiet. “Yes. You do.”

She went to the table and began the midday compounding, because there were afternoon patients and the work didn’t stop, and she’d always found work a good place to put feelings too big for standing still. After a moment he pulled the second stool from the wall and sat beside her. He didn’t help. He sat, present, paying attention to everything and performing none of it.

“Tell me what you’re making.”

“A cough mixture. Loquat leaf, apricot kernel, liquorice.”

“Why the liquorice?”

She ground for a while. “It harmonises the others. And it’s sweet, so the children take it. Why are you asking?”

“Because I want to know what you do all day and I’ve only ever read about it,” said the General.

She stopped grinding. She leaned sideways until her shoulder was against his, and stayed there, and after a while started grinding again with her shoulder still against his, and he didn’t move away.

This, she thought, was what it looked like on the other side of all of it: a preparation room in Qingzhou in midday light, jars on the shelves, the white mortar in her hands and the General of the northern army on a stool beside her with his shoulder warm against hers, asking about liquorice. It was exactly right.

chapters.title: The Dinner Her Mother Had Planned for Months
chapters.desc: He brings her father three lost books, and her mother asks whether he eats alone.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve no family in the capital? No household to go back to in the evenings?”
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
Her mother had been preparing for this dinner since the capital. Shiyu understood that the moment she saw the table: the good lacquerware, her grandmother’s dishes, the chrysanthemum tea made at exactly the right temperature and not a degree warmer. None of it was performed. Lady Ren had just done it, in the quiet, absolute way she did everything that mattered, and the table said you’re welcome here without saying it, which was the only way it counted.

“Mother, there are eleven dishes.”

“There are nine. Two are sauces.”

“For six people.”

Lady Ren moved a bowl a finger’s width to the left. “Seven. Your uncle’s riding down with the review party. And Captain Chen eats like a man who’s been fed by an army.”

“He has been fed by an army.”

“Then tonight he’ll be fed by me,” said her mother, and moved the bowl back.

The General arrived exactly when he’d said he would. She’d come to understand this was a structural feature of him: not punctuality as a show, but as respect for other people’s time. He came with Chen Ye, who was there in some capacity never specified. Chen Ye always found a role in rooms he arrived in.

Her father met them at the gate. Shiyu watched from the courtyard doorway, because going to the gate herself would have been correct, and she wasn’t entirely in command of her face.

“General. You honour the house.”

“Governor. Thank you for having me.”

“I’m afraid I don’t know quite how one greets—”

“The way you’d greet anyone who’s come to eat your wife’s cooking and is grateful to be asked,” said the General.

Her father, flustered and warm, bowed anyway. The General returned it, then held out the gift his household had prepared: a set of herbal classification texts, the Tang edition, the companion volumes to the ones her father had read at the Imperial Medical Library.

Her father looked at the texts. Then at the General.

“You found the companion volumes.”

“I was told there was a gap in the set.”

“There’ve been three volumes missing from every catalogue in the empire for sixty years.”

“There were two in a monastery in the western hills, and one in Lü Yue’s grandmother’s attic. She was glad to see it go to someone who’d read it,” said the General.

Her father held the books like something long sought, and couldn’t say anything for a while, and didn’t need to.

Shiyu stepped into the courtyard. The General saw her the moment she moved. His attention followed movement in a room the way a strategist follows position on a map, and it went to her and stayed, the way it had been staying since the clinic that morning.

“Physician.”

“General. You found the books.”

He glanced past her. “Mei Yun told me which ones. Three weeks ago, by letter. She signed it ‘a well-wisher’.”

Mei Yun, behind the door, made a small strangled noise and vanished.

Chen Ye caught Shiyu’s eye on the way in with the air of a man who’d been right about something for three years and was enjoying it professionally.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was excellent, in the practical sense and in the particular one: everyone at the table was exactly themselves.

Her father had recovered from the books and was in full form, which meant he was explaining the Tang way of classifying with sustained enthusiasm and its implications for Qingzhou’s herb farms. The General listened, actually listened, the engaged focus of a man following something worth following.

He set down his cup. “Then your secondary identification of the fritillary would change what the river farms grow?”

“It would double the yield on the eastern terraces!”

“Have you told the provincial office?”

“I’m the provincial office. Ren. I’m the provincial office,” said her father, and stopped, startled by his own logic.

“You are, dear. Eat your fish,” said her mother.

Chen Ye, at the far end, had fallen into talk with Mei Yun, who’d been invited on the grounds that she was practically household. They had the look of two people both sharper than the setting needed, who’d recognised it in each other.

“You wrote to him,” Chen Ye said to her, low.

“I wrote to a general about a gap in a set of books.”

“You signed it ‘a well-wisher’.”

“I wished him well. Pass the greens,” said Mei Yun.

Shiyu was aware, the way she’d been aware for three and a half years, that the man across the table was three seats closer than the formal arrangement would have put him, and that her mother had done the seating.

At the second course her mother turned to him with the gentle precision of a woman who chose her moments.

“You’ve no family in the capital? No household to go back to in the evenings?”

A short pause, the kind that from him meant thought, not discomfort.

“My household’s run by staff. My parents died when I was fifteen. The Emperor’s household took their place afterwards, as much as it could.”

“Then you eat alone in the evenings.”

Not quite a question.

“When there is an evening,” said the General.

Her mother refilled his tea without comment, but she did it with the care she kept for people she’d decided to feed properly. Shiyu saw it, and put down her chopsticks for a breath.

“Lady Ren. The duck,” said the General.

“Yes?”

“I’ve eaten at His Majesty’s table since I was fifteen. I’ve never had duck like this.”

“It’s my mother’s. Ginger, five-spice, three days in the brine. I’ll write it down for your cook,” said Lady Ren.

“My cook will resign out of shame.”

“Then you’ll have to come here for it,” said her mother, serenely, and Shiyu had to look at her soup.

At the dessert course her father produced his notebook to show the General the herb from the capital road. It was possibly not a conventional dinner offering. The General took it and studied it with the same attention he’d given the duck, and her father’s face, when someone took his notes seriously, was the face of an entirely happy man.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, in the courtyard, with the summer night closing in and the lanterns turning everything gold, she stood beside him while the others were busy: her father drawing her uncle into the notebook, Chen Ye and Mei Yun arguing about something near the gate, her mother visible through the window, present and deliberately not watching.

“Your father’s going to read those books tonight,” he said.

“He started before the dessert was finished. I saw his hands.”

“I liked him before. I like him more now.”

“Because he talked to you about fritillary for an hour?”

“Because he talked to me about fritillary for an hour as though I’d want to hear it. Nobody’s assumed that about me in a long time,” said the General.

“My mother’s going to feed you every time you’re in Qingzhou.”

“I gathered.”

“She’s decided you’re too thin.”

“I’m not too thin.”

“You eat alone when there’s an evening. She’s going to fix that. So am I,” said Shiyu.

He turned from the garden to look at her, and there was the thing without a name in his face again. She’d been watching it for months. She still wasn’t immune.

“I’m glad you came. For the review. And for the other reasons,” she said.

“So am I.”

She reached for his hand in the half-dark, below the line of the window, and he took it and turned it over and pressed his mouth to the inside of her wrist, quick and warm, where her pulse was, and let it go.

From the gate came Mei Yun’s voice, low. “Chen Ye. Don’t look.”

“I’m not looking.”

“You’re looking.”

“I’m looking at the sky.”

“There’s nothing in the sky.”

“There’s a great deal in the sky. I’m looking at it very hard,” said Chen Ye.

He left at the right hour: not early, which would have said he was managing something, and not late, which would have been a statement of its own. When he said good night at the gate he gave it the whole of his attention. She watched the gate close.

Her mother appeared beside her.

“He found the companion volumes,” said Lady Ren.

“He did.”

“For your father. He found out what your father needed, and he went to a monastery and an attic, and he brought it to dinner.”

“Mei Yun told him.”

Her mother pressed her hand once. “Mei Yun told him what. He did the rest. I’ll write down the duck.”

She went in. Shiyu stood in the courtyard a moment longer and let herself feel the whole specific warmth of it: the books, the question about eating alone, his mouth at her wrist. Then she went inside and set out the next morning’s preparations, and was, if she was honest, happier than she’d been in a long time.

chapters.title: Peng Yao
chapters.desc: A pleasant new secretary delivers papers in person and looks at the wrong side of the cabinet.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody asks about camphor, Miss. Nobody who isn’t a carpenter.”
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
She met Peng Yao on the second day of the General’s review visit.

He came to the clinic mid-morning with the commission’s paperwork for the seasonal filing. It could’ve gone through the garrison post. He brought it himself, with a politeness so complete it was hard to fault anything in it. Thirty-one, she guessed. Scholar’s hands, well kept; the grooming of a man who’d spent time in the capital’s offices; a pleasant, intelligent face, and the bearing of someone who’d been in rooms with important people long enough to know how to move in them.

“Physician Yun. Peng Yao, of the commission’s secretariat. I’ve brought the seasonal filing.”

“You could have sent it with the garrison post, Secretary.”

He smiled, exactly warm enough. “I could. But I’ve read so much about the Qingcloud Medical Hall that I wanted to see it. Forgive the indulgence.”

“There’s nothing to forgive. Please sit.”

The papers were perfect: in order, nothing missing, the preparation of a capable man. She asked two questions about the format for the baseline records.

“Why does the new form want the patient’s district as well as the street?”

“So the capital can compare districts across provinces. It was the deputy minister’s suggestion.”

“And the column for ‘previous physician’?”

He paused. “To see which patients come to you after being treated elsewhere. And how they fared there. A measure of comparison.”

Both answers came quickly and were correct. She found nothing wrong with either. She also found herself paying the kind of attention she paid patients whose symptoms wouldn’t quite settle into a picture: the attentiveness of someone who’d learned to trust the thing that didn’t resolve.

“Thank you, Secretary. I’ll have it back to the garrison by the end of the week.”

He rose and bowed. At the door he turned. “There’s no hurry at all. Your cabinet’s beautiful. Camphor?”

“Camphor. The best carpenter in Qingzhou.”

“It shows,” said Peng Yao, and went.

Mei Yun had been in the preparation room the whole time. She appeared in the consultation-room doorway with the face of someone composing a sentence.

“He looked at your bookshelves.”

“Most visitors do.”

“He looked at the commission cabinet.”

Shiyu looked up from the filing.

“The general commission papers are on the left. The method records and the direct correspondence are on the right. He looked at the right. For longer than the left,” said Mei Yun.

“How much longer?”

Mei Yun folded her arms. “While you were reading page two of the filing. And again when he asked about the camphor. Nobody asks about camphor, Miss. Nobody who isn’t a carpenter.”

Shiyu was quiet.

“Note it,” she said, and went back to the filing.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wrote it to her uncle that evening, through the commission channel, in the plain language she used for observations she couldn’t yet sort. His reply came the next morning.

Peng Yao joined the commission’s staff eight months ago, from the Ministry of Revenue, on the recommendation of Deputy Minister Kang. No military background. In his first month he submitted an internal review proposing that the commission’s standards were insufficiently rigorous, and that its chief civilian physician’s credentials be verified by a capital academic board instead of being accepted on the strength of field outcomes.
I rejected it. I didn’t tell you. I thought it was friction. I’m less sure of that now, and I should have told you sooner.

She read it twice. Then she filed it in the section of her correspondence box for things she wasn’t going to act on yet, but wasn’t going to put down either.

That afternoon was the second day of the review. The work was good and the figures useful, and at the end of the session she told the General what her uncle had written, in the neutral, clinical way she trusted most. He listened without expression.

“The deputy minister’s name?”

“Kang.”

Something moved in his face: barely, a degree, the tightening of a man connecting new information to something he already knew.

“You know him.”

He didn’t say what. “I know of him. I’ll look into it.”

“I’m not asking you to act. I wanted you to know.”

He was quiet. “I know. It’s the same reason I tell you things. Has he been here before today?”

“No. Why?”

He looked at the cabinet across the room. “Because Kang’s office has been asking the garrison for copies of your clinic’s correspondence since the spring. The garrison’s been refusing, on my orders. I didn’t think it was worth troubling you with. I was wrong. I’ll trouble you with everything from now on.”

“Everything?”

“Everything. Including the weather,” said the General.

She laughed, because she couldn’t help it, and the tightness went out of the room. He reached across the table and took the season’s file out of her hands, as he had in the capital, and turned her hand palm up on the wood and held it.

“Lock the right-hand side of the cabinet.”

“It’s a medical cabinet. It doesn’t have a lock.”

“It’ll have one by tonight. Chen Ye’s very good with locks. I’ve never asked where he learned,” he said.

They went back to the summer analysis, and for an hour the world outside the consultation room wasn’t the priority. It was only afterwards, walking home through Qingzhou in the afternoon light, that she let herself think about the name Kang and the right side of the cabinet, and about a pleasant man who’d come himself, with papers that could have been posted.

She filed it next to what her uncle had written. Then she went home and found Chen Ye in her clinic courtyard with a bag of tools, fitting a brass lock to a camphor-wood door, whistling.

“Captain.”

“Physician. Don’t ask where I learned.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Good, because it’s a much better story if you never find out,” said Chen Ye.

chapters.title: The Third Day
chapters.desc: The last day of the review: what he sees in her records, and a kiss for the shelves.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll admire your shelves more often.”
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
The third day of the review was the last the General had scheduled in Qingzhou before he went north again. She’d written it in her planning book with the same mark she gave every other date, and hadn’t let herself annotate it. She’d been practising that: not shrinking feelings, but not letting them bend the shape of the days that held them either. The day was what it was. She’d be in it.

The morning session was good in the way their sessions had always been good. The summer figures for the circulation treatments were strong, stronger than the first year’s projections, which had been cautious on purpose.

“You’ve never once overestimated a clinical outcome in three years of records,” he said.

She looked up.

“Every projection in the baseline is conservative. Every actual outcome beats it. It’s consistent enough to be a method, not caution.”

“I know what the work can do. I don’t always know what the patient’s life will allow.”

“You trust the work. You don’t trust the variables outside it.”

She thought about it. “That’s probably accurate.”

“It makes for better records. It’s also how you treat people.” The gap between the two sentences was shorter than his gaps usually were.

“How do I treat people?”

“You assume they’ll do less than they can, and then you’re delighted when they don’t. Old Master Feng. Your father. Mei Yun. Me.”

“I never assumed you’d do less.”

“You assumed I wouldn’t come.”

“I assumed you’d come in three months because you said three months, and you’re a man who means what he says. I didn’t assume you’d come and kiss me in front of Mei Yun before you’d taken your gloves off,” said Shiyu.

“That was not in the projections,” said the General.

She put the file down. He was looking at the table with the slight downward angle he had when he was being precise about something he’d thought through, and then he looked up.

“The next review’s in three months. The summer baseline comparison will be worth looking at together.”

“Yes.”

“I’ll come earlier. If that’s acceptable.”

“Three months is a long time.”

It was honest, and the most she was prepared to say in a consultation room at midday with patients due in an hour.

“It is,” he said. From him, that was a great deal.

“How much earlier?”

“Lin Wenyuan’s drawing up a reason for me to inspect the southern garrisons in the eighth month.”

“Do the southern garrisons need inspecting?”

“They will by the eighth month. Lin Wenyuan’s very thorough,” said the General.

They worked through the remaining items with the care they both gave to things worth doing properly. At the end, when the papers were done and she was collecting the clinic’s copies, he didn’t stand straight away. He sat at the table with the quieter stillness she’d come to connect with him here: someone present in a room, not managing it.

“The shelves,” he said.

He was looking at the herb cabinet, at the new brass lock on the right-hand door, and at the jars.

“You built all of this. From nothing.”

“From a plan and three years. And my father’s patience and my uncle’s records and a carpenter who did excellent work.”

“From you,” he said.

She stood at the preparation table with the season’s file in her hands and the midday light in the eastern window, and thought: I’ve wanted for years to be seen. Not as the physician’s useful helper, not as the governor’s unusual daughter, not as the girl in the supply cart. As exactly what I am. He sees it.

She came round the table. He stood, and she put the file down on the chair and took his face in both her hands, the way he’d taken hers in the capital, and kissed him slowly in her own consultation room with the door shut and the noon bell ringing over the river.

“That’s for the shelves,” she said.

“I’ll admire your shelves more often.”

“There are four more in the back room.”

“Then I’ll need to stay for the afternoon.”

“You’ve a horse saddled at the gate and four hundred li to ride.”

He didn’t let go of her waist. “Four hundred and twelve. Chen Ye’s holding it. He’s very patient. He’ll tell me so for the whole first day.”

“Go. Go, or the southern garrisons will never need inspecting,” said Shiyu, laughing.

“Three months.”

“Two and a half. If Lin Wenyuan’s as thorough as you say,” said Shiyu.

She didn’t watch him leave from the doorway. She went back to the preparation room and made the afternoon compound with steady hands, and let herself feel what she felt without making it smaller, and the afternoon was warm and good and entirely real.

chapters.title: Peng Yao, Again
chapters.desc: Peng Yao keeps asking about the letters, and she asks the General not to manage around her.
chapters.epigraph: Yes. You’re right. I won’t manage around you again.
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
The weeks after the General went north had the quality she’d come to trust: the productive quiet of a life that was mostly hers. The summer load followed the patterns she’d recorded for three years. River workers with sunstroke. Farmers with worn shoulders. And the east district’s endless dehydration, which she was still arguing about with Well-Master Hu.

“Covers, Master Hu. Wooden covers, on every well in your street.”

“My grandfather never covered a well in his life, Physician.”

“How many of your grandfather’s children lived past five?”

Well-Master Hu thought about it. “Four. Of nine.”

“Cover the wells and catch the rain in clean jars, and next summer come and tell me how many children on your street had the flux,” said Shiyu.

He came back in the eighth month, red to the ears, to say two. Last year it had been nineteen.

His letters came every week, as he’d promised. She didn’t count the days between them. She noticed, accurately, when they arrived.

Peng Yao came to the clinic twice more in that time. Both visits had papers that were, technically, due in the commission’s cycle. Both were in person, in the smooth, pleasant manner she’d learned to read beneath without ever finding a grip.

After the second, Mei Yun came to her with the look of someone whose observation needed more than her usual sidelong delivery.

“He asked me whether the direct correspondence between the clinic and the command is a standard commission arrangement or special to this site.”

Shiyu put down her brush. “What did you say?”

Mei Yun’s mouth thinned. “That I manage the supplies, not the administration, and he should send paperwork questions through the garrison. He asked again. Twice. Different words each time.”

“What words?”

Mei Yun looked at her steadily. “First ‘channel’. Then ‘arrangement’. Then ‘the General’s personal letters’. He didn’t get that last one from me, Miss. He already had it.”

“He isn’t interested in our methods.”

“No. He’s interested in your post bag,” said Mei Yun.

She wrote to her uncle that evening, not about the questions, which she’d handle by keeping her own records clean and giving nothing that could be misread, but about the summer baseline and two real method questions it had raised. In the last paragraph she wrote: I’m being careful. I want you to know I’m paying attention. His reply came two days later.

I know you are. So is he. Be well.

She opened the clinic. She treated Old Master Feng’s knee and a river worker’s shoulder and the merchant woman’s headaches, which she’d decided after three careful assessments came from the blood vessels and would answer to the preparation she’d refined over the year.

“Is it working, Madam Sun?”

“Two headaches this month. Last year it was ten.”

“Write them down when they come. What you ate, how you slept.”

“My husband says I write everything down now.”

“Your husband has fewer headaches than you, and doesn’t need to,” said Shiyu.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told the General too, in the direct channel, that the summer papers had been arriving in person instead of by garrison post. She put it as a fact. She didn’t frame it as concern.

He wrote back in three days, which wasn’t his usual week. He answered every commission question first, correctly. Then:

I know about Peng Yao. Deputy Minister Kang has interests in the capital that run against the commission’s expansion: his family holds the licence for army medical supplies in four provinces, and your method costs them a fortune in salt they don’t sell. I should have told you this the day you gave me his name. I’m telling you now. He’s being watched. If anything changes in how he approaches the clinic, write to me the same day.

She read it three times. He’d known. He’d known since the second day of the review, more than she’d known, and had made the same calculation he made in the field, what to act on when and through which door, and chosen to tell her now and not then.

She understood it. The logic was his, sound and whole. She also felt the scrape of wanting to be inside a situation instead of managed round it.

“You’re frowning at a love letter,” said Mei Yun, passing with a tray.

“It isn’t a love letter.”

“It’s from him.”

“It’s about the salt licence for four provinces.”

“Then it’s a love letter about the salt licence,” said Mei Yun, and carried the tray off.

Shiyu wrote back:

Thank you for telling me. In future I’d like to have relevant information when it becomes relevant. I understand your reasoning. I want you to understand mine.

She sealed it and sent it. His answer came in three days.

Yes. You’re right. I won’t manage around you again.

She read it in the morning light at the clinic window. Then she turned it over. On the back, smaller, in the same hand:

I’ve been reading your letter about the headaches. Madam Sun’s husband sounds like a sensible man. I’ve started writing down what I eat. Lin Wenyuan thinks I’ve been poisoned.

She laughed out loud at the window, alone, at eight in the morning.

He didn’t give ground easily. When he gave it, it was real. She thought: this is what knowing someone actually means. She went back to work.

chapters.title: The Storm
chapters.desc: A notice arrives to stop their letters. She writes to ask, plainly, whether he allowed it.
chapters.epigraph: Not authorised by me. I’ve countermanded it.
chapters.volume: Volume Seven: The Dinner and the Storm
chapters.content:
The storm came on the ninth day of the seventh month. That wasn’t unusual for Qingzhou in summer: the province was known for its rains, and the city had been built over centuries to manage water, its stone streets tilted towards the river district’s drains. What was unusual was the letter that came that morning.

It came through the garrison under official seal, and it wasn’t from her uncle and it wasn’t through the direct channel. It was from the commission’s administrative office. She knew the secondary seal: Peng Yao’s desk. It was a formal notice that, from the next cycle, all correspondence between civilian physicians and commanding officers would pass through the secretariat for documentation. All existing direct correspondence would be archived in the commission’s records.

She read it twice, and went still. Mei Yun came to the doorway, saw her face, and said nothing, which was the most useful thing she could have done.

“Mei Yun. Where are his letters?”

“In the right-hand cabinet, Miss. Behind Captain Chen’s lock.”

“How many?”

Mei Yun came in and shut the door. “Sixty-one from this year. All of last year’s are in your room. Archived means they want to read them.”

“Archived means they want to read them out loud to someone who matters,” said Shiyu.

She picked up her brush and wrote in the direct channel. No commission language at all.

I’ve had a formal notice from Peng Yao changing how our letters travel. I don’t know whether you authorised it. I’m asking directly.

She sealed it and took it to the garrison herself, in the early morning, with the storm building in the west: the kind of cloud she knew from three years of Qingzhou weather was serious, not seasonal. On the way back she passed Old Master Feng’s corner. He wasn’t there; the wind had driven him in.

She thought about the notice and the deputy minister’s salt licence and the way Peng Yao had looked at the right side of the cabinet. He wasn’t interested in what they’d built. He was interested in what the direct channel held, and what it implied: who’d written to whom, in what register, and what could be made of that in the right ears.

The storm broke in the afternoon, while she was seeing patients. Rain came the way it came to Qingzhou, decisively, without apology, a season let go all at once. The clinic’s drains ran properly. She treated a child’s fever and a carpenter’s torn hand.

“Will I lose the finger, Physician?”

“No. Hold still. You’ll lose a week’s work, and you’ll keep the finger.”

“My wife’ll say I lost it on purpose.”

“Tell your wife the physician says you’re to keep your hand dry for seven days and that if she has any objections she can bring them to me,” said Shiyu.

“She’ll bring them. She’ll bring them with dumplings,” said the carpenter darkly.

“Then I’ll look forward to it.”

The storm was outside and she was inside, and both were where they should be.

✦ ✦ ✦

His reply came two days later by relay rider, faster than any letter had ever come, which told her something about how he’d taken the question.

Not authorised by me. I’ve countermanded it. The direct channel stays as it is.

His private seal, not the commission’s. Countermanded. Not reviewed, not considered: struck out, which meant the notice hadn’t reached him before it went out, and that someone was already looking into how it had. Below the seal, in a quicker hand:

I’m sorry it frightened you. It frightened me. I read it at the river crossing and turned the horse round before I’d finished the second line. Chen Ye says I startled a ferryman.

She wrote back:

Received. Thank you. The method changes Peng Yao proposed in his first month and this notice point the same way. I believe he’s trying to build a written record that looks like impropriety between the commission’s physician and its commanding officer. I think you should know exactly what I believe he means to do.
And I wasn’t frightened. I was angry. There’s a difference, and you should know that too.

She took it to the garrison herself again, with Mei Yun beside her under the big oiled umbrella. The storm had softened into the steady rain that would last three days, the kind Qingzhou was made for, filling the herb gardens and the river and the cisterns.

“You’re walking very fast, Miss.”

“I’m walking at my ordinary pace.”

Mei Yun tilted the umbrella. “Your ordinary pace is for when someone’s bleeding. Are you frightened?”

“No.”

“Then what are you?”

“Certain. He’s shown which way he’s going, Mei Yun. Whatever he means to do, it’s moving,” said Shiyu.

She wasn’t afraid. She felt, with the precision she’d brought to three years of diagnosis, that something had crossed a threshold. Peng Yao had shown his direction. Whatever he meant to do, it was moving.

She went home and ate with her parents. Her father had his nose in the companion volumes. Her mother asked careful questions about the commission, and Shiyu answered them honestly, including, because her mother always knew anyway, that there was a complication.

“Are you safe?” said Lady Ren.

“Yes. The complication’s administrative.”

“Administrative.”

“A secretary. Some letters.”

“Your letters?”

“His letters. To me.”

“Ah. All right. Eat,” said her mother, in the tone of a woman who’d been reading situations her whole life and whose idea of administrative was a good deal larger than her daughter’s.

She ate. She slept. She didn’t know that in three weeks everything would change.

chapters.title: What Peng Yao Does
chapters.desc: A formal complaint names them both, and Peng Yao comes to the clinic to watch her hear about it.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t assure me. I’m writing this down.”
chapters.content:
The document reached the Emperor’s Censorate three weeks after the storm. She didn’t know it at the time. She’d learn it later, from her uncle, from Chen Ye, from the General himself, in the broken way the truth puts itself together after something has moved faster than any account of it.

What she knew in the week before was this: Peng Yao had been to the garrison three times. He’d talked to two officers she didn’t know. He’d sent a formal request to the commission’s administration for the complete record of direct correspondence between the clinic and the command.

Her uncle refused it on procedural grounds, correctly and properly documented. What Peng Yao had done instead, with the patience of a man who’d spent his whole career in offices, was collect the outline of the letters without their contents. How many. How often. The weekly pattern. The fact that they came in the General’s own hand. He didn’t need the contents. He had their shape, and the shape was enough.

The document he sent to the Censorate was a concern, not an accusation: carefully framed, precise, neutral in the way of a man who knew neutral framing was its own kind of weapon. It suggested an administrative irregularity in the Northern Army’s civilian medical commission: a direct correspondence between its commanding officer and a provincial physician, unusual in form, sustained over a long period, in a pattern suggesting the relationship had moved beyond the commission’s intended scope.

It named her. It named him. And it asked, with the measured neutrality of a man asking a question he already knew the answer to, whether His Majesty was aware of the nature of the relationship between the General of the Northern Army and the physician of the Qingcloud Medical Hall.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning it was sent she was seeing patients. The carpenter’s hand was healing cleanly. Old Master Feng’s knee had answered well to the summer change in his massage. A young woman from the east district came in tired and pale, and after a careful assessment Shiyu told her what it was.

“Thin blood. It’s very common. It’s very treatable.”

“Am I dying?”

Shiyu wrote as she talked. “No. You’re eating rice and pickles and not much else, and you’re working twelve hours on the dye vats. Liver once a week, if you can get it. Dark greens every day. Dates. And this preparation, morning and night.”

“Liver’s dear.”

“Chicken liver isn’t. Ask the poulterer by the bridge for the ones he throws away. Tell him the physician sent you, and that she’ll fix his back for nothing next time it goes.”

“Will he do it?”

“His back goes every winter. He’ll do it,” said Shiyu.

She did her work, and the morning was ordinary. Then Peng Yao came.

He came at midday, which was unusual. He came alone, without papers, which was more unusual. He stood in the consultation room with the pleasant manner fully in place and looked at her like a man who’d done the thing and was now watching the consequences arrive.

“Physician. I wanted to let you know, as a courtesy, that a concern has been submitted to the Censorate regarding the commission’s administrative structure. It’s a procedural matter. I’m sure it’ll be resolved without difficulty.”

“I see.”

“I’m sure the General will manage it efficiently. He manages most things efficiently.”

“He does.”

Something shifted under the pleasant surface: not cruelty, but the satisfaction of a man who’d put something exactly where he meant it to go.

He smiled. “His Majesty will be informed, of course. These things always go up. I expect the commission itself won’t be affected. The physician’s involvement may need to be reviewed.”

She looked at him. She’d given serious diagnoses to hundreds of patients across that same table, and she’d learned to read the people opposite: fear, denial, the held stillness of someone who already knew. She read Peng Yao now and found something she hadn’t expected. Not cold ambition. Something personal, and more dangerous because of it.

“You wanted my post,” she said.

His face didn’t move. It didn’t need to.

“The deputy minister recommended you to the commission and you expected to run it. Then it went to a provincial physician with no capital credentials, and the General put her name on the first page of the field manual where the Emperor would read it first. And there wasn’t anything you could do about the work, because the work’s sound. So you found the one thing you could do something about,” said Shiyu.

“Physician, I assure you—”

“Don’t assure me. I’m writing this down.”

Something moved in his expression: a fraction of something that was almost surprise.

“Thank you for telling me. I’ll make a note of this visit in the clinic records,” said Shiyu, perfectly level.

“Of course,” said Peng Yao, and left.

She wasn’t frightened. She was, with complete cold clarity, furious.

Mei Yun was in the doorway the moment the outer gate shut.

“I heard.”

“I know.”

“Are you—”

Shiyu was already uncapping the ink. “Bring me the correspondence log. And the commission filing record. I’m going to record this conversation and every visit before it and every query, in order, with dates and exactly what was said, and it’s going to be accurate and complete, and it’s going to exist before anything else happens.”

Mei Yun brought the log without another word. She wrote for two hours. Every visit, every question, every filing, every look at the right side of the cabinet, in her own hand, in the clinic records that had run unbroken for three years. When it was done she sealed it and wrote a cover letter to her uncle, by garrison post, marked urgent.

Then she wrote to the General in the direct channel. She told him everything Peng Yao had said, in the order he’d said it, as clinically as a medical report: accurate, without annotation, giving it its true weight and no more.

At the bottom she put one more line, because she’d promised him the weather too:

It’s raining again. The carpenter’s wife brought dumplings. I’m all right.

She carried it to the garrison herself. On the way back she passed the Jade Phoenix. Its gate lanterns were lit in the late afternoon, and the city moved round her with its ordinary permanence.

He’d known what he was doing. He’d chosen the thing that would hurt, and the thing he’d chosen was them. She breathed, and went home.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.desc: Four pages in his hand, a word he’s never written before, and her mother on men who say it late.
chapters.epigraph: “Some men don’t say it until they’ve something to put behind it.”
chapters.content:
The General’s reply came in two days, fast enough that she knew he hadn’t slept before writing it. It was four pages. She’d never had four pages from him; the longest before had been a page and a half, after the capital, with the commission’s rules attached. Four pages in his compressed, careful hand, the characters closer together than usual, the way they went when he wrote quickly.

“Four pages,” said Mei Yun, at her shoulder.

“Go away.”

“I’m not reading it. I’m counting it.”

“You’re reading it upside down.”

“I can’t read upside down,” said Mei Yun, who could, and went.

Mei Yun came back ten breaths later with a tray she didn’t need to carry.

“What does it say? Just the first page. The first page is the commission. I’m allowed the commission.”

“He went to the Emperor. The Censorate had it inside a day; His Majesty read it himself.”

“And?”

“And His Majesty said the commission’s structure is sound, the physician’s qualifications are a matter of documented record, and the concern will be dealt with through the proper channel.”

“Which channel’s that?”

“Him. His Majesty’s handed it straight back to the General,” said Shiyu.

Mei Yun put the tray down slowly. “That’s the cleverest thing I’ve ever heard. Peng Yao went over his head, and the head sent it back.”

“Go away now. The second page isn’t the commission.”

“I knew it,” said Mei Yun, and went.

I’m coming back to Qingzhou. Not for the review. I need to be there while this is dealt with.
I should have moved on Peng Yao after his first intervention. I watched when I should have acted. That was my mistake, and you won’t pay for it.

And on the fourth page, without any commission language over it at all:

I know that what he sent names us both, and calls it something irregular. I want you to know that my answer to His Majesty, and to any review that follows, will be the same. There’s nothing irregular about it. It’s what it is. I love you. I’ll say so formally, and without qualification, to anyone who asks.

She read that section three times. Then she put the letter flat on the table and put both her hands over it, as if it might go somewhere.

He’d say it to the Emperor. To anyone. He’d decided already. The letter wasn’t him working towards it; it was the announcement.

He’d never written the word before. Not once in three years. She’d known it the way she knew the shape of a fever before the column confirmed it, and it was still a different thing entirely to see it in ink. She went to find her mother.

Lady Ren was in the garden cutting chrysanthemums. She looked at her daughter’s face and put the shears down.

“He’s written.”

Shiyu stopped. “He’s coming back. Peng Yao went to the Censorate. The Emperor’s sent it back to him. And he wrote—”

“I can see what he wrote. It’s all over you,” said her mother gently.

“He’s never said it.”

Lady Ren picked up the shears again. “Some men don’t say it until they’ve something to put behind it. Your father said it to me the day he was given the governorship. Not before. He said a man who couldn’t keep a roof over a wife had no business telling her he loved her. I told him he was an idiot. He agreed. We were married in the autumn.”

“Mother.”

“Write back. Say it back, if it’s true. And then come and help me with these, because your father’s going to want them on the table and he’s never once noticed they’re there,” said Lady Ren.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wrote back four pages, which seemed right, for once. She answered everything, including the last section.

I know what it is. I’d say the same, formally, if anyone asked. I’m not afraid of any of it. I’m angry that he aimed at the clinic, because the clinic isn’t mine to gamble the way my own standing is. But the clinic’s records are three years of unbroken work, and they’re sound. He can’t damage what’s true.
I love you. I’ve loved you since the cart, I think, though I’d have denied it with my last breath in that tent. My mother says some men don’t say it until they’ve something to put behind it. I don’t need anything behind it. I only needed you to say it, and now you have, and I’m sitting in my clinic with ink on my sleeve, happy, and furious, both at once.
Come when you can. The figures will be ready. And when this is settled, I want to talk: not through the channel, not across the consultation table. There are things I’ve been waiting to say, and I think the right time is coming.

“Mei Yun.”

“Miss?”

“Take this to the garrison. Don’t read it.”

Mei Yun held out her hand for it, and looked at her face, and her own face changed. “I’d never. Oh, Miss. He said it.”

“Take it to the garrison!”
