“I’m going. I’m going, I’m gone, I’m not crying, it’s the rain,” said Mei Yun, already at the door.

She slept well, which surprised her. The situation was real and serious and she wasn’t making it smaller. She was also steady at the bottom of it, in a way she hadn’t been at eighteen in a tent or at twenty-one in a capital courtyard. The thing she’d been building wasn’t only the clinic. It was the ability to carry something large without being bent by it.

She woke before dawn, as always. She made tea and did the morning preparations, with the letter in her sleeve.

She didn’t know that in two days everything would break in a direction nobody had seen coming.

chapters.title: The Riverbank
chapters.desc: A child falls at the second bend. She goes alone, and Peng Yao is waiting on the path.
chapters.epigraph: “Move aside, please.”
chapters.content:
The emergency came from the western district. A child had fallen from the bridge abutment at the river’s second bend, the old stone bridge the river children used as a diving platform in high summer, which the city had meant to fence for as long as anyone could remember. The water hadn’t caught him; the abutment’s edge had.

The boy who brought the message could barely breathe. “Head wound. He went quiet. His mother’s screaming.”

“How long since he went quiet?”

“I ran straight here!”

“Then he’s been quiet a quarter of an hour. Mei Yun?”

“I’m stitching Madam Gao’s foot, Miss. I can’t leave it open.”

“Finish her. I’ll go.”

Shiyu took her bag and went alone. She’d done it before and would do it again: the situation needed speed, and she had speed. Not running. Running on Qingzhou’s stone streets risked exactly the kind of fall she was going to treat. The fast, deliberate pace of someone who knew how to cover familiar ground.

The bridge was crowded: river workers, neighbours, two garrison soldiers who’d come for the commotion. The child was conscious. She saw that from ten paces: a small body turning towards his mother’s voice, which was the most important thing.

“Let me through. I’m the physician.”

“It’s the physician from the Qingcloud Hall—”

“Let her through!”

Left temple, bleeding hard but not spurting. Possible concussion. She knelt.

“What’s his name?”

The mother was weeping. “Xiao Bao. He’s seven. He’s seven, Physician—”

“Xiao Bao. Look at me. How many fingers?”

“Three,” said the boy, crossly.

“Good. Very good. Don’t move your head. Madam, I need you to hold his hand and talk to him. Tell him about supper. Anything. Keep your voice ordinary.”

“I can’t—”

“You can. He’s listening to you, not to me. You’re the medicine just now.”

The mother took a breath and began, shakily, to talk about noodles.

Shiyu didn’t notice Peng Yao at first. She was with the child. She only saw him when she stood up to tell one of the soldiers how to lift the boy, and found him at the edge of the crowd, not watching the child. Watching her. His expression was something she didn’t have time to read.

“Like this. One hand under the neck, one under the back. Don’t let his head roll.”

“Yes, Physician.”

She walked beside the boy to the nearest house with a suitable room, and didn’t look back.

She was with him an hour. She didn’t hurry the assessment; the stakes were exactly as high as they looked. She cleaned the wound and closed it with the care she gave every closure, wherever it was. He followed her finger. His eyes were even. There was no sign of bleeding inside the skull. She wrote the night-watch instructions on a slip of paper and made his mother say them back.

“Wake him every two hours.”

“Every two hours.”

“Ask him his name and where he is.”

“His name and where he is.”

“If he’s sick, or can’t wake, or one eye’s bigger than the other, send for me at once. Any hour. Don’t wait for morning.”

The mother clutched the paper. “Don’t wait for morning. Physician. Thank you. Thank you.”

“He’ll be cross with you by tomorrow afternoon. That’s how you’ll know he’s better,” said Shiyu.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out into the river street with her bag on her shoulder. Peng Yao was there.

He stood alone where the river path met the street, and his face had changed since the bridge. The pleasant surface wasn’t quite in place. Under it, more openly than she’d ever seen, was the look of a man who’d lost something he’d been counting on, and who’d decided, the way people do who’ve run out of things to manage, to do the last thing left.

No greeting. “The Censorate accepted the General’s reply. It’s been noted. But noted isn’t resolved. The commission’s future isn’t certain. What the physician does next will be watched.”

The river was loud at this part of the bend, the summer water high.

“I’m going back to my clinic.”

He paused. “I’d suggest that a very public distance from the command would settle things faster. For the clinic. For the commission. For the General’s standing with His Majesty.”

She understood exactly what it was. Not a threat: nothing that could be reported as one. A suggestion, dressed as advice and working as pressure, aimed at the place he’d decided was softest, the chance that what she had with the General would cost him.

She went still. She was also two paces from the river at the edge of the path, and Peng Yao was between her and the street back, and the afternoon had gone grey ahead of a second rain, and the soldiers from the bridge had gone.

“Move aside, please.”

He stepped towards her instead. Not raising his hands. Only a man closing distance, and she registered it with the clarity of someone who’d judged physical situations in emergencies and knew the space between danger and safety could be a single breath.

She stepped back. The edge of the path wasn’t where she’d judged it to be.

She didn’t fall. She was pushed. She wouldn’t be able to prove it later. She’d be certain anyway, and keep that certainty to herself for months, because certainty and proof weren’t the same. What she knew, in the one clear instant of the bank giving way, was the pressure on her shoulder: deliberate, specific, not her own momentum, not the earth. Then the river.

The water at the second bend was fast. She’d known that in the abstract; she’d lived in Qingzhou for twenty-one years and walked the river path a thousand times. Knowing and being in it were different. She didn’t panic. Long ago, in that other life, she’d been taught how to survive water, and her body remembered: sweep sideways, find the surface, breathe when you can, don’t fight the current. The water was cold for summer. Her bag went; she felt the strap tear, which was right, because the weight would have finished her. She kicked for what she thought was up.

She surfaced once. A breath, and a bearing. The current was taking her east, towards the lower bend, the stretch before the river narrowed into the gorge. She needed the south bank, inside a hundred paces.

She swam. The cloud-embroidered pouch tore loose from her sash. Her grandmother’s jade pin went with the current. She knew about the losses somewhere at the back of the absolute present tense of staying alive.

She nearly made it. The rock at the mouth of the gorge caught her shoulder, a hard spinning blow that turned her over in the water, and she lost the bearing, and the current had her, and she was going into the gorge. The last clear thing she knew before the roar took everything else was: he’ll look for me. She held on to that, and went under.

chapters.title: What the General Knows
chapters.desc: The report reaches him on the road: no body recovered. He doesn’t stop for the night.
chapters.epigraph: “We’re not stopping for the night. We move now.”
chapters.content:
He had the report on the fourth day.

He’d been on the road. He’d written that he was coming back to Qingzhou and he’d moved on it at once, because that was how he worked: decide, move. He was two days out when the first dispatch caught him. Not through the commission channel. Through the garrison’s emergency post, from Chen Ye, who’d ridden ahead and had been in Qingzhou six hours when the news came in.

The physician of the Qingcloud Medical Hall. Riverbank incident, western district, second bend. One witness. No body recovered.
No body recovered isn’t confirmed. The current at the gorge mouth makes recovery uncertain. The search has started. I thought you should know before you arrived.

He read it once. He read it again. He folded it and put it inside his coat, next to the four pages she’d written him, which he’d been carrying for two days. Lin Wenyuan was watching his face.

“General. The horses have done forty li since noon. If we stop at the relay—”

“We’re not stopping for the night. We move now.”

“Yes, General.”

“Send ahead to every relay on the road. Fresh horses at each, saddled and waiting. Nobody sleeps.”

“Yes, General.”

No one questioned it. He reached Qingzhou before dawn.

✦ ✦ ✦

The search was running. Two garrison teams; river-district men who knew the water; and her father, who hadn’t slept. Yun Chengde stood at the second bend like a man whose whole idea of what was possible had been violently rearranged and hadn’t yet found a new shape. Her mother was at the house, managing something enormous by managing the smallest things: the tea, the lamp, the gate left open.

He went to the river first. Chen Ye met him on the bank.

“One witness. A river man, some way off. He saw someone struggling in the water and raised the alarm.”

“Peng Yao?”

Chen Ye’s voice was flat as a slate. “Was here. He left before the garrison came. He went back to his lodging. He hasn’t come out since.”

The General looked at the second bend and the mouth of the gorge. He judged the current: speed, direction, the weight of summer water, what it did to a body. He thought about her. The steadiness of her hands. She’d have swum for the bank, he was sure of it; she wouldn’t have panicked, she’d have calculated. He thought about the private terror of not knowing whether calculation had been enough.

“Keep him there. Don’t let him know he’s being kept. Don’t let him leave the city.”

“Yes, General.”

“The search goes on. Every man we’ve got. The gorge mouth and the lower bend above all. If she cleared the gorge she’d have come out on the north or east bank, and the current favours east.”

Chen Ye didn’t move. “Yes, General. Lingyun.”

He hadn’t heard Chen Ye use his name since they were boys at the old general’s camp.

“What?”

Chen Ye’s jaw was tight. “She swims. Mei Yun says she swims like an eel. She taught the river children in the second summer, when two of them drowned at the ford. She knows this water better than any of us.”

“I know.”

“I know you know. I’m telling you anyway.”

He’d spent every year since he was fifteen learning to be a man whose face didn’t say what he felt, because in his world feeling shown was ammunition given away. He’d been excellent at it. Some part of him admitted now that he’d been too excellent at it for too long. He wasn’t managing his face this morning. There was no one to manage it for. Chen Ye had seen it, and Chen Ye wasn’t someone it needed managing for.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went to her father.

Yun Chengde was a gentle man and a scholar. He’d spent fifty-five years in a world where governance and medicine and the quiet arts of administration were the substance of life, and nothing in that world had prepared him for this. He was trying. He stood at the bend watching the search teams with the stillness of a man who’d decided that the only thing left to him was to be present at the place. His notebook was in his hand. He wasn’t writing in it.

The General stood beside him.

He had words. He had many: the assessment, the odds, the search he’d ordered, which was as thorough as he could make it. He had the language of a commander who’d told families things before and learned that honesty served better than comfort, because false comfort made everything worse.

“Governor.”

Her father didn’t look away from the water. “General. You came very fast.”

“Not fast enough.”

His voice shook once, and steadied. “She wrote you a letter. Two days ago. Four pages. Mei Yun told her mother, and her mother told me. Did it reach you?”

“It reached me.”

Yun Chengde turned the notebook over in his hands. “Good. I’m glad. I’m glad it reached you. She said it, didn’t she? In the letter.”

“She said it.”

He laughed, horribly, and stopped. “She’d only say a thing like that if she meant it. She’s never said anything she didn’t mean. Not once. Not as a little girl. It was very inconvenient. General, I don’t know the river. I know plants. Tell me honestly.”

The General looked at the gorge. “Honestly, I don’t know. But she knows how to fight for it. She’s been doing it her whole life.”

Yun Chengde looked at him then, and something in his face, grief-masked and sleepless and a little bewildered, the face of a man who’d always known his daughter was more than he quite understood, changed into something else. It had recognised, in those words, another man who knew her. He nodded once.

They stood at the second bend together until dawn came up over the river hills.

chapters.title: Dead or Alive
chapters.desc: An inquiry, a jade pin in a fishing net, and a ride to the Emperor for leave to cross the border.
chapters.epigraph: “Bring her back, Lingyun.”
chapters.content:
He gave it three days.

Not because he believed she was dead. He didn’t, and it wasn’t the denial of a man refusing what the evidence suggested. It was the considered judgement of a man who’d read situations for thirteen years and trusted his reading. She’d been close to the south bank. She was strong and calm and didn’t panic, and he’d seen her face things that would have broken people with less of her particular clarity. Three days meant: let the search be thorough, and then move.

The search was thorough. He ran it himself, pulling teams he’d never usually have pulled, and everyone who took his orders understood exactly what weight they carried.

On the second day he dealt with Peng Yao.

He did it formally, in the garrison’s administrative chamber, with witnesses and a clerk and the full structure of a military inquiry. Lin Wenyuan sat at his left with the papers. Chen Ye stood by the door.

“Secretary Peng. Where were you at the third hour of the afternoon, two days ago?”

“In the western district, General. I’d been at the bridge, like half the city. A child had fallen.”

“You didn’t go to the child.”

“I’m not a physician.”

“No. You went to the river path. The witness puts you there.”

“I wished to speak to Physician Yun on a commission matter. I spoke to her. She left.”

“Left where?”

“She walked away along the path. I went back to my lodging.”

“Before the alarm was raised.”

“I didn’t know there’d be an alarm.”

The General didn’t raise his voice. “Didn’t you. Lin Wenyuan. The secretary’s first review of the commission.”

Lin Wenyuan turned a page. “Submitted in the first month of his posting, General. Recommending the chief physician’s credentials be examined by a capital board. Then the notice changing the correspondence, which you countermanded. Then the request for the complete letters, which the Chief Physician refused. Then the Censorate.”

“Each of those was a proper administrative—”

The General didn’t move. “Each of those was proper. Each of them was aimed at one woman. And two days ago you stood between her and the street on the river path, at the fastest stretch of water in the province, and now she’s in it. Tell me again where she walked.”

Peng Yao’s pleasant manner held through the first hour. It didn’t hold through the second. He didn’t confess; a man like him never would. But his careful explanations didn’t survive patient, step-by-step logic, and he became defensive in the way of someone who hadn’t expected the other side to be quite this prepared. He’d built a career in rooms where friction was smoothed with surface and connections, and he was facing a man for whom surface counted for nothing.

The inquiry closed. The General sent the full record to the Emperor by the formal channel, with a personal letter he wrote once and didn’t revise.

The evidence points one way. I’m submitting it for your review. I’m not asking for a particular outcome, only that the review be complete. I trust your judgement on the formal consequence. On my own answer to this man and what he did, I ask your permission to act personally.

The reply came in a day. The Emperor had, as always, read everything and made up his mind before writing.

The formal consequence will be handled by the Censorate. He won’t be in a position to do this again. Your permission is granted. Do what you need to do. I’d suggest doing it memorably, and without diplomatic complications. And Lingyun: find her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the jade pin on the third day.

A fishing family at the lower mouth of the gorge had pulled it out of their net two days before: small, jade, carved with clouds. He knew it. He’d watched her mother’s hand press it into her hair in the capital. He held it in his palm.

“She cleared the gorge,” he said.

Chen Ye looked at the pin. “East bank.”

The General nodded. East of the gorge lay forty li of riverside country before the first real settlement, and beyond that the border, administered on paper and porous in summer, when high water moved the old crossings. His search teams had already reached the marker on the east bank, and there they’d stopped. Imperial soldiers didn’t cross it. He wouldn’t order them to.

He rode for the capital that night, changed horses at every relay, and was in the palace on the second evening. The Emperor had arranged for the audience not to be hurried. He sat with the Qingzhou letter in front of him and looked at his nephew with the expression of a man who’d already arrived somewhere and was waiting for the other person to catch up.

“You want to go across.”

“The pin puts her at the gorge mouth on the east bank. The current would have taken her to the settlement at the border marker, or past it. If she’s alive, she’s somewhere on that line.”

“If she’s alive.”

“She’s alive.”

He said it without qualification. He knew how it sounded. He didn’t take it back.

The Emperor studied him with the attention of a man who’d been watching people for thirty years and could tell certainty from desperation. What he saw, it seemed, was certainty.

“You can’t enter the border country officially. Not with your title. The implications alone—”

“Not officially. One man in plain clothes, following the river east, looking for a physician from a provincial clinic who was swept downstream. There’s nothing political about a private man following a river.”

“You’re not a private man.”

“I will be, for this.”

The Emperor was quiet. He looked at his nephew: the stillness, the set jaw, the dark eyes that weren’t performing patience but had none left on this subject. In thirteen years the boy had never asked him for anything personal. Authority, yes; supplies for campaigns; the machinery of a command. Never this.

“She wrote to you. Before,” said the Emperor.

“Yes.”

The Emperor turned his cup. “And you to her. I’ve read your letter to the Censorate. ‘It’s what it is.’ I’ve known you since you were a child who wouldn’t cry at his own father’s funeral. I wondered whether anyone would ever get through. I’ll admit I didn’t expect it to be a girl in a supply cart.”

“Neither did I.”

“Chen Ye goes with you.”

“Yes.”

“Travelling as what? Merchants are too obvious in the border villages.”

“Not merchants.”

Something that wasn’t quite amusement crossed the Emperor’s face. “Physicians, then. How appropriate.”

“Travelling scholars. It holds in the settlement country. We’ve documents enough.”

The Emperor picked up his brush and signed. “Travelling scholars. You’ll have full imperial authority the moment you’re back on this side. On the other side you’re a private man following a river. Bring her back, Lingyun.”

He took the papers from his uncle’s hand.

“I intend to.”

chapters.title: The Letter at the Border Post
chapters.desc: At the flooded border, a letter in charcoal and a pouch embroidered with clouds.
chapters.epigraph: “She says not to let anyone cross for her. I’d point out that you’re anyone.”
chapters.content:
He rode south out of the capital with the travel papers in his coat and Chen Ye half a length behind, and neither of them spoke until the first relay station. There Chen Ye handed him a bowl of soup and waited until he’d drunk half.

“You should sleep for two hours.”

“No.”

“Then I’ll sleep for two hours, and you can watch the horses.”

He didn’t answer. Chen Ye slept for two hours on a bench by the stable wall. The General sat on the step outside with the jade pin in his hand and watched the horses, and when Chen Ye woke they rode on.

They came back through Qingzhou at dawn on the eleventh day. He didn’t stop at the governor’s house. He stopped at the second bend, because Yun Chengde was there, as he’d been every morning, standing on the bank with his notebook.

“Governor. The Emperor’s given permission. I’m going across myself. I’ll send word the moment I know anything at all.”

Her father listened to all of it. Then he took off his outer coat, the governor’s good coat with the embroidered collar, and held it out.

“She’ll be cold. If you find her. The river’s cold even in summer.”

“When I find her.”

“When you find her,” said Yun Chengde, and his mouth shook, and he made it stop.

The General tied the coat behind his saddle.

✦ ✦ ✦

They rode the forty li in the afternoon. Halfway, Chen Ye brought his horse up alongside.

“What will you say to her?”

“I haven’t thought.”

“You’ve thought of nothing else for eleven days.”

“I’ve thought about the current. The depth at the gorge mouth. The east bank. Whether a woman with a bad shoulder could reach the reeds below the pool,” said the General.

“And whether she did.”

“Yes.”

Chen Ye rode beside him a while. “When you find her, don’t give her a report.”

“I don’t give her reports.”

Chen Ye looked straight ahead. “You gave her a report on the weather. Two pages. She told Mei Yun, and Mei Yun told me. Lingyun. Say something that isn’t the weather.”

“Such as?”

“You’ll know. You’ve never once not known, with her. You just never said it in time,” said Chen Ye.

✦ ✦ ✦

The border marker stood forty li downstream, where the river came out of the hills and spread wide and brown across a gravel plain. There was a settlement of perhaps thirty houses, a ferry landing with no ferry, and a small post with two clerks and a flag. The search teams had camped beside it for a week. They stood when the General rode in and saw what he was wearing: a scholar’s plain grey robe, no insignia, no armour. Being soldiers, they carefully didn’t mention it.

The ford was under water. You could see where it ought to be, two posts on this bank and two on the far one, and between them a stretch of river fast enough to roll stones along its bed. The far bank was another country on paper. In practice it was hill farms and fishing villages that paid tax to whoever came asking and had a strong opinion of neither side.

“How long since the water was low enough to cross?”

The senior clerk was a thin young man with ink on his cuffs who’d plainly been told who the scholar in grey was and was trying not to stare. “Twenty days, sir. Twenty-two. It usually drops at the end of the eighth month. We’re close.”

“Has anything come across?”

“Nothing by the ford. A salt trader came over the hill path two days ago, from the villages on the other side. He left a letter for the post to send on. It’s for the Governor of Qingzhou, so I put it in the next garrison bag, but the bag doesn’t go until—”

The General was already walking to the post.

The letter was in the bag under the window, between a tax return and a complaint about a goat. It was folded small and tied with a strip of blue cloth, with no seal, because whoever wrote it had had nothing to seal it with. Something else was tied into the cloth. He knew what it was before he had the knot undone.

A little pouch of faded silk, embroidered with clouds. River water had stiffened it and the sun had bleached it pale. One corner of the stitching had come loose.

He’d watched her press her fingers to that pouch for nearly four years. In the medical tent, when a conversation went somewhere she hadn’t planned. At the inn, when she thought no one was looking. In the capital, once, in the breath before she walked into the presentation hall. She did it when there was something she couldn’t say. He’d never asked her about it. He’d just known, the way he knew which of his officers rubbed his jaw before a lie.

He opened the letter. It was written in charcoal on the back of a page torn from a trader’s account book, the characters cramped and slanted because she’d been lying down to write them. But they were hers. He’d have known them anywhere.

To Yun Chengde, Governor of Qingzhou.
I’m alive. I’m at the fishing village of Wide Water, a day and a half by the hill path from the border marker, on the east bank. My left shoulder came out in the river; it’s back in. I had a fever; it’s gone. The people here pulled me out of the water and have been kind to me.
The ford’s closed until the water drops. Please don’t let anyone cross for me in high water. I’ll come home as soon as I can walk the hill path.
The pouch is so you know it’s me.
Shiyu

He read it once, and again. Then he sat down on the clerk’s stool, because his legs had decided before he had, and held the letter in both hands.

Chen Ye came in, looked at him, looked at the letter. He didn’t ask. He went back out and told the soldiers to stand down and the search teams to strike camp. Then he came back in and waited.

The General’s voice didn’t sound like his own. “She’s alive. She’s at a place called Wide Water. She put her shoulder back in herself.”

“Of course she did.”

Chen Ye sounded perfectly calm. He also had to turn and look out of the window, and the General let him.

“She says not to cross in high water.”

Chen Ye looked at the ford, which was roaring, and then at the General, who was looking at the ford.

“She says not to let anyone cross for her. I’d point out that you’re anyone.”

There’d been a time, not long ago, a few months, when he’d have weighed the river against the risk and crossed anyway, and called it a decision. He thought about the letter she’d written him in the summer. I’d like to have relevant information when it becomes relevant. And his own answer: I won’t manage around you again.

She’d told him what she wanted. In charcoal, lying down, with her shoulder just put back.

“Find the salt trader. We’ll take the hill path,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The salt trader was a broad, cheerful man called Tuo, with a laugh like a dropped pot and two mules that hated each other. He was in the settlement’s only tea house.

“Wide Water? Tonight? It’s a day and a half on foot, master scholar, and nobody walks the hill path in the dark.”

The General put a silver ingot on the table.

Tuo stopped laughing and looked at it. “Now I think of it, the moon’s nearly full.”

They left an hour after sunset. The path climbed out of the plain into steep terraced hills, tea bushes in rows, dogs barking at them from every farm. Tuo talked the whole way: salt prices, his mules, his wife’s brother. Somewhere past midnight, when the General had stopped listening, he started on the river doctor.

He squinted sideways. “Old Nai pulled her out of the shallows below Wide Water. Her and her son. Thought she was dead. Bruise on her face like a plum. Two days later she’s sitting up telling Old Nai’s son how to pull her own arm back in. Then she’s walking. Then she’s lancing the headman’s hand. Now every child in the village follows her about like ducklings. You’re her family?”

“No.”

Tuo waited.

“Not yet,” said the General.

Behind them Chen Ye made a small sound that might have been a cough.

They slept three hours in a shepherd’s hut at the top of the ridge, because Tuo said the mules wouldn’t go on otherwise and Chen Ye said the General wouldn’t, and the General, who hadn’t slept properly in eleven days, argued with neither of them. He slept with the pouch in his hand.

They came down into Wide Water in the late afternoon of the second day. It was exactly what its name promised: the river came out of the hills and opened into a broad slow pool, reeds along the edges, fishing boats pulled up on the mud. The village sat on the slope above it, forty or fifty houses of dark wood and grey stone, drying racks of fish, chickens in the lane, smoke from cooking fires.

He heard the children before he saw them. A whole flock came shrieking and laughing down the main lane towards the river, and in the middle of them, walking more slowly, with her left arm bound to her body in a sling made from fishing net and a dozen small hands holding her skirt, was a woman in a borrowed blue jacket too big for her.

She was thinner. A fading bruise ran along her cheekbone, yellow at the edges. Her hair was tied up with a strip of cloth instead of a pin. She was saying something to the children in a dialect he didn’t know, and they were laughing at the way she said it, and so was she.

A little girl near the front, running backwards to look at her, caught her heel on a stone and pitched towards the ground. A hand shot out, her right hand, quick and sure, caught the child by the back of her jacket, and set her on her feet before she’d finished falling. He stood still for one breath. Then he moved.

chapters.title: The River Doctor
chapters.desc: Thirteen days on the far side of the river, a shoulder put back on a stranger’s floor, and one question: who was behind her?
chapters.epigraph: “Look where you’re going, little goose.”
chapters.content:
She didn’t remember the end of the gorge. She remembered the rock and the spin and the roar, and the thought she’d held on to as she went under. After that there was only cold and dark and the sense of being flung about inside something enormous that didn’t know she was there. At some point there’d been wood under her arms, a branch or a piece of tree, and she’d held it because her body wouldn’t let go. At some point there’d been light.

The next thing she knew for certain was a smell: smoke, fish, and the bitter green of some herb on the boil. Then a ceiling of dark beams, low enough to touch, with nets hung from it. Then a face: an old woman, brown and creased as a walnut, with no front teeth, peering down and saying something in a dialect so thick that Shiyu caught only one word.

“Alive. Alive, alive,” said the old woman again, louder, and patted her cheek.

Her voice came out as a croak. “Yes. Thank you. Where—”

Then she tried to move, and her left shoulder told her a great deal at once, and for a while she didn’t ask anything at all.

The old woman was Old Nai. Her son, whom everyone called Second Son, his mother included, had pulled Shiyu out of the reeds at the edge of the wide pool below the village two mornings before. They’d taken her for a drowned body until she coughed. Old Nai had stripped her wet clothes, rolled her in a quilt and spooned hot broth into her while she lay there not waking. Shiyu worked it out slowly over the first afternoon, from gestures and repetition and the handful of hill words close enough to Qingzhou speech to guess at.

The shoulder was out. She knew the moment she was clear-headed enough to feel it with her good hand: the flat wrong shape at the top of the arm, the head of the bone sitting forward where it shouldn’t. Two days out of the socket, and every hour made it harder to put back. She couldn’t do it alone.

She drew what she needed in the ash of the hearth with one finger. Second Son, a big quiet man of about thirty who mended boats, looked at the drawing with deep reluctance.

“Pull?” He mimed it, appalled.

“Pull. Slowly.”

“Hurt.”

“Yes. Very much. Don’t stop.”

He looked at his mother. Old Nai said something short and fierce, and he nodded.

She lay on the floor. Old Nai folded a quilt into a long roll, passed it under Shiyu’s arm and round her chest, held both ends and braced her feet against the doorframe. Second Son took Shiyu’s wrist in his two big hands.

She’d taught him the word an hour before. “Slowly. Slowly. Keep pulling. Don’t stop when I make a noise.”

He pulled. She made a noise. He looked ready to stop.

“Slowly,” said Shiyu, through her teeth.

He kept on, steady, the way he’d draw a boat up a bank, and somewhere in the long burning stretch of it she felt the muscles give and the bone slide and then a deep dull clunk she felt in her jaw.

She lay on the floor and breathed. Second Son sat back on his heels, grey in the face. Old Nai said something that was plainly a prayer.

“Good. That was very good. Thank you,” said Shiyu.

And then, because her body had been waiting for permission, she cried a little, with her face to the wall. Old Nai patted her hair and didn’t ask why.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fever came that night and stayed two days. She knew what it was: the cut on her scalp where the rock had caught her, river water in it, a body worn down to nothing. She talked Old Nai through what she needed. Boiled water. Salt. Clean cloth. The willow bark drying on the rack.

“This?” Old Nai held up the bark.

“That. Boil it. Bitter. Good.”

“Bitter good,” agreed Old Nai, who seemed to think this was a fine summary of medicine, and boiled it.

In the fever she went back over the riverbank, the way she’d go back over a case that had gone wrong: carefully, in order, skipping nothing. Peng Yao at the corner of the path, in front of her, between her and the street. His face. His hands held a little out from his sides, open, the way a man holds his hands when he wants you to see they’re empty. The step he took towards her. The step she took back.

And then the push. Low on her back, under the shoulder blade, flat and hard and meant. From behind.

Peng Yao had been in front of her. Both his hands had been in front of her, where she could see them. He’d made sure she could see them. So someone else had been behind her.

On the second night an image came to her that she didn’t trust: the back of a man’s hand, with a shiny pink scar across the knuckles like an old burn. She didn’t know where it came from. Perhaps it was the soldier she’d told to lift the child at the bridge; she’d watched his hands as he picked the boy up, worried he’d jar the neck. But she’d been feverish when she remembered it, and she knew exactly what a fevered memory was worth. She put it to one side. Not thrown away. Labelled, the way she’d label a sample she wasn’t sure of yet.

The fever broke on the fifth morning after the river. On the sixth, she sat up. On the seventh, a salt trader came to Old Nai’s door: a big, loud, cheerful man with two mules.

“Border. Tomorrow. Him,” said Old Nai, pointing over the hills.

“He’s going to the border marker?”

“Border Letter? You?” said the trader himself, beaming, and then a great deal more she didn’t follow, and then, slowly and kindly, as if to a child.

“Yes. Yes, please. Paper?”

He had an old account book and a stub of charcoal. She tore out a page and wrote to her father lying on her side, because sitting up for long still tipped the room. She wrote what had happened and where she was. She wrote that the ford was shut. She thought about who would read it, her father, her uncle, and one other person who’d certainly read it whatever its address, and she wrote: Please don’t let anyone cross for me in high water.

She knew him. She knew what he’d want to do. She wrote it anyway, because she wanted him to know what she wanted.

Then she needed something to prove it was hers. She had nothing left. The river had taken her bag, her shoes, her grandmother’s pin. She had the borrowed jacket and the quilt and, still knotted into the sash Old Nai had dried by the fire, the cloud-embroidered pouch. It had kept its stitches through the gorge. She didn’t know how.

Her mother had made it for her when she was six, the year after the fever, when her daughter woke up strange and quiet and too clever and her mother didn’t know what had happened to her and loved her anyway. It was the only thing Shiyu owned that had no use. She’d pressed her fingers to it ten thousand times.

She tied it into the letter with a strip of blue cloth and gave it to the trader.

“Important,” she said, in one of her five words of dialect.

The trader nodded solemnly and put it inside his shirt, and patted it twice.

After he’d gone, her hand kept going to her sash, to the place where the pouch wasn’t. She let it. There was no one to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth day the headman of Wide Water came to Old Nai’s door holding his right hand in his left: swollen to the wrist, red and hot and shiny, from a fish-hook three days old. Old Nai had told the whole village by then that the woman from the river knew medicine.

“Knife. Boil,” said Shiyu.

“Boil knife?” said the headman, alarmed.

“Boil knife,” said Old Nai, firmly, and boiled it.

She lanced the hand with a fishing knife, drained it, packed it with salt and boiled cloth, and told him through Old Nai to come back every morning. He came back the next morning and the swelling was down, and he looked at her differently.

After that, people came. A fisherman with a cough. An old man with a rash. A boy who’d trodden on a nail. She did what she could with one arm and the herbs on Old Nai’s rack and the things Second Son fetched from the hillside when she drew them for him. She learned the words for pain, and where, and better, and tomorrow. She learned twelve children’s names.

The only person who didn’t come was the village midwife, Auntie Fen, a tall, sharp-eyed woman who’d set every broken bone and brought every child in Wide Water for thirty years, and who stood at the end of the lane with her arms folded and watched the river doctor go by.

“She doesn’t like me,” said Shiyu to Old Nai.

“Fen. Fen likes Fen,” said Old Nai, and made a face like a sour plum.

Little Ke, the smallest, appointed herself the river doctor’s assistant on the ninth day, and brought her every word she thought Shiyu ought to know.

“Fish,” said Little Ke, pointing.

“Fish.”

“No. Fish.” A different sound entirely.

“Fish,” said Shiyu, trying.

Little Ke pointed at a goose with enormous condescension. “Better. Goose.”

“Goose.”

Little Ke pointed at Shiyu, delighted. “You. Goose.”

The children decided Shiyu was theirs. They followed her from house to house, laughed at her accent, and called her something she eventually understood meant the river doctor. They wanted to hear over and over how she’d come down the river on a tree. She told them, in dreadful dialect, with a great deal of waving of her good arm. The tree got bigger every time.

On the tenth night, at the hearth, Old Nai pointed her pipe at Shiyu’s sash, where her hand kept going to the place the pouch had been.

“Man?”

Shiyu laughed. “Why do you ask?”

Old Nai mimed it, pressing her own sash. “Hand. Girls do this. For a man.”

“Physicians do it too.”

Old Nai’s scorn was deep. “Physicians. Man. Where?”

“North. A long way north.”

“Good man?”

Shiyu thought about it: a chair moved in an inn, a gate checked in the dark, four pages in a cramped hand. “Very good.”

“Fisherman?”

“Soldier.”

Old Nai made a face like a pike. Second Son, mending a net by the door, said something low and amused.

“What did he say?”

“He say soldier come over mountain for you. Soon. He say, if soldier come, he hide the boat,” said Old Nai.

“Why would he hide the boat?”

Old Nai cackled until her pipe went out. “So soldier not try cross the river. Soldiers. Stupid. All soldiers.”

“This one isn’t stupid.”

“Then he come over mountain, like Second Son say,” said Old Nai.

At night she lay on Old Nai’s floor and counted. A day and a half for the trader to cross the hills. Longer, Old Nai said, because he’d salt to sell in every village. Then however long a letter took from a border post to Qingzhou. Her father would read it. Her mother. Mei Yun. And he’d have been told by now. He’d been on the road to Qingzhou when she fell. He’d have arrived to find her gone.

She thought about his face reading the report and couldn’t bear it, and thought about it anyway. She didn’t think: he’ll come. She thought: he’ll want to. She’d asked him not to cross in high water. She didn’t know whether he’d listen. She thought he’d try hard to, and lying in the dark with the river outside she found she loved him for it so much it hurt worse than the shoulder had.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the thirteenth day, at noon, Auntie Fen fell off her own roof.

She’d been mending the thatch. A rung went. She came down on the stone edge of the yard, and when Shiyu got there, running, with seven children behind her, the midwife was sitting in the dust with her face the colour of ash and her right shin bent where no shin should bend. The bone had come through the skin.

“Don’t touch. I set bones. I’ll set it,” said Auntie Fen, in hard clear dialect that even Shiyu understood.

“You can’t set your own leg.”

“I’ll set it.”

“You’ll faint before you’ve started and then you’ll lose it,” said Shiyu.

The midwife looked at her. Shiyu knelt in the dust, splinted the leg where it lay with a roof slat and a strip of her own sash, and held Auntie Fen’s eyes until something in them gave.

“Tonight. It must be cleaned and set before tonight, or the fever takes it. I need light. I need Second Son to pull. I need you not to fight me,” said Shiyu.

“Your lamps are fish-oil. They’re dim and they smoke. You’ll see nothing,” said Auntie Fen bitterly.

“Then I’ll find a better lamp.”

She walked back from the midwife’s house in the late afternoon, with the net sling cutting into her neck and seven children hanging on her skirt, thinking about the bone and the wound and what she could do with one arm by fish-oil light.

Little Ke, the smallest, was running backwards in front of her, telling a long story about a goose. She caught her heel on a stone.

Shiyu’s hand went out before she’d decided anything. She caught the child by the back of her jacket and set her on her feet.

“Look where you’re going, little goose.”

The children shrieked with laughter. She looked up, smiling, over their heads.

At the bottom of the lane, where the path came down from the hills, two men in plain grey scholars’ robes had stopped beside a salt trader’s mules. One of them was standing perfectly still. Then he wasn’t.

chapters.title: A Lamp for the Midwife
chapters.desc: He finds her. Then he holds a lamp for four hours while she sets a midwife’s broken leg with one arm.
chapters.epigraph: “Hold a lamp. Where I tell you. For as long as it takes. And not faint.”
chapters.content:
He didn’t run. Afterwards she thought that was the most like him of anything he did that day. He came up the lane at a pace that was nearly a run and wasn’t one, and the children scattered out of his way like hens, and he stopped a single pace from her and looked at her.

She’d seen his face do a great many things in four years, all of them small. She’d learned the corner of his mouth and the set of his jaw and the half-breath before he answered a question he hadn’t expected. She’d built a whole language out of the little he let show.

None of it was any use now. Nothing was held back. He looked like a man who hadn’t slept in two weeks and had walked over a mountain in the dark and had just found the one thing he’d been afraid he’d never see again, and he didn’t try to make it look like anything else.

“You told them not to cross.” His voice was rough.

“Did you?”

“We came over the hill.”

She let out a breath she seemed to have been holding for thirteen days. “Good. That’s good.”

He reached into his robe and brought out something small, and held it out on his open palm. The pouch. She took it with her good hand. The silk was stiff and faded, the stitching loose at one corner, and her fingers closed over it and pressed before she’d decided anything at all.

“You do that when there’s something you can’t say.”

She looked up at him. “How long have you known?”

“Since the tent.”

Since she was eighteen. Since the interrogation, when she’d stood in front of him and his five officers and told the truth because she couldn’t think of a lie good enough. He’d been watching her hands even then.

She’d been steady for thirteen days. She’d put her own shoulder back and sweated out a fever on a stranger’s floor and lanced a headman’s hand with a fishing knife. She’d been steady because there’d been nobody to be anything else in front of.

Now there was. She stepped forward and put her forehead against his chest and stood there with the pouch crushed in her fist and her bad arm trapped between them, and shook. Not crying, exactly. Shaking, the way a body does when it finally puts something heavy down. His hand came up and rested on the back of her head. Not steady either.

“I’m here,” he said into her hair. He said it twice.

Behind them in the lane a dozen children stood in solid, staring silence.

Chen Ye cleared his throat. “Who’d like to see a scholar do a trick with a copper coin?”

They didn’t understand a word of his careful Qingzhou speech. They understood the coin. He led them off down the lane towards the river with the air of a man who’d done this before, and Tuo followed with the mules, laughing his dropped-pot laugh.

She stayed where she was a while longer. Then she stepped back, wiped her face with the heel of her good hand, and looked at him properly.

“You look terrible.”

“I haven’t slept.”

“For how long?”

He thought about it. “Some time.”

“How long is some time?”

His eyes went to the bruise on her cheek, the sling, the borrowed jacket, and something moved in his jaw. “Since the dispatch. Your shoulder.”

“Second Son pulled it and I told him not to stop. It’s in. It’ll be weak for a month. I had a fever; it’s gone. I’m thin and my head aches in the mornings. That’s all of it. I promise.”

She watched him not ask the next question. “Peng Yao. He didn’t push me,” she said instead.

The General went still.

She held his eyes. “His hands were in front of me. He made sure I saw them. Someone was behind me. I can’t prove it. I’m telling you because I said I’d tell you things when they’re relevant.”

His voice was low. “I know he didn’t. The witness saw two men on the path. Not one. I’ve had every man who was on that bridge brought in since. I’ll find him.”

“There was a soldier who lifted the child. I think he had a scar on his hand. A burn, across the knuckles. I was feverish when I remembered it.”

“Then I’ll look at every soldier’s hands in the Qingzhou garrison and you can tell me whether the fever was right,” said the General.

He nodded slowly, as if filing each thing where he could find it again. Then his face changed.

“Your father sent his coat. He said you’d be cold.”

That nearly undid her a second time. She pressed the pouch instead.

“Is he—”

“He goes to the second bend every morning. Your mother keeps the gate open. Mei Yun’s kept the clinic running. They’re all well. They’ll be better when they see you.”

“Then we’ll go tomorrow. First light.”

She saw him start to say now, and decide not to.

“Tomorrow. Tonight you’ll eat something and sleep.”

“Tonight I can’t,” said Shiyu.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him about Auntie Fen as they walked up the lane. The midwife’s shin had broken through the skin at noon. It had to be cleaned and set before dark, or the fever would take the leg, and a midwife who couldn’t walk to a birth couldn’t work, and a woman who couldn’t work in Wide Water couldn’t eat.

“She doesn’t trust me. She’s set every bone in this village for thirty years, and she thinks I’m a girl who fell in a river.”

“You are a girl who fell in a river.”

“I’m a physician who fell in a river. I’ve only got one arm. Second Son can pull, he’s done it before. But I need light, and their lamps are fish-oil. They’re dim and they smoke,” said Shiyu.

He was quiet for a few steps. “What can I do?”

He didn’t say you should rest, or let someone else. She’d known he wouldn’t, and it still went through her like warmth.

“Hold a lamp. Where I tell you. For as long as it takes. And not faint.”

“I’ve never fainted.”

“You’ve never held a lamp for a bone coming through skin.”

“I’ve held worse things than lamps.”

“Not for me. Not with your hands steady,” said Shiyu.

Auntie Fen didn’t want a man in the room. The headman didn’t want a stranger in the room. Shiyu stood in the doorway with her arm in a sling and told them, in her five words of dialect and a great deal of pointing, that she needed light and hands she trusted, and that this man had sat up with wounded soldiers through worse nights than this and was good at holding things still. All of which was true.

The midwife looked at him a long while, propped on her pallet with her leg in its roof-slat splint. He looked back with a face so plainly serious that she threw up her hands.

“Him?” said Auntie Fen, to Shiyu.

“Him.”

“He’s a scholar. Scholars faint.”

“This one won’t.”

“If he faints on my leg I’ll set his nose,” said Auntie Fen.

Chen Ye, outside, translated that from Tuo’s translation, and the General inclined his head to the midwife with perfect gravity.

“Madam. If I faint, you may.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He held the lamp for four hours. Tuo had dug a proper oil lamp out of his saddlebags, brass with a glass chimney, traded long ago from a capital pedlar, and the General held it where she told him, high and steady, and moved it when she said move, and didn’t look away from anything.

He watched her wash the wound with boiled salt water until it ran clean, talking all the while in her bad dialect to the midwife, who swore at her in good dialect and then, slowly, stopped swearing and started answering. He watched her pick grit and splinters of bone out with a boiled needle, one at a time, her one good hand sure.

“Lower. Left. Hold it there.”

“Here?”

“There. Don’t breathe on it.”

“I’ll try not to breathe.”

“Try hard,” said Shiyu, not looking up.

He watched her lay the leg straight and set Second Son at the foot of the pallet and Old Nai at the head, the quilt roll passed under the midwife’s arms as it had once passed under her own. He watched her put her good hand flat on the break.

“Fen. Look at me. Not the leg. Me.”

“I’m looking.”

“When I say, he pulls. You’ll want to scream. Scream. Don’t move.”

“I’ve told a hundred women that.”

“Then you know it’s true. Second Son. Slowly.”

The midwife screamed. She didn’t move. Somewhere in the long dreadful stretch of it the bone went home under Shiyu’s palm with a sound the General would remember for the rest of his life, and Shiyu said stop and hold and good, and the room let out its breath.

She stitched the skin closed by his lamplight with silk unpicked from the hem of her own borrowed jacket, eleven stitches, small and even. She splinted the leg properly with two boards Second Son planed while they waited. She packed the wound with salt and boiled cloth and told Old Nai, slowly, three times, how to change it.

Auntie Fen lay grey and sweating on the pallet and looked at the river doctor.

“You’ll walk. Not this month. By the new year. You’ll limp in the rain. But you’ll walk to every birth in this valley,” said Shiyu.

The midwife said something short. Old Nai began to cry.

“What did she say?” asked the General.

“She said I can come back and deliver the headman’s grandchildren any time I like. That’s an enormous compliment. She’s never let anyone into a birthing room in thirty years,” said Shiyu.

He put the lamp down on the shelf. He found he had to.

She sat back on her heels on the earth floor. Her hair had come down. There was blood to her elbow. She looked up at him, and her face was grey with tiredness and completely happy.

He crouched beside her so their eyes were level.

“Is it always like that?”

She thought about it. “No. Sometimes it’s easy. Sometimes it’s worse.”

He looked at the midwife, already dozing under the willow-bark draught, and back at her.

He paused. “I’ve watched you work before. At the camp. At the inn. I thought I knew what it was. I didn’t.”

She didn’t know what to say to that. So she held out her good hand, the one with blood to the elbow, and he took it without hesitating and helped her up, and when she was on her feet he didn’t let go. He bent his head and kissed her, there in the midwife’s doorway, gently, with the lamp still smoking on the shelf and the whole of Wide Water asleep.

“You smell of fish,” he said against her mouth.

“You smell of mule.”

“Tuo’s mules. They hate each other. I’ve been between them for a day and a half.”

“Kiss me again anyway.”

He did. Outside, the sky over the wide water was turning grey. Chen Ye sat on the midwife’s step with a sleeping child against each shoulder. He looked at the two of them in the doorway: her hair, the General’s sleeves, their hands, which neither of them had yet remembered to let go.

He said nothing whatsoever. He didn’t need to. His face said it for him.

chapters.title: Two Things She Had Not Said
chapters.desc: By a fire on the ridge she says two things out loud: that she loves him, and where she really comes from.
chapters.epigraph: “Everyone’s a little frightened of me. You never were.”
chapters.content:
They left Wide Water at noon, after she’d slept four hours on Old Nai’s floor and checked Auntie Fen’s leg twice and the headman’s hand once and the boy’s nail wound for the last time. Old Nai wouldn’t take silver. The General tried three times, and on the third she slapped his hand, quite hard, and said something that made Shiyu laugh until she had to hold her bad shoulder.

“What did she say?”

“That you’ve lovely manners for a scholar, and if you try to pay her again she’ll feed you to the pike.”

He bowed to Old Nai, low, the way he’d have bowed to a duchess. Old Nai looked deeply pleased with herself. In the end he left the silver with the headman, for the village, and nobody slapped him for that.

Auntie Fen had herself carried to her door on a plank to watch them go.

“River doctor,” she called, and then something else.

“What was that?” said the General.

“She says next time I come I’m to bring the scholar with the lamp, because he’s the only man she’s ever met who doesn’t talk.”

“I’ll come.”

“She also says you’ve a face like a magistrate and she’d marry you herself if she were thirty years younger.”

“Tell her she’d have to fight you for me,” said the General, and Shiyu translated it, and Auntie Fen laughed so hard she nearly fell off the plank.

The children walked them to the foot of the hill path, and Little Ke cried, and Shiyu crouched and promised in her terrible dialect that she’d come back when the water was low and her arm was better. She meant it. She’d already decided.

The path was steep and her legs were weaker than she wanted. He didn’t offer to carry her. He walked on the outside edge where the slope fell away, and when she stumbled his hand was at her good elbow before she’d finished stumbling, and when she was steady it went away again. Chen Ye and Tuo and the mules walked ahead and somehow always happened to stop and wait just when she needed to sit down.

✦ ✦ ✦

They reached the shepherd’s hut on the ridge at dusk. Chen Ye made a fire outside it and cooked rice and dried fish in Tuo’s pot, and then announced that he and Tuo would sleep on the far side of the hut with the mules, because the mules liked company, and went off with a briskness that fooled nobody.

The night was clear. Below them the hills fell away in folds of dark, and far off to the west a faint smudge of light might have been the border post. Her father’s coat was round her shoulders. It smelled of his study, ink and dried herbs, and she kept turning her face into the collar.

They sat by the fire without talking. It was the kind of quiet they’d always been good at.

“There are two things I haven’t said,” she said at last.

He turned his head.

She looked at him across the small fire. “The first is easy. I wrote it. I’ve never said it out loud. I love you.”

He didn’t move. She watched it reach him.

“I wanted you to hear it in my voice. Not charcoal, not ink. In case the river ever tries again.”

“The river won’t try again.”

“You can’t order a river, Lingyun.”

His voice was rough. “I can have a fence built at the second bend, and I’ve already sent the order. Say it again.”

“I love you.”

“Again.”

“You’re very greedy for a man who wrote it in a letter to the Censorate.”

He reached across and took her good hand. “I wrote it to you. The Censorate only had the summary. I love you. I’ll say it out loud as often as you like. I’ve been saving it.”

“For how long?”

“Since a supply box.”

She laughed, and then she didn’t, because the second thing was harder.

She pressed the pouch where it hung at her sash again. Then she made herself take her hand away.

“His Majesty told me something at the capital dinner. While you were talking to Lü Yue. He said you’d told him you didn’t know where I’d learned to think the way I do.”

He went still. Not the way he had over Peng Yao. Differently.

“He told you that.”

She looked at the fire. “He told me he’d asked you, and you’d said you didn’t know, and you’d decided it wasn’t your business. He seemed to find that interesting. You’ve never asked me. Not in the tent, not at the inn, not in any letter. I used to wonder why.”

He spoke slowly. “Because I thought if I asked, you’d have to choose between telling me and lying to me. And I didn’t think you’d lie to me. So I didn’t want to make you choose.”

She had to look away.

She drew her father’s coat tighter. “I’m going to tell you now. Because I don’t want there to be anything I haven’t told you, and because if I don’t say it tonight, up here, I don’t think I’ll ever find a better place. You can decide afterwards that I’m mad. I’ll understand.”

“Tell me.”

So she told him. About a city he couldn’t picture, where the streets were lit all night and the buildings stood taller than the palace walls. About a hospital as big as the Northern Army’s whole camp, where she’d been a surgeon, a physician who cuts, for fifteen years, putting people back together after carts and falls and fires and fights. About how good she’d been at it, and how tired, and how alone. About driving home through rain after two days without sleep, and lights coming the wrong way out of the dark, and nothing after that.

And then waking at five years old, in a fever, in her mother’s arms in Qingzhou, with a whole other life behind her eyes and no idea how she’d got there.

She told it plainly, the way she’d explain a diagnosis, and didn’t dress it up. She watched his face the whole time. It told her nothing at all, and she kept going anyway.

She spread her good hand. “I’ve never told anyone. Not my mother. Not my uncle. They know I’m strange. They decided long ago to love me without knowing why. That’s where I learned to think the way I do. I didn’t learn it. I brought it with me.”

The fire cracked. On the far side of the hut a mule shifted. He was quiet so long she began, despite everything, to be afraid.

“Was it a good life?” he said.

She stared at him. Of everything she’d imagined him saying, and she’d imagined a great deal, in four years of dark, she’d never once imagined that.

Her voice did something she didn’t mean it to. “It was a busy one. I was good at my work. I helped a lot of people. I was very lonely. I didn’t know how lonely until I came here and had a mother who fussed and a father who forgot to eat and an uncle who argued with me about everything.”

He nodded slowly. “And when you went into the river. Did you think—”

He stopped. She saw him understand all of it before he’d finished the sentence.

She was crying now and didn’t try to stop. “Yes. I thought: I died once and woke up somewhere else. What if it happens again? What if I wake up there, and none of this is real, and I’m alone again with all the lights? And I thought, I don’t want to go back. Everything I want is here. And I held on to that branch.”

He took her good hand in both of his. They were warm from the fire.

“Then I’m grateful to the branch.”

It was so exactly what he’d say, so plain, so serious, so unlike anything anyone else in either of her lives would have said, that she laughed through the crying and couldn’t stop.

“You don’t think I’m mad.”

He turned her hand over and looked at it, at the little calluses from the mortar and the brush. “I’ve read every report you’ve written since you were eighteen. I told the Emperor I didn’t know where you learned to think like that. I’ve spent four years not knowing. It’s a relief, a little, to know. It explains the first report.”

“It explains the first report,” she repeated, and laughed again.

“And it explains why you were never frightened of me. I couldn’t understand it. Everyone’s a little frightened of me. You never were.”

“I was frightened of you all the time. I just wasn’t frightened of what you’d do to me.”

He was quiet. “I won’t tell anyone.”

“I know.”

“Not His Majesty. Not Chen Ye.”

“Chen Ye will guess.”

“Chen Ye guesses everything. That isn’t the same as being told.”

“Lingyun.”

“Yes.”

“Kiss me. Before I think about it too much and decide I’ve made a terrible mistake.”

He leaned across the little fire, careful of her shoulder, and kissed her: slowly, and then again, his hand at her jaw, until the wood popped between them and they both drew back laughing.

“You’ll set your sleeve alight,” she said.

“It wouldn’t be the worst thing that’s happened to it this fortnight.”

They sat afterwards with her hand in his, watching the fire burn down. At some point she fell asleep against his shoulder with her father’s coat round her. He didn’t move until morning. He told her later it was the best night’s sleep he hadn’t had in years.

chapters.title: The Second Bend at Dawn
chapters.desc: Home at dawn: her father on the riverbank without his coat, and a soldier with a burned hand.
chapters.epigraph: “Every patient. Every day. The same format. I didn’t miss one.”
chapters.content:
The moment they came off the hill path onto the river plain, he stopped being a private scholar following a river. She watched it happen. One step he was beside her in a grey robe with mud to the knees. The next he’d seen the flag of the border post, and something in his shoulders settled into place, and by the time they reached the post he was giving orders.

“A rider to Qingzhou. Now. The fastest horse. To the governor’s house: she’s safe, she’s with me, we’ll be home by morning.”

“Yes, sir.”

“A second rider to the garrison commander. The duty roll for the day of the riverbank. The names of every soldier sent to the bridge at the second bend. Both those men found and held, separately, before nightfall. Don’t tell them why.”

“Yes, sir.”

“And a carriage. With every quilt in this post. The physician has one working arm and she isn’t riding forty li.”

“I can ride,” said Shiyu.

“I know you can. You’re not going to.”

She opened her mouth.

“Please,” he said.

She shut it. He’d never said please to her before. She got into the carriage.

Chen Ye didn’t. He took the second-best horse and a copy of the order to the garrison, and looked at the General.

“The right hand. A burn across the knuckles,” said the General.

Chen Ye nodded once, and was gone down the river road before the first rider’s dust had settled.

✦ ✦ ✦

They travelled through the night. The carriage was hard and the road was bad, and she slept anyway in snatches, her head against the window frame and her father’s coat round her. Each time she woke he was riding beside the window. Once she woke and he was looking in at her, and he didn’t look away when she caught him. He kept looking, like a man who’d decided he was allowed to now.

“Go to sleep,” he said.

“You go to sleep.”

“I’m on a horse.”

“You’ve slept on horses. Chen Ye told me. At the eastern pass, three days, and you fell off at the end.”

“Chen Ye is going to be posted to the southern garrisons,” said the General.

“They don’t need inspecting.”

“They will now,” he said, and she fell asleep smiling against the window frame.

They came into Qingzhou from the east along the river path as the sky turned from black to grey. She knew where they were before she saw it. The river had a different voice at the second bend: louder, harder, the water piling against the rocks before the gorge. She’d never in her life been afraid of that sound. Now her whole body went tight, and she was angry with herself, and she breathed through it the way she’d taught a hundred frightened patients to breathe.

“Stop here.”

He didn’t ask why. He stopped the carriage. She climbed down carefully. The bank was wet with dew.

Fifty paces on, right at the edge where the path ran beside the water, a man stood alone with his back to them, looking at the river. He wasn’t young. His shoulders were rounded. He had a notebook in one hand and no coat on, and it was cold at dawn by the river.

She walked towards him. Her legs weren’t steady and she didn’t care.

“Father.”

He turned. She’d seen her father surprised many times: by plants, by old books, by a well-argued footnote. She’d never seen his face do what it did now. It went loose and young and open all at once, like a child’s, and the notebook fell out of his hand into the wet grass. He didn’t say anything. He took two steps and put his arms round her, carefully, minding the sling, and held on.

Her voice had gone to pieces. “You haven’t got your coat on. It’s cold. You’re freezing.”

He held her tighter. “I gave it away. To a young man going over a mountain. I knew you’d be cold.”

Behind them the General had stopped by the carriage and was looking at the river.

After a while her father let go, wiped his face with his sleeve and bent stiffly for his notebook. He brushed the wet grass off it with great care. Then he turned to the General, and didn’t bow, and did none of the correct things a governor does when a supreme commander stands on his riverbank.

“Thank you.”

“She came back by herself. I only walked beside her.”

Yun Chengde gave him the slightly bewildered look he gave things that were more than he’d expected.

“Yes. That’s what I meant.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother was at the gate. The gate stood open. A lamp hung beside it, still lit in the grey light, with the look of a lamp that had been lit every night for weeks. Her mother stood under it in her house robe with her hair down, which Shiyu hadn’t seen since she was small.

She didn’t run either. She waited until her daughter was close enough to touch, and then put a hand on each cheek, careful of the bruise, and looked at her.

“You’re thin.”

“I know.”

“You’ll eat.”

“Yes, Mother.”

Her mother nodded. That settled everything. Then she put her forehead to her daughter’s and stood like that, saying nothing, while the lamp burned beside them. When at last she stepped back, she looked past Shiyu to the General, who’d stopped outside the gate.

“You’ll come in. You’ll eat too. You look worse than she does.”

Not a question. He came in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mei Yun came an hour later, running, hair half pinned, a clinic apron still on. She stopped in the doorway of the room where Shiyu sat with a bowl of congee and her uncle prodding her shoulder, and looked at her for one breath with a completely naked face.

Then she burst into tears, loudly, like a child.

Then she stopped, scrubbed her face fiercely with the apron, and lifted her chin. “I kept the records.”

“I know you did.”

Her voice wobbled and she ignored it. “Every patient. Every day. The same format. I didn’t miss one. Old Master Feng came every morning and asked. I told him you’d gone to the capital. He didn’t believe me. He brought pears anyway. There are a great many pears.”

Shiyu put down the congee and held out her good arm, and Mei Yun crossed the room in three steps and hugged her so hard that Uncle Xiang said, “The shoulder, girl,” and was ignored by both of them.

Her uncle had ridden down from the camp the day the news reached him and had spent the last ten days, according to her mother, being rude to everyone. He examined the shoulder now with fingers less steady than they should have been.

“Adequate. For a fishing village.”

“Second Son did it beautifully.”

“Second Son can have a post in the army medical service any time he likes. This sling is a disgrace.” He made her a new one himself, and tied it, and didn’t say anything else for a while. When he’d finished, he put his hand on her head, the way he had when she was seven, and went out of the room fast.

She read Mei Yun’s records that afternoon, in bed, because her mother wouldn’t let her up. They were excellent. The handwriting was neater than her own. In the margin of the eighth day, beside a note about a child with a fever, Mei Yun had written in tiny characters: She’d have tried the willow bark first. I tried the willow bark first.

Shiyu put her hand over the line and lay still for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Ye came to the house at dusk. He found the General in the courtyard, where he’d been since the afternoon, not sleeping though Lady Ren had told him twice to sleep, but sitting on the bench under the window of the room where Shiyu was resting. Chen Ye didn’t remark on it.

“Duan Ping. Garrison infantry, six years’ service. Right hand burned across the knuckles as a boy. He was one of the two men sent to the bridge. He asked for leave the morning after the riverbank and he’s spent it in a gambling house in the river district, losing more silver than a soldier earns in a year.”

The General didn’t move.

Something cold crossed Chen Ye’s face. “I had him brought to the garrison. I sat down across the table from him. I hadn’t said a word. He started talking before I’d finished sitting down. Peng Yao paid him. Peng Yao told him where to stand. He says he only meant to frighten her. He says he didn’t think the bank would give.”

“And the silver.”

Chen Ye held out a folded paper. “From a man who came to him in the river district a month ago. A steward, he says, from a great house in the capital. He knew the face. I showed him some faces. It’s the steward of Deputy Minister Kang.”

The General took the paper. He didn’t open it. He knew the name. He’d known it since the day she first told him where Peng Yao came from.

“She knew. Didn’t she. About the hand,” said Chen Ye.

The General looked up at the window. “She worked it out on a stranger’s floor, with a fever. And then she told me she wasn’t sure.”

Chen Ye followed his gaze.

“Of course she did.”

Above them the window opened, and Shiyu leaned out on her good elbow in her mother’s quilt, with her hair down.

“I heard all of that. Was it the scar?” she said.

“It was the scar.”

She looked down at the General on his bench. “Then the fever was right. Lingyun. My mother’s told you twice to sleep.”

“I’m going to.”

“You’re going to sit on that bench until morning.”

“I’m going to sit on this bench until morning, and then I’ll sleep.”

“There’s a room made up for you on the east side.”

He didn’t get up. “I know. Your mother showed me. It’s a very good room. It hasn’t got you at the window.”

She looked at him. Then she said, “Chen Ye, go away,” and Chen Ye went, grinning, and she stayed leaning on the sill, and he stayed on the bench below, and they talked in low voices about nothing much until the lamp at the gate was the only light in the house.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.desc: A dry old censor, a careful witness, and the General answering the word “irregular” in public.
chapters.epigraph: “I love her. If the Censorate needs a word for that, the word it’s looking for isn’t impropriety.”
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
The Censorate sent a censor called Fang Mingshan, who arrived in Qingzhou eleven days later with two clerks, a chest of documents, and a reputation for once having made a provincial governor cry in open court. He was a small, dry, elderly man with spotless fingernails. He took the garrison’s administrative hall for the hearing, had the benches moved so nobody could sit at the back, and announced that he’d hear everything in one day, in order.

“Anyone who wastes my time will be noted in the record as having wasted it. The record is permanent. I have a long memory and a longer archive.”

Shiyu liked him at once. Her shoulder was out of the sling by then, though not yet strong. She wore a plain dark jacket, not the green coat, which was for presenting and this wasn’t that kind of day, and she sat on the witness bench with her hands in her lap and her mother’s voice in her head. Eat. Sleep. Tell the truth. Don’t let them hurry you.

The General sat across the hall among the officials, in full uniform for the first time since the riverbank road. He hadn’t come near her that morning. He’d told her the night before that he wouldn’t, so nobody could say afterwards that he’d spoken to her before she gave evidence.

“That’s very sensible, and I hate it,” she’d said.

“So do I. I’ll be across the hall. I’ll be looking at the censor. I won’t be looking at you.”

“Not once?”

“Not once, and it’ll be the hardest thing I’ve done this year, including the mountain.”

Peng Yao was brought in under guard. She hadn’t seen him since the riverbank. He looked smaller. His robe was clean, someone had let him shave, and he’d put the pleasant expression back on, though it no longer quite fitted. He bowed to the censor correctly. He didn’t look at her. Duan Ping came in after him and looked at no one at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The censor took the riverbank first. The river worker who’d raised the alarm said what he’d seen from the far end of the path.

“A woman in the water, Your Honour. And a man in a garrison coat going up the slope. Fast, but not running.”

“Not running.”

“No, Your Honour. Walking fast. Like a man who doesn’t want to be seen hurrying. I thought he was going for help.”

“Did he come back with help?”

“He never came back at all.”

The garrison commander read out the duty roll. Two soldiers sent to the bridge. One back at the garrison inside the hour. One not back until the next morning, and then asking for leave.

A clerk read Duan Ping’s confession into the record, slowly, every word. The silver. The instructions. Where to stand. He said she’d step back. He said all I had to do was be there when she did. Duan Ping sat with his burned hand in his lap and his head down and denied none of it. Once, when the clerk read out I only meant to frighten her, his shoulders shook.

Then the censor called her. She walked to the front. She told it the way she’d told the General by the fire: in order, without colour, exactly as much as she knew and no more. The child at the bridge. The two soldiers. Peng Yao at the corner of the path. What he said. Where he stood. Where his hands were.

“And the push,” said the censor.

“From behind. Low on the back. A flat hand.”

“Did you see whose hand?”

“No.”

On the far side of the hall Peng Yao lifted his head.

“You didn’t see.”

She kept her eyes on the censor. “I didn’t see. I was facing Peng Yao. Afterwards, in a fever, I remembered a burn scar on the back of a man’s hand. I told the General at the time that I couldn’t swear to it, because I was feverish when I remembered it. I still can’t. I can swear to the push. I can swear Peng Yao was in front of me the whole time, and both his hands were in front of him, open, where I could see them.”

Peng Yao spoke in his pleasant voice. “The physician admits she doesn’t know who touched her.”

The censor turned his head slowly and looked at him, and Peng Yao stopped.

He looked back at Shiyu. “You’ll have your turn. It isn’t now. Why do you mention his hands, Physician? A man may hold his hands where he likes.”

She showed the censor, exactly as she’d shown the General. “He wanted me to see them. That’s why I remember them. He held them a little out from his sides, like a man showing you he isn’t carrying anything. I’ve stood opposite a great many frightened people, and a great many who were lying to me. Nobody stands like that by accident. He was making sure that whatever happened next, I’d remember it wasn’t his hands. I did remember. It’s how I knew someone was behind me.”

The hall was silent. The censor wrote something down. It took him some time.

✦ ✦ ✦

When it was Peng Yao’s turn, he did well, for a while. He was calm and reasonable and regretful.

“I went to the riverbank to give the physician advice, Your Honour. About the commission’s future. Nothing more. Duan Ping is a gambler and a liar who pushed a woman into a river for reasons of his own, and is now trying to save his neck by blaming a man of good family. It’s a tragedy. I’m deeply sorry for it.”

“Thank you. How does a garrison infantryman on a soldier’s pay come to be carrying silver stamped with the mark of the capital’s Western Mint?” said the censor.

“I’ve no idea.”

“How do you explain that a steward of Deputy Minister Kang’s household was seen in the river district of Qingzhou on three separate days in the month before the riverbank, and lodged in the same house as you?”

“Qingzhou is a large city.”

The censor turned a page. “It is. On the morning after the riverbank you wrote to Deputy Minister Kang. The courier station kept a copy, as courier stations do. It contains the sentence The difficulty in Qingzhou has resolved itself. What difficulty?”

Peng Yao didn’t answer.

“I’m waiting, Secretary. The record’s waiting. The record is very patient,” said the censor.

The pleasant expression didn’t so much fall off Peng Yao’s face as slowly stop being there. What was left wasn’t frightening. It was tired and bitter and wholly ordinary.

✦ ✦ ✦

The General was called last. He stood in his uniform, and every official in the hall sat a little straighter, and he walked to the front and faced the censor and didn’t look at her once.

He spoke for a few sentences about the inquiry he’d held and the records he’d sent the Emperor; about Peng Yao’s first review, the attempt to stop the letters, the concern sent to the Censorate. He used the flat plain voice he used for battle reports, and it was devastating, because it so plainly wasn’t trying to be.

“The concern Peng Yao submitted to this office describes your correspondence with the physician as an irregularity. You’ve said you wish to answer that formally,” said the censor.

“Yes.”

Shiyu’s hands tightened in her lap.

For the first time his voice wasn’t quite flat. “There’s nothing irregular about it. I wrote to the physician every week for most of a year. Some of the letters were about the commission. Some weren’t. I wrote them because I wanted to write to her. She answered them, I believe, for the same reason. I love her. If the Censorate needs a word for that, the word it’s looking for isn’t impropriety.”

Nobody in the hall moved. The censor looked at him over his spotless fingernails for a long breath. Then he looked across the hall.

“Physician. Do you wish to add anything?”

She stood. Her knees weren’t entirely reliable. She didn’t care.

“Only that he’s right. I answered them for the same reason.”

She sat down. On the far side of the hall, Chen Ye was studying the ceiling with the face of a man trying hard not to look at anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

The censor gave his findings at sunset.

Duan Ping: to the Ministry of Justice for sentence, with a note that he’d confessed fully and without pressure, and that the physician he’d injured had asked in writing that his sentence take account of his mother in the river district, who depended on him.
