Shiyu had written that note in the morning. She still wasn’t sure whether she’d done it because it was right or because she wanted to be someone who did it. She thought perhaps those weren’t so different.

Peng Yao: stripped of rank and post and sent to the Ministry of Justice for the attempted murder of an imperial appointee, with the censor’s recommendation of exile to the far southern frontier, for life.

Deputy Minister Kang: a report to the Emperor, every document attached.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, late, the General came to the clinic. She was in the preparation room, because she couldn’t sleep and her hands wanted something to do. He sat on the stool beside her without being asked.

“His Majesty’s answer about Kang will take a week. He’ll be dismissed. He’ll be allowed to say it’s for his health.”

“That seems generous.”

He watched her grind mugwort. “It’s the kind of generous that leaves no complications. His Majesty gave me permission, weeks ago, to answer for this personally. I’ve decided how.”

She put the pestle down.

“You told me on the ridge you’d ordered a fence.”

His face was perfectly grave. “I did. I didn’t tell you who’d pay for it. Stone posts and a timber rail, the whole length of the path, and along the abutment where the children jump. The city’s been meaning to build it for as long as anyone can remember. It’ll be built this autumn. At the end of it there’ll be a stone saying who paid. Deputy Minister Kang is going to pay. Out of his own household. I’ve already written to explain to him that he’d like to.”

She stared at him. “The stone will have his name on it.”

“In large characters. Clearly cut. Where every child who sits on that fence will be able to read it.”

“That’s petty.”

“Yes,” he agreed.

She started to laugh. She couldn’t help it. She laughed until her shoulder ached and she had to hold it, and he sat on the stool and watched her with an expression she’d never seen on his face. It took her a moment to work out what it was. He was pleased with himself.

She could barely get the words out. “You said it. In front of the Censorate. In front of a clerk who writes down every word.”

“I said I’d say it to anyone who asked.”

“He didn’t ask.”

“He was about to. I saved him the trouble. He’s a busy man,” said the General.

She leaned over and kissed him, with mugwort on her fingers, and he caught her face and kissed her back, and the white mortar rocked on the table between them and nearly went over, and neither of them did anything about it.

chapters.title: Something for Himself
chapters.desc: For the first time in his life, he asks for something that isn’t for the army. She has conditions.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll try. I’ll be bad at it. You’ll have to tell me when I’m being bad at it.”
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
He was meant to go north at the end of the ninth month. He’d been away from the camp six weeks. Dispatches came every day. Wei Tiecheng had written twice in his short blunt hand. The first said Everything is in order. The second said Everything is still in order. Come back anyway. From Wei Tiecheng that was close to a plea.

She knew all of it. She knew he couldn’t stay. She’d known from the first letter that this was how it would always be: a season of him, then the road north, then letters. She’d told herself she could live with it. She thought she probably could.

On the morning before he was due to leave he came to the clinic at midday, when the waiting room was empty and Mei Yun had gone to market, and found her in the preparation room with the mortar. He pulled the second stool from the wall and sat beside her, the way he had on his first morning in Qingzhou at the start of the summer, which felt a lifetime ago. He didn’t say anything for a while. She ground. He watched.

“I’ve never asked anyone for anything,” he said.

She stopped.

He was looking at the herb cabinet, not at her. “I’ve asked for things for the army. Men. Grain. Horses. Authority. I’ve asked His Majesty for a great many things, and all of them were for the army. When I was fifteen, after my parents died, he asked me what I wanted. I didn’t understand the question. I said I wanted to be useful. He gave me a sword and a tutor and sent me north. I’ve been useful ever since.”

She put the pestle down without a sound.

“What did he say?”

He turned his head and looked at her. “He said, ‘That’s not what I asked.’ I didn’t understand that either. Chen Ye says I don’t know how to want things for myself. He’s usually right about me. He’s right about this. I’m trying to learn. I’m not very good at it yet. So I’m going to say this plainly, because I don’t know any other way to say it.”

She waited. She’d always known how to wait for him.

“I want to marry you. If you’ll have me.”

The preparation room was quiet. Out in the lane someone was calling the price of chestnuts. She found she’d known he’d say it, had known for weeks, perhaps since the fire on the ridge, and that knowing made no difference at all. It still went through her like the first warm day of spring.

“Before you answer. I’ve thought about the rest of it. I don’t want you to say yes and then find out what you’ve said yes to,” he said.

“Tell me.”

“I’ve written to His Majesty asking to divide the year. Winter on the frontier, when the passes close and the fighting stops and the army sits in winter quarters. That’s when the camp most needs a physician who can teach. The rest of the year in Qingzhou, with the southern garrisons under my command.”

“The ones that need inspecting.”

“The ones that will always need inspecting. And the frontier under Wei Tiecheng, who’s been asking for it for two years and will hold it better than anyone. Lin Wenyuan’s drawn up the dispatch routes. Lü Yue’s read the plan and called it sound, which from Lü Yue is a blessing,” said the General gravely.

“And the clinic?”

“When you’re in the north, Mei Yun runs it. If you think she’s ready.”

“She’s ready. She’s been ready for a year. I just hadn’t told her.”

He paused. “And when you’re here, you work. As you work now. As much as you like. I wouldn’t know how to stop you. I wouldn’t want to be the kind of man who tried.”

She looked at him. “You’ve been thinking about this for a while.”

“Since the inn. Before the inn, if I’m honest. I didn’t let myself think it in words until the capital.”

“And His Majesty said yes? To dividing the year?”

“His Majesty hasn’t answered. I didn’t want to ask him for the rest of it until I’d asked you.” The corner of his mouth moved.

She laughed, a short shaky sound, and then stopped, because she’d cry if she didn’t, and she’d cried enough that month.

“I have conditions.”

He nodded at once, as though he’d expected nothing else. “Tell me.”

“I keep my name on my work. Always. Not yours. Mine.”

“Yes.”

“The camp gets a proper medical building. Not a tent. A building, with a floor. And real lamps. Not fish-oil.”

“Yes.”

“I go back to Wide Water when the water’s low. Every year, if I can. Old Nai’s going to need her knees looked at, and Auntie Fen’s leg, and I promised Little Ke.”

“I’ll come with you. I owe a man a great deal of silver for a hill path, and a midwife wants to marry me.”

“She’ll have to fight me.”

“I’ve told her so. She was delighted.”

She stopped. The next one was harder. She made herself say it anyway, because she’d decided in a tent four years ago that she’d always tell him the truth.

“And you have to tell me. When something’s wrong. When you’re hurt, or frightened, or tired, or you don’t know what to do. You can’t keep it all behind your face for me. I’ve spent four years learning to read what you don’t say. I don’t want to spend the rest of my life doing it.”

He was quiet for a long breath.

“That one’s difficult.”

“I know.”

He held her eyes. “I’ll try. I’ll be bad at it. You’ll have to tell me when I’m being bad at it.”

“I will. Often.”

“Then yes. To all of it.”

She looked down at the mortar and the herbs half ground in it, and her own hands, which had been steady through a gorge and a fever and a broken shin by fish-oil light, and weren’t steady now.

“Then yes. I’ll marry you,” said Shiyu.

He didn’t move. She thought perhaps he hadn’t quite believed she’d say it, even now, after everything.

Then he took her face in his two hands, carefully, the way a man holds something he’s been told is fragile and knows isn’t, and kissed her. It didn’t stay careful for long. When it ended she found she was holding the front of his coat in both fists, bad shoulder and all, and didn’t remember deciding to. He rested his forehead against hers.

“You’ve herbs on your fingers.”

“I was working.”

His voice had gone low. “I know. I’ve always liked watching you work. I liked it in the medical tent. I liked it at the inn. I liked it at four in the morning by fish-oil, God help me, with a midwife threatening to break my nose.”

“You never said.”

“I’m telling you now. I’m practising.”

“Practise more.”

“I like the way you push your sleeve up with your wrist when your hands are dirty. I like that you talk to the mortar when you think no one’s listening. I like that you’ve never once let me win an argument about the fever column,” said the General.

“You’ve never been right about the fever column.”

“I know,” he said, and kissed her again.

The clinic’s front door opened and shut. Baskets clattered.

“The chestnut man was robbing everyone, so I got pears instead, there are—”

Mei Yun stopped in the preparation-room doorway. She looked at the two of them: Shiyu’s hands on his coat, his hands on her face, the mortar forgotten on the table. Her own face did something complicated and then went perfectly, serenely blank.

“I’ll be in the front. Sorting pears. For some time.”

She went. A moment later, from the front room, came the sound of someone trying not to make a sound and failing.

Shiyu put her face against his shoulder and laughed until she couldn’t breathe.

chapters.title: A Very Formal Letter
chapters.desc: Her father asks one question. The Emperor reads a letter twice and smiles.
chapters.epigraph: “I fell in love with her watching her work, sir.”
chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
He didn’t go north the next morning. He sent a dispatch to Wei Tiecheng instead. Chen Ye carried it to the garrison and told Shiyu afterwards that it said only: One more month. Then I bring you a physician for the winter. You’ll understand.

Wei Tiecheng’s answer came back by relay rider four days later and was shorter still. It said: Finally. That afternoon he went to see her father.

There were correct ways to do this. Shiyu knew them, and so did he. A matchmaker should go first, with gifts and the eight characters of his birth; the families should consult an almanac; and nobody should say anything directly to anybody for at least a month. Her mother had explained all of it at breakfast with great seriousness.

“And then the matchmaker comes back a second time with the almanac’s answer, and the families exchange gifts, and—”

“Mother.”

Lady Ren stopped, and looked at her daughter. “—and then, in the spring, if the signs are good— He isn’t going to do any of that, is he.”

“No, Mother.”

Her mother sighed. “Good. I never liked the Wang family’s matchmaker anyway. She sniffs.”

He went to her father’s study alone, in the plain dark coat he wore in Qingzhou, carrying nothing. Shiyu wasn’t in the room. She sat in the courtyard outside it on the edge of the herb bed, with a book open in her lap that she wasn’t reading. Her mother was in the corridor on the far side of the study door, arranging and rearranging a vase of chrysanthemums that hadn’t needed arranging the first time.

Through the window Shiyu could see her father at his desk among the Tang companion volumes, his nose two finger-widths from the page, the way he always read. He looked up when the General came in and blinked several times. Then he took off his outer robe, which he only did for people he considered family, and hung it over the back of his chair.

She couldn’t hear most of what they said. The General’s voice, low and even, for some while. Her father saying “Ah,” once, and then that yes, he’d wondered. And then, after a long pause, a question.

Everyone in the house heard the question. Her father had a scholar’s voice, made for reading aloud in large halls, and when he was serious he forgot to lower it.

“Will you let her work?”

A silence. Then the General’s answer, quieter, but not so quiet it didn’t carry through a paper window.

“I couldn’t stop her if I tried. I wouldn’t want to be the kind of man who tried. I fell in love with her watching her work, sir. It would be a strange thing to marry her and ask her to stop.”

Shiyu closed the book in her lap and sat still in the autumn sun.

In the study her father was quiet a long time. Then he spoke in his ordinary voice, the slightly vague one.

“Good. Good. That was the only thing, really. She’s been working since she was five, you know. Even before that she was— well. She was always herself. I never understood her, entirely. I hope you don’t expect to.”

“No, sir. I expect to spend the rest of my life trying.”

Her father seemed delighted. “Ha! Yes. That’s the right answer. That’s exactly what I’ve been doing. It’s very interesting. You’ll never be bored. Her mother will say yes before I do. She’s been outside that door for a quarter of an hour.”

The study door opened. Her mother came in carrying the chrysanthemums, as if she’d just happened to be passing with them, and set the vase on the desk on top of the Tang volumes, which made her father give a small anguished cry.

“Yes,” said Lady Ren.

“I hadn’t asked you yet,” said the General.

She looked at him. “I know. I’m saving you the trouble. You’ll eat with us tonight. And every night you’re in Qingzhou. I won’t have you eating alone.”

Something happened to the General’s face that Shiyu, through the window, had to look away from, because it seemed too private to watch.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wrote the letter to the Emperor that night at the table in the governor’s guest room. He wrote it four times. The first three he burned in the brazier.

He told her about it afterwards. “The first was too short. The second was too long. The third sounded like a request for winter supplies.”

“What did the fourth sound like?”

“Like a nephew asking his uncle for something he’s wanted for four years and been too proud to name.”

“Was it formal?”

He paused. “Very. Every correct phrase. Two pages of correct phrases. And then one sentence that wasn’t.”

“What was it?”

“I’ll tell you when he’s answered in case he says no and I have to pretend I never wrote it,” said the General.

He sealed it with his own seal and gave it to the relay rider before dawn.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Emperor received it six days later in the small study behind the audience hall, where he read the dispatches that mattered. It was raining in the capital. He had a cold. He’d spent the morning listening to the Ministry of Rites argue about precedence at the winter sacrifice, and the afternoon reading Deputy Minister Kang’s letter of resignation, which was long and full of references to his health. He wasn’t in a good temper.

His secretary put the Qingzhou letter on top of the pile without being told.

The Emperor broke the seal. He read the first part, about dividing the year between the frontier and the south, and nodded. It was sound. He’d expected it. He’d approve it.

Then he read the second part. He read it again.

His secretary, who’d served him twenty-two years and seen him receive news of victories and plagues and the deaths of three brothers, would say afterwards that he’d never seen what happened next. The Emperor put the letter down. He sat back in his chair. And he smiled: not the thin careful smile he gave ministers, but something broad and sudden that took ten years off his face.

“Well. It took him long enough,” he said, to nobody.

“Majesty?”

The Emperor tapped the last line. “My nephew wishes to marry. He writes: ‘You once asked me what I wanted, and I said to be useful. I’ve found the answer to the question you actually asked.’ All these years I’ve waited for that boy to answer me properly. Bring me the good paper. And the vermilion.”

His reply reached Qingzhou eight days later by an imperial messenger in full ceremonial dress, who had to ask three people in the river district for the governor’s house and was given four different answers.

The decree was correct in every way. It granted the division of the year. It granted the marriage, in the long formal language of the throne, with the names and titles of both parties written out in full. And it named the physician Yun Shiyu a Lady of the Fourth Rank in her own right, for service to the Northern Army and the people of Qingzhou, so that nobody could ever say she’d been given a title only for whom she married.

At the bottom, under the imperial seal, in the Emperor’s own hand, was one more line, and not in the language of the throne.

Bring her to dinner at the new year. I want to ask her about page seven.

“Page seven. He remembers,” said Shiyu, reading over his shoulder.

“He remembers everything.”

“Did you tell him?”

“Tell him what?”

“About the old official with the grey beard. The one who gave me the list.”

The General folded the decree. “I didn’t have to. He gave you the list because His Majesty asked him to find out whether you were real. You were.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Two nights before the wedding he gave her mother something. Shiyu didn’t see it happen. Her mother told her much later, on the morning of the wedding itself.

He’d come to find Lady Ren in the courtyard while she was taking in the lamp from the gate. She still lit it every night, though there was no longer any reason. She said she’d got used to it. He’d held out his hand, and on his palm lay a small jade hairpin carved with clouds.

“A fishing family found it below the gorge. I’ve been carrying it. I thought you should be the one to give it back to her.”

Her mother took it and looked at it a long while by the lamp.

“You could have given it to her yourself. Weeks ago.”

“Yes. I wanted you to have the chance to put it in her hair again,” said the General.

Her mother said she hadn’t been able to say anything to that. She’d only nodded, and closed her hand round the pin, and gone inside. She’d put it away in her own jewel box, in the drawer where she kept the things that mattered, to wait.

chapters.content:
They were married in Qingzhou in the tenth month, when chrysanthemums lined every wall in the city and the river had gone back to its ordinary autumn brown.

The Five arrived three days before, which Shiyu hadn’t expected, since somebody had to hold the frontier. It turned out Wei Tiecheng had left it with his second-in-command and a long list of instructions, and had told the whole camp that anyone who sent him a dispatch during the wedding would be digging latrines until spring. Lin Wenyuan had drawn up the duty rosters for the journey. Zhou Hua had complained about the length of it every single day. Lü Yue had said nothing the whole way, which Chen Ye said meant he was deeply moved.

They came to the clinic the first afternoon, all five in plain clothes, and stood in her front room looking at the shelves.

“So this is where it all comes from,” said Zhou Hua, with enormous satisfaction, and knocked over a jar of dried chrysanthemum.

“Captain Zhou. Your leg.”

“Perfect, Physician. I climbed a wall last month.”

“Why were you climbing a wall?”

“There was a wall and you’d said I’d never climb one again, so I had to,” said Zhou Hua.

“I said you’d never climb one again if you took the splint off early.”

He beamed. “I didn’t take it off early. I took it off on the exact day. Lin Wenyuan counted. Then I climbed a wall.”

Wei Tiecheng had brought her a box. He held it out without looking at her, the way he’d once stood in the entrance of her medical tent with his arms crossed, preparing to say something he didn’t want to say. It was a medicine case of dark camphorwood with twelve small drawers that fitted perfectly, and a brass catch shaped like a cloud. The joints were so fine she couldn’t see them.

“Who made this?”

Wei Tiecheng looked at the ceiling.

“He did. All summer. In the evenings. He wouldn’t let anyone see it. He cut his thumb on the third drawer and wouldn’t let anyone see that either,” said Zhou Hua.

“Let me see the thumb.”

“It’s healed,” said Wei Tiecheng.

“Let me see it anyway.”

He held it out, scowling. She looked at it, a neat white line, properly closed.

“Who cleaned it?”

His scarred face went dull red. “I did. Wine first. Then salt water. The way you said. For the twelve men from my unit. I said I’d noted it. I wanted it noted properly.”

She held the box in both hands. She didn’t trust herself to say anything long.

“It’s been noted. Thank you.”

He nodded once, sharply, and went to look hard at the herb cabinet.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of the wedding her mother put the jade hairpin in her hair.

She did it in the same room where she’d done it before the capital, with the same small quick movements, and said nothing while she worked. When it was done she stepped back and looked at her daughter in the red wedding robe, and her eyes filled.

“There,” said Lady Ren, in a voice that wasn’t steady at all.

Shiyu put her hand up and felt it. “Mother. Where did you—”

Her mother told her: the courtyard, the lamp, what he’d said. Shiyu sat still for a while afterwards, and her mother held her hand, and neither of them spoke, and it was one of the best moments of the whole day.

✦ ✦ ✦

The red veil meant she saw little of the ceremony: her own feet, the hem of her robe, the floor of her father’s great hall. She heard a great deal. Her father reading the blessing in his large-hall voice, losing his place once and finding it again. Old Master Feng in the front row telling everyone round him that he’d known from the first day, when he heard two voices in the consultation room. Mei Yun sniffing loudly, and Chen Ye beside her handing over a handkerchief under his breath.

When the families bowed to each other, she heard her uncle say, low, to the General, “I’m still deciding whether to be angry with you.”

“Take as long as you like, Chief Physician. I’ll still be here.”

Then a hand lifted the veil. The hall was bright after the red dark, and full of faces. She didn’t look at any of them. She looked at him, standing in front of her in red with the veil in his hand. His face wasn’t managing anything. It hadn’t been, she realised, since the lane in Wide Water. He’d just stopped. He looked at her in front of everyone.

“You came back,” he said, under his breath.

“I said I would.”

“You said it in charcoal.”

“Charcoal counts,” said Shiyu, and somewhere behind her Zhou Hua cheered before anyone had told him to, and the whole hall laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The feast lasted most of the afternoon and well into the evening and was louder than anything the governor’s house had held in a hundred years. Zhou Hua danced, badly, on his healed leg, and insisted it was a northern dance, and Wei Tiecheng told everyone it wasn’t. Her father showed the Tang volumes to Lin Wenyuan, who turned out to have read them, and the pair of them vanished into a corner for an hour.

Tuo the salt trader came all the way over the hill path with his two mules, uninvited, carrying a sack of salt as a wedding gift and a message from Old Nai. Shiyu translated it with some care, and the guests decided it was a blessing.

“Was it a blessing?” the General asked her, low.

“Mostly. She says if the scholar doesn’t treat me well she’ll come down the river herself.”

“On a tree?”

“On a very large tree.”

“Tell her I’ll treat you well out of respect for her, and fear of the tree,” said the General.

Lin Wenyuan had written the wedding couplets. They hung either side of the hall door in his precise, beautiful hand, and everyone who came in stopped to read them.

The cloud that came down with the rain stayed to heal the city.
The cloud that rose with the battle came back to stand beside her.

Shiyu read them twice on her way in. She found Lin Wenyuan afterwards and thanked him, and he looked down at his ink-stained fingers.

“I’ve been writing that one in my head since the inn. It seemed a waste not to use it.”

Late in the evening Lü Yue came to find her. He was the eldest of the Five and the most serious, and in four years he’d never said anything to her that wasn’t strictly necessary. He stood in front of her in his good grey robe, and she half thought he’d say nothing at all. Then he bowed: not the bow a man gives a general’s new wife, but the slow, full bow a junior physician gives a senior one.

“The logic was sound. The first time you explained it to me, in the tent. I’ve thought so ever since. He chose well. So did you,” he said, straightening.

He went before she could answer. She stood there some time afterwards holding her cup, and found it hard to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

Near the end of the night she went out into the courtyard for air and found Chen Ye there, leaning against the wall by the gate, watching the lanterns. Mei Yun was there too, on the edge of the herb bed. They weren’t talking. They had the look of two people who’d just finished talking about something and hadn’t decided yet what they thought.

Shiyu stopped in the doorway. Neither of them had seen her.

“Are you going to say your one true thing now and then leave?” said Mei Yun.

Chen Ye considered it. “Not tonight. I thought I might stay.”

Mei Yun looked at him. Then she moved over on the edge of the herb bed, a fraction. Not enough to mean anything. Exactly enough to mean something. He sat down.

Shiyu went back in without a sound and told no one. She thought Mei Yun would tell her eventually, probably at great length.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, when the guests had finally gone and the lanterns were burning low and the house had gone quiet, they sat together on the edge of the bed in the room her mother had made ready, still in their wedding red. For a while neither of them spoke. It was a good silence, one of theirs.

She spoke at last. “I’ve been trying to think what I’ll call you now.”

He turned his head.

She smiled. “In the tent you were General. In the letters you were General, and then Lingyun when no one else was reading. In front of His Majesty you were the General again. I’ve had four years of names for you. Tonight there’s one I’ve never used.”

“Tell me.”

“You tell me first. You’ve called me Physician, and Shiyu, and nothing at all, and once, on the ridge, something in your sleep I won’t repeat.”

“I don’t talk in my sleep.”

“You talked in your sleep. Chen Ye heard it too. He was very kind about it.”

He was quiet. Then he looked at her in the low lamplight: the hairpin, the red robe, the bruise on her cheekbone long gone.

“Wife,” he said.

It was the way he said everything that mattered: flat and certain, a plain fact. She had to take a breath before she could answer.

“Husband.”

She felt it land. She watched it go all the way through him. He closed his eyes, and when he opened them he didn’t say anything. He didn’t need to. For once in his life everything he felt was in his face, and he let her see all of it, and didn’t look away.

She leaned in and kissed him, slowly, and he took the jade pin out of her hair with great care and set it on the table, and her hair came down round both of them, and the lamp burned lower, and that was all anyone in the house heard of them until morning.

chapters.desc: Two years later she watches the army ride in from the same balcony. This time he looks up.

chapters.volume: Volume Ten: The Song of Clouds
chapters.content:
Two years later, in the spring, the Northern Army came back through Qingzhou on its way south from winter quarters, and Yun Shiyu went up to the balcony of her father’s house to watch it pass.

She didn’t need to. She’d come down from the frontier herself three weeks before, ahead of the army, the way she did every spring now, to open the clinic for the season and read Mei Yun’s winter records, which were, as always, better kept than her own. She knew exactly when the procession would arrive, which road it would take, and who’d be riding at the front. She could have waited at the gate like a sensible woman.

She went up anyway. She liked it there. It was where it had started.

Little Lan came up behind her with a tray, as she’d done six years ago, older now and married to a carter, and back for the day because she said she wouldn’t miss it.

“Miss. You’ve come up to watch the army.”

“I’ve come up for the air.”

“You said that last time.”

“I meant it last time too.”

Little Lan set the tea down. “You didn’t, Miss. You’d been reading about him for a year. Lady Ren says you’re to come down for the greeting, and not stand up here making a spectacle.”

“Tell my mother I’m not making a spectacle. I’m standing still.”

“She says that’s how it started,” said Little Lan, and went.

The spring rains had stopped two days ago and the city smelled of wet stone and herbs. Below her the street was filling the way it always did when the army came through: shopkeepers in doorways, children on walls, old women with stools, Old Master Feng at his corner with a basket of loquats he’d certainly try to give her later. Further off, towards the river, she could see the long grey line of the fence along the second bend, with a row of small figures sitting on it kicking their heels.

At the end of the fence there was a stone, as promised, clearly cut. In two years the river-district children had worn the characters smooth climbing on it. Deputy Minister Kang, she’d heard, had retired to the country for his health and didn’t visit the south.

✦ ✦ ✦

Little Lan came back up with the honey she’d forgotten, and didn’t leave. She stood at the railing beside her old mistress the way she had six years before, and looked at the fence.

“Is it true the deputy minister paid for every post?”

“Every post. And the rail. And the stone.”

“My husband says the children call it Kang’s Bench.”

Shiyu poured the tea. “Your husband’s right. I’ve sat on it. Deputy Minister Kang retired to the country for his health. He doesn’t visit the south.”

“And the camp? Mei Yun says you’ve a whole hall now. With a floor.”

Shiyu smiled. “With a floor that can be scrubbed, and windows facing south, and lamps that burn good oil. I insisted on the lamps.”

“And the shelves?”

“Wei Tiecheng built the shelves. In the evenings. He cut his thumb again.”

“Did he let you see it?”

“Not until I sat on him. I’ve taught eleven army physicians to clean a wound with boiled salt water and write down what happens after. Three of them already argue with me about method,” said Shiyu, and Little Lan laughed until she had to put the tray down.

“Is that bad?”

“Uncle Xiang says it’s the surest sign they’ve been listening.”

Little Lan’s eyes were round. “And the palace, Miss? At the new year? My husband’s cousin says the Emperor talked to you for two whole courses.”

“About page seven. For most of the first course and the whole of the second. He asked why I counted.”

“What did you say?”

Shiyu turned her cup. “That nobody else had. He said that wasn’t a reason. I said it was the only reason anyone ever starts counting anything. He laughed out loud, and three ministers dropped their chopsticks. Then he asked me to teach one month a year at the Imperial Medical Academy.”

“And you said yes.”

“On conditions. My own records, my own assistant, and nobody calls me the Fairy Physician.”

“Did he agree?”

“To the first two,” said Shiyu.

“And Wide Water? You still go?”

“Every autumn, when the river drops. Old Nai’s knees are bad and getting worse, and she complains about them with enormous satisfaction to anyone who’ll listen. Auntie Fen walks the whole valley again, limping in the rain and swearing at her leg like an old friend. And Little Ke’s eight now. She says she’s going to be a river doctor too.”

“Like you.”

Shiyu smiled at the fence. “She follows me from house to house with a notebook made of trader’s paper and writes down everything in characters nobody else can read. The General comes every time. He pays Tuo far too much for the mules.”

“Does Tuo mind?”

“Tuo laughs his dropped-pot laugh and takes it,” said Shiyu.

And he was learning. He was bad at it, as he’d said he’d be. But in the second winter, when a patrol was caught in the passes by a snowstorm and didn’t come back for three days, he’d come to the medical hall at midnight and stood in the doorway.

“Lingyun?”

“I can’t sleep. I’m afraid for them,” He’d said it plainly, the way he said everything that mattered.

She’d put down her brush and sat with him until dawn, and the patrol had come in on the fourth morning, frostbitten and alive.

Afterwards he’d been a little stiff about it. “It helped. To say it.”

“I know.”

She hadn’t told him it was the best thing he’d ever said to her, because he’d have been unbearable about it.

The clinic had changed too. There was a second sign over the door of the Qingcloud Medical Hall now, beside the old one, with Mei Yun’s name on it as physician of record. Mei Yun had wanted it smaller. Shiyu had made it exactly the same size and refused to discuss it. In the winters Mei Yun ran the Hall alone and was, by every account, terrifying. She was also, since the new year, betrothed to a certain captain of the personal guard, who’d asked her in the governor’s courtyard and then, as he told the General afterwards with great dignity, had stayed.

And there was a song. Shiyu hadn’t known about it until the first autumn after the wedding, when she heard it from the children in the river district.

“Mei Yun. What are they singing?”

Mei Yun had been delighted. “Oh, Miss. Haven’t you heard? It’s about two clouds.”

“Two clouds.”

Mei Yun beamed. “One came down with the rain and stayed to heal the city. One rose with the battle and came back to stand beside her. And in the last verse the two clouds meet over the river, and the river stops being afraid. It doesn’t rhyme. It’s got six endings, depending which street you’re in. They sing it on the fence.”

“It’s excessive.”

Mei Yun had been serene about it. “You’re not meant to like it, Miss. It isn’t for you. It’s for the people who watched.”

They called it the Song of Clouds.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard the procession before she saw it: hooves, harness, a crowd going quiet and then loud again. The first riders came round the corner below the balcony, and behind them, on a black horse, in black armour edged with silver and his helmet carried at his side, came the Supreme Commander of the Northern Army.

He looked older than he had at twenty-eight, the first time she’d seen him from this railing. There were two grey hairs at his temple that she’d found in the winter and refused to pull out. And he looked less cold. People in the crowd who’d seen him come through before said so to each other; she heard them.

“He looks different.”

“He looks—”

They didn’t quite have the word, and she didn’t supply it.

Her father’s household came out of the gate to greet him, as it always did. Her father was in front, with ink on his sleeve and the first printed copy of his herb survey under his arm, which he’d carried everywhere for a week. Her mother beside him. Her uncle, down with the army, three horses back and already arguing with Lin Wenyuan about something.

The General turned his head to receive the greeting. And then, before he’d finished nodding to her father, he looked up.

He looked straight up at the balcony, at her, the way he hadn’t looked the first time, because the first time he hadn’t known she was there. He knew now. He always knew where she was in a room. He’d told her once it was the first thing he did, entering anywhere: find the door, find the danger, find her.

His face didn’t do anything anyone else in that street would have noticed. But she’d spent six years learning it. She saw the corner of his mouth and she saw his eyes, and she knew exactly what they said.

She pressed the back of her hand to her cheek. Warm.

“It’s the sun,” she said to no one. This time there was sun.

Then her other hand went, without her deciding, to the cloud-embroidered pouch at her sash, and pressed.

Down in the street, he saw it. She watched him see it, and understand that she was pressing it here, now, with nothing wrong anywhere in the world, and what that had to mean. There was something she didn’t yet know how to say.

He said something to her father. Her father looked up at the balcony, startled, and then waved, delighted, with the ink-stained sleeve. And the General handed his reins to Chen Ye, who took them without any expression whatsoever, and walked in through the gate.

She heard him on the stairs. He’d never in his life taken stairs two at a time. He did now. He came out on the balcony and stopped a pace from her, still in his armour, smelling of horses and road dust and the north.

“You’ve something to tell me.”

“How do you know?”

He looked at her hand, still on the pouch. She laughed and let go of it. Her eyes had filled. She didn’t mind.

“I didn’t know how to put it in a letter. I wanted to see your face.”

“Then tell me. I’m looking at you.”

So she told him.

She held his eyes. “Uncle Xiang’s retiring at the end of the year. He wrote to His Majesty before he wrote to me. His Majesty wrote back with one name for the post. Chief Physician of the Northern Army. In my own name. Not as anybody’s niece or anybody’s wife. By the first snow it’ll be official. Nobody will ever be able to send me home in a supply cart again.”

She saw it land, the way she’d watched everything land in him for six years: the half-breath, the stillness, and then the slow change all the way through. Except that this time he held none of it back. He didn’t even try. He put his hands either side of her face, armour and all, there on the balcony in full view of half Qingzhou, and kissed her.

“Lingyun. The whole street.”

“Let them look. They’ve been watching since the cart,” said the General.

Down in the street the crowd had gone completely silent. Then, from somewhere near the river, faint and badly out of tune, a row of children on a stone fence began, with great enthusiasm, to sing.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, when the house was quiet, she went to the chest at the foot of her old bed and took out a notebook she hadn’t opened in years: the one she’d carried on the road south from the camp when she was eighteen, with her bundle and her uncle’s parting advice and a feeling in her chest she’d had no name for. Most of it was notes on patients. On the second evening of that journey she’d written two lines about the General. Only two.

She found the page. The characters were small and careful, a girl’s hand trying hard to be steady.

It was worth having done.
He kissed me first.

He came in while she was still looking at it, sat on the end of the bed beside her and read over her shoulder. She felt him go still.

“You wrote that. On the way home.”

“On the second evening. I thought it was the end of the story. I thought I was being very grown up about it.”

“You put it under your pillow.”

“How do you know that?”

“Because you’ve just gone red and you’re about to tell me it’s the sun,” said the General.

She laughed and held out the brush from the writing box. He understood. He wrote under her lines in the compressed, careful hand she’d first seen in the margins of her reports, the hand she’d waited for every week at the window, in the good light.

It still is.
She kissed me back.

He gave her the brush. She looked at the lines together for a long while, the girl’s and his. Then she dipped the brush, and under all of them, in her own hand, steadier now, a woman’s, a physician’s, she wrote the only thing left to add.

Every time.

She closed the notebook and put it back in the chest and blew out the lamp. Outside, from somewhere down by the river, somebody’s child was still singing.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
In another life, Yun Shiyu was a trauma surgeon. In this one she’s eighteen, the governor’s daughter in a rainy southern river city, and she has just watched the Emperor’s nephew ride past her balcony.

She does something very foolish to see him again. It turns into six weeks in an army medical tent, a kiss in the command tent the night before she leaves, three years building a clinic of her own, and a love carried in letters, until someone decides to use those letters against them both.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
A sweet romance. Some chapters include:

• Battle wounds and field surgery, described from a physician’s point of view

• A near-drowning and an attempted murder (The Riverbank)

• A dislocated shoulder put back in, and a fever (The River Doctor)

• A broken leg set by lamplight (A Lamp for the Midwife)

• Grief and fear while a loved one is missing

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
I started this one because I wanted a romance where two people fall in love by watching each other be good at their work. She stitches his arm. He reads her reports at night. They kiss before they’ve said half of what they mean, and everybody around them notices anyway.

He isn’t cold. He’s careful. She isn’t quiet. She’s honest. That’s most of the story, really.

It ran longer than I planned. I kept thinking they were nearly there and then one of them would write another letter. Thank you for waiting with them all the way to the end.

A small note: names are written without tone marks in the chapters so they’re easier to read. If you want to know how to say them, the Characters and Names & Terms pages have the Chinese.

— 甜慕

characters.title: Characters
characters.content:
✦ Yun Shiyu (云诗雨 · Yún Shī Yǔ)
Role: Female Lead
Age: 18 at the start, 21 for most of the story
Appearance: Slight, dark-eyed, usually with herb stains on her fingers. Wears a green coat for important days.
Personality:
Honest even when lying would be easier
Patient in the long way
Thinks like a surgeon, talks like a governor’s daughter
Presses a cloud-embroidered pouch when she can’t find words
Strengths:
Calm in emergencies
Keeps careful records
Sees what patients aren’t saying
Weaknesses:
Hides her feelings inside her work
Hates being protected without being told
Nickname: The Fairy Physician

✦ Zhan Lingyun (战凌云 · Zhàn Líng Yún)
Role: Male Lead
Age: 28 at the start, 31 for most of the story
Appearance: Tall, dark-eyed, black armour with silver edging. A face that gives away very little.
Personality:
Precise, quiet, and very hard to read
Shows care by quietly arranging things
Reads every report, all the way through
Orphaned at fifteen and has been useful ever since
Strengths:
Clear thinker under pressure
Keeps his word exactly
Weaknesses:
Keeps everything behind his face
Has never learned to ask for anything for himself
Nickname: The General

✦ Uncle Xiang (云翔医 · Yún Xiáng Yī)
Role: Shiyu’s uncle · Chief Military Physician
Age: 48
Personality:
Proud of his niece and exasperated by her, usually at once
Argues about method in long letters
The least subtle matchmaker in the empire

✦ Little Lan
Role: Shiyu’s maid at home in Qingzhou
Personality:
Tells the kitchen everything
Helps pack a bundle and a letter for a very foolish plan

✦ Mei Yun
Role: Shiyu’s assistant at the clinic
Age: 15 when she arrives
Personality:
Sharp-eyed and unembarrassed
Narrates life as if it were a love story
Keeps better records than anyone admits

✦ Chen Ye
Role: The General’s personal guard · one of the Five
Personality:
Sees through people and says one true thing on his way out of the door
Very pleased with how this story is going

✦ Wei Tiecheng
Role: Vice-Commander · one of the Five
Age: 35 at the start
Appearance: Broad, with a scar on his left cheek.
Personality:
Suspicious first, loyal forever
Says the hard thing in as few words as possible

✦ Lin Wenyuan
Role: Strategist · one of the Five
Appearance: Scholar’s bearing, ink-stained fingers.
Personality:
Speaks rarely and sees everything
Writes beautiful calligraphy

✦ Zhou Hua
Role: Scout · one of the Five
Age: 29 at the start
Personality:
Restless and talkative
The first of the Five to warm to Shiyu
Takes an arrow in the leg in Qingzhou

✦ Lü Yue
Role: Senior officer · one of the Five
Personality:
Weathered and morally serious
His approval is worth more than most people’s praise

✦ Yun Chengde
Role: Shiyu’s father · Governor of Qingzhou
Age: About 52 at the start
Personality:
Gentle scholar, always with ink on his sleeve
Has been hunting the same herb texts for eleven years

✦ Lady Ren
Role: Shiyu’s mother
Personality:
Conventional, composed, and always right about the window
Loves her daughter without needing to understand her

✦ Emperor Zhan Hong
Role: The Emperor · Lingyun’s uncle (his late father’s elder brother)
Personality:
Shrewd, not cruel
Helps without appearing to

✦ Peng Yao
Role: Secretary at the Civilian Medical Commission, placed there by Deputy Minister Kang
Personality:
Pleasant until it is indistinguishable from sincere
Believes he was overlooked, and wants someone to pay for it

Has never learned to ask for anything for himself

chars.name: Uncle Xiang
chars.personality:
Proud of his niece and exasperated by her, usually at once
Argues about method in long letters
The least subtle matchmaker in the empire

chars.name: Little Lan
chars.role: Shiyu’s maid at home in Qingzhou
chars.personality:
Tells the kitchen everything
Helps pack a bundle and a letter for a very foolish plan

chars.name: Mei Yun
chars.personality:
Sharp-eyed and unembarrassed
Narrates life as if it were a love story
Keeps better records than anyone admits

chars.name: Chen Ye
chars.role: The General’s personal guard · one of the Five
chars.personality:
Sees through people and says one true thing on his way out of the door
Very pleased with how this story is going

chars.name: Wei Tiecheng
chars.appearance: Broad, with a scar on his left cheek.
chars.personality:
Suspicious first, loyal forever
Says the hard thing in as few words as possible

chars.name: Lin Wenyuan
chars.personality:
Speaks rarely and sees everything
Writes beautiful calligraphy

chars.name: Zhou Hua
chars.personality:
Restless and talkative
The first of the Five to warm to Shiyu
Takes an arrow in the leg in Qingzhou

chars.name: Lü Yue
chars.role: Senior officer · one of the Five
chars.personality:
Weathered and morally serious
His approval is worth more than most people’s praise

chars.name: Yun Chengde
chars.personality:
Gentle scholar, always with ink on his sleeve
Has been hunting the same herb texts for eleven years

chars.name: Lady Ren
chars.personality:
Conventional, composed, and always right about the window
Loves her daughter without needing to understand her

chars.name: Emperor Zhan Hong
chars.role: The Emperor · Lingyun’s uncle (his late father’s elder brother)
chars.personality:
Shrewd, not cruel
Helps without appearing to

chars.name: Peng Yao
chars.role: Secretary at the Civilian Medical Commission, placed there by Deputy Minister Kang
chars.personality:
Pleasant until it is indistinguishable from sincere
Believes he was overlooked, and wants someone to pay for it

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Qingzhou — Shiyu’s home city in the rainy south, known for herbs and river trade. Her father is its governor.
The capital — Where the Emperor and the court live, about four days north of Qingzhou by carriage.
The northern camp — The Northern Army’s base on the frontier, three days from Qingzhou. Uncle Xiang runs its medical tent.
Qingcloud Medical Hall (清云医馆) — The clinic Shiyu opens at nineteen.
The Fairy Physician — What Qingzhou calls Shiyu. She thinks it is excessive.
The Five — Zhan Lingyun’s most trusted officers: Wei Tiecheng, Lin Wenyuan, Zhou Hua, Lü Yue and Chen Ye.
The Civilian Medical Commission — The army’s new office for bringing civilian physicians and records into its medical work. Shiyu becomes its chief civilian physician.
The hour of the Rabbit — The old name for the two hours around dawn, roughly five to seven in the morning.
Li — A distance of about half a kilometre. Five hundred li is a long journey.
Relay station — Post stations along the main roads where riders change horses, so urgent letters can travel hundreds of li in a day.
The Censorate — The court office that investigates complaints against officials.
The Ministry of Revenue / Ministry of Justice — Two of the great government ministries in the capital.
The second bend — A fast stretch of river in Qingzhou’s western district, just above the gorge.
Wide Water — A fishing village across the border, where the river spreads out and slows down.
The cloud-embroidered pouch — A small silk pouch Shiyu’s mother made for her. She presses it when there is something she can’t say.
Saying the names — Shiyu: “shir-yoo”. Lingyun: “ling-yoon”. Zhan: “jahn”. Xiang: “shyahng”. Lü Yue: “lyoo yweh”. Qingzhou: “ching-joe”.
